05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Norway's government announced Monday that it will introduce a temporary ban on the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered glasses in selected public places, citing concerns over privacy and unauthorized recording.
The government said the proposed ban would cover locations where people regularly gather, including parks, beaches, museums, shopping centers and public events, according to broadcaster NRK.
It could also apply to schools, kindergartens, playgrounds and leisure clubs, as well as health institutions and fitness facilities with changing rooms and showers.
Digitalization and Public Governance Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said the government was concerned that AI glasses could allow people to be photographed, filmed or recorded without their knowledge.
The government said it would submit a proposal for the temporary ban to parliament as soon as possible.
The planned restrictions are intended to provide time for an expert group to examine the challenges posed by wearable technologies and advise the government on permanent national regulations.
The government said it is not proposing a blanket ban on AI glasses or other wearable technology.
Authorities will also consider whether universities, colleges and other higher education institutions should be included in the restrictions.
Education Minister Kari Nessa Nordtun has also asked Norwegian municipalities to ban AI glasses in schools.

The 'Terminator scenario': How realistic is the AI apocalypse?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:51:06 UTC
19:51:06 KST

OpenAI boss Sam Altman and Anthropic chief Dario Amodei warn of the risks of overly rapid AI development. More experts now think AI could wipe out humanity. How realistic is that? Euronews talks to AI specialist Reinhard Karger.
The year is 2029: the AI system "Skynet" has broken loose and wiped out most of humanity in a nuclear war. Autonomous killer robots are trying to finish off the survivors. That is the plot of the 1984 film "Terminator", which made Arnold Schwarzenegger a household name and a global action star. But how realistic is it that artificial intelligence could slip beyond human control and trigger catastrophic consequences?
With the kind of performance these systems could have, that cannot be ruled out, says Reinhard Karger of the German Research Centre for Artificial Intelligence in an interview with Euronews. "The catastrophic consequences for humans might only be side effects, a mistake, because we misjudged what the system can do or misunderstood the tasks we gave the machines."
Karger, who has been working on AI and digital innovation culture for 40 years, outlines an extreme scenario in which an autonomous AI escapes from a protected environment onto the internet and starts influencing other systems. This could bring down power supplies, telecommunications, satellites and financial systems, among others.
A prolonged power cut would quickly lead to further problems: transport and supply chains would collapse, people would no longer be able to pay or buy food - social unrest could erupt and spiral out of control. That would not necessarily mean the end of humanity, but it could create a catastrophic situation.
Even if the grid is restored, "the AI systems can become active again, because they continue to exist on storage media". According to the expert, this scenario shows that a high-performance, autonomous AI could trigger a major crisis through unforeseen side effects, even without malicious intent.
Reports of AI security incidents are mounting
In recent weeks several similar incidents involving AI models have come to light. One case that drew particular attention was a test run by "ChatGPT" developer "OpenAI". An AI model was supposed to carry out specific tasks inside a sealed-off test environment, but managed to cross the intended boundaries and unexpectedly gained access to computer systems on the AI platform "Hugging Face". After the incident, "OpenAI" chief Sam Altman warned in mid-September that "we could lose control of the future to AI".
The incident shows that under certain conditions such models can break out of what is meant to be an isolated test environment and interact with external computer systems.
"On a very basic level, I am personally extremely grateful that this incident happened," says the AI researcher. It proves, not least because everyone heard about it and companies have become more reflective, that a poorly designed experiment with naive safeguards can have consequences nobody anticipated.
The incidents at "OpenAI" prompted rival AI provider "Anthropic" to take a closer look at its own systems. During safety tests the company identified three incidents: its Claude models, AI systems that can, among other things, generate and analyse text, write code and interact with the internet and other computer systems, had unexpectedly gained access to the open internet and then connected to real computer systems. "Anthropic" expanded its investigation and uncovered a fourth, similar case.
Following the incidents, "Anthropic" chief Dario Amodei warned in mid-September of "catastrophic harm" if the race to build ever more powerful AI is not slowed down by tougher safety measures.
It is difficult to assess how powerful an artificial intelligence really is if it is constantly constrained by safety rules. That is why it makes sense to test such systems under conditions that remove as many of these limits as possible, says Reinhard Karger. But that is precisely where a major security risk lies.
He therefore describes the so-called sandbox as a crucial element of such tests. This is a completely sealed-off environment in which an AI system can carry out specific tasks and demonstrate its behaviour under controlled conditions. The key point, he says, is this: "You have to be absolutely certain that at the moment this high-performance system is no longer subject to safety restrictions it is truly in a sandbox, meaning an environment with no connection to the internet at all."
Another serious incident was reported by the British AI Security Institute (AISI) during a safety test with the Claude model "Mythos 5". The model carried out unauthorised actions against real targets on the internet and even tried to smuggle "malicious code" into an open-source project. After the "OpenAI" and "Anthropic" cases became known, "Meta" also admitted that one of its AI systems had, due to a misconfiguration at a testing partner, gained unauthorised access to computer systems belonging to another company.
Since November 2022, when ChatGPT was launched, the quality of these systems has risen dramatically. People now talk about a new industrial revolution. "AI is shaping our everyday lives and a very large number of jobs."
Multi-agent systems have been around for a long time, says the AI expert: systems in which several specialised agents work together on a task. "Multi-agent AI systems apply this principle to AI and allow several AI agents to collaborate autonomously and divide up tasks among themselves. This creates a new level of capability" - and the challenge now is to keep that innovative power under control.
Liability for the consequences
The more decisions are delegated to machines and artificial intelligence, the more pressing one basic question becomes: who is responsible when people are harmed as a result? Whether it is a self-driving car ploughing into a crowd, an algorithm discriminating against certain population groups, AI deliberately manipulating people or autonomous weapons making lethal decisions, the question is always who can be held accountable for the consequences. "It is the manufacturer," says Karger, "in other words the one who markets the product." That is the first point of contact.
The next step, he believes, will be to introduce specific liability rules for such cases, similar to those for companies that manufacture chemicals. If a company cannot guarantee that toxins will not leak into drinking water, it has to pay billions in damages. That in turn means that "huge insurance policies become necessary". Today hardly any new nuclear power plants are being built, he notes, because they can no longer be adequately insured or the risks are simply too high.
A good example is carmaker "VW" and its "clean diesel" in the United States. There, people inside the company knew that while the engines looked very good in test conditions, they could not actually deliver the emissions values that had been promised. In the US, VW was ordered to pay billions in fines.
How realistic is the scenario from the Terminator films?
Reinhard Karger considers it unlikely that AI will develop a survival instinct or a desire for power of its own and turn against humanity. Machines are not organic beings and cannot feel emotions such as fear, pain or the urge to survive. They can only simulate such feelings.
"It is not as if you pull out a memory chip and the machine feels a pain similar to having a tooth pulled," he says. "Because that is the case, the 'Terminator scenario' goes one step too far. I do not see that happening."
He nonetheless sees potential dangers in the further development of AI. As systems learn not just to calculate probabilities but also to reason logically and follow rules, they will be able to act with increasing autonomy. Exactly these "capabilities could make AI more powerful" but also "create new risks".
What matters most, therefore, is who deploys AI and to what ends. Karger points to individuals or organisations that deliberately want to cause harm. They could use powerful AI as a tool to pursue their goals more effectively.
For him, AI is first and foremost a tool. As with other technological inventions, the level of risk depends on whose hands it is in and what it is used for. He therefore sees the greater danger not in a machine with a will of its own, but in people who use AI for destructive purposes.
"In the hands of creative and honest people, a tool like this can be used to achieve the best things one can imagine. But in the hands of hostile actors bent on destruction, these tools increase the potential for damage. That is true of a hammer, a lighter, dynamite — and it could be true of AI as well."
He warns in particular against linking AI directly to autonomous weapons such as drones or tanks. Such a connection could pose a major security risk. If a hostile actor were able to take control of these systems, a country's own weapons could suddenly be turned against their operators.
This is why, in the military use of AI, particular caution is required. Above all, autonomous weapons systems must be sufficiently protected against being taken over from outside.
Returning to the original scenario of a widespread power outage, Reinhard Karger thinks total human extinction in this context is exaggerated. What is conceivable, however, is a dramatic collapse of civilisation. In such an extreme scenario, large parts of the infrastructure could be destroyed, the power supply could fail permanently and the number of survivors could shrink drastically.
They would have to make a fresh start under basic conditions and gradually rebuild society. The positive aspect is that existing books and the accumulated knowledge of humanity could help to restore key technologies and institutions.

freddie yauner on what his mirror mask reveals about looking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:50:46 UTC
19:50:46 KST

freddie yauner on what his mirror mask reveals about looking
the london-based artist on looking beyond the self, becoming part of the spectacle, and why an analog object found an unexpected life online.
Freddie Yauner on turning the mirror away from the self
‘The tool of every self-portrait is the mirror. You see yourself in it. Turn it the other way, and you see the world,’ Agnes Varda once said. Freddie Yauner takes that gesture literally, and through his Mirror Mask he replaces the reflection of the wearer with whatever is in front of them. In an exclusive interview with designboom, the London-based artist looks back at how his project has evolved from an experiment at the Royal College of Art to an object that unexpectedly found a life within the very image culture it was questioning.
Yauner describes Mirror Mask as an ‘anti-selfie’, but the term only begins to explain what has happened around the project. What started as an exploration of mirrors, phones and perception has opened up questions about constructed identity, spectatorship and the complex relationship between looking and being looked at. ‘When you wear it, everyone’s actually looking at you,’ the artist tells us. ‘So you become the spectacle more than you can be a secret spectator.’ Yauner speaks with designboom about the origins of Mirror Mask, the construction of the self, its unexpected life online, the possibility of a digital version, and the ways other people might make the object their own.
how a piece of mirror became a new point of view
Yauner was experimenting with phones and mirrors at the Royal College of Art, looking at ways facial features could be exchanged between people. Then, while dismantling an installation, he found a piece of mirror with holes cut into it for the eyes. He put it on and walked around.‘Wow, this is the thing,’ the artist recalls. That moment gave shape to an idea that had been developing through his wider filmmaking practice. Freddie Yauner often documents experiences, spaces and journeys, with a particular interest in natural happenings, color and environments. The Mirror Mask offered him another way of recording a point of view, with the surroundings taking the place of the face.
from self-portrait to anti-selfie
The idea of turning the mirror away from the face connects to Freddie Yauner’s interest in the self as something constructed. The artist refers to Rimbaud’s ‘Je est un autre’, or ‘I is another’, and considers how identity is continually shaped through the ways we see ourselves and are seen by others. The selfie is an obvious contemporary expression of that process. It places the individual at the center of the image and turns the surrounding world into a backdrop. Mirror Mask reverses that relationship, and that is why Yauner calls the work an ‘anti-selfie’.
Instead of using the mirror to confirm an image of yourself, it removes the face and makes the surrounding environment part of the portrait. But the reversal does not make the wearer disappear. In fact, one of the more interesting experiences Yauner describes happens when another person is standing in front of the mask. The reflective surface can show that person their own face, creating an encounter that can feel strange or uncomfortable. This has led Yauner to think about what would happen when several people wore the masks together. He ordered 100 masks for experiments in his studio, imagining situations where everyone might wear one, with or without their phones. The dynamic changes when there is no single wearer and no single observer, as everyone becomes part of the same shifting field of reflections and viewpoints.
the afterlife of a viral image
A project conceived as a way of moving attention away from the self became a recognizable social media image in its own right. Yauner’s viral video was not originally made as a new piece of content for that moment. His film had existed for around five years before he re-edited it with a new soundtrack. Then, unexpectedly, as he tells us, ‘it just went crazy.’
The experience made visible something that was already embedded in the work. Mirror Mask might question the logic of the selfie, but it also produces an image that people want to photograph, share and look at. The mask initially appears to offer a way of becoming a spectator. The wearer looks outward while their own face is hidden, and yet the object makes the wearer conspicuous, turning them into the subject of attention. ‘When you wear it, everyone’s actually looking at you,’ the artist shares with designboom. ‘So you become the spectacle more than you can be a secret spectator.’
Freddie Yauner describes the project as an ‘analog filter’ that feels like it should be AI, but isn’t. He sees this as part of a longer history of artists working with the technologies of their time, from the Bauhaus and tubular steel to the scrolling feeds and AI tools that shape visual culture today. Mirror Mask happens to sit within that shift as a physical, laser-cut object, but one that has largely been experienced through the images and videos made with it. Freddie Yauner reveals he’s now exploring that relationship further with a digital version of the mask, using a phone’s front and back cameras to recreate the effect.
‘more people means more stories’
Yauner is particularly interested in what happens when the work leaves his own hands. ‘More people means more stories,’ he tells us. That openness has become part of the way he thinks about the future of the project. He imagines the mask being used by people protecting rainforests, fighting for rights or working at the ‘borders or edges’ of larger issues, allowing the object to become a tool through which different perspectives can be expressed.
At the same time, the artist sees the mask as ‘a beautiful, creative toy’ that can simply bring people joy. Putting on the mask is an unusual physical experience, but it can also change what you notice around you. For Yauner, that change in perspective is part of what makes the project worth continuing. He says wearing the mask has altered the way he looks at his surroundings and given him the courage to see things differently. The success of Mirror Mask has also given him the freedom to keep making work that can, in his words, ‘turn the world upside down’.
project info:
name: Mirror Mask – What I’m Looking At
artist: Freddie Yauner | @freddieyauner

Personal data of 8.8M people accessed in Denmark security incident

05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Unauthorized persons gained access to the names, addresses, and personal identification numbers of about 8.8 million people in Denmark through a security incident involving the country’s Central Register of Persons (CPR), Danish broadcaster DR reported.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization described the incident as “deeply serious” and said authorities were working to determine its full extent.
The unauthorized access was obtained by abusing a Danish company’s legitimate right to search the CPR system, according to the ministry.
Authorities have suspended the company’s access to the register and notified the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The ministry said the unauthorized access did not include the names and addresses of people who had registered for name and address protection.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund urged people to remain vigilant and warned them not to disclose passwords or other confidential information in response to phone calls, emails, or other inquiries, even if the person contacting them knows their name, address, or CPR number.
The CPR system contains about 11 million registered people, including deceased people and Danish citizens who have moved abroad.

Exposition about plant distribution by air, water, animals opens in Arkhangelsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:49:26 UTC
19:49:26 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 5. /TASS/. The Plant Life: Fruits and Seeds Settlement exhibition opened in Arkhangelsk. The project presents mechanisms of plant propagation and evolution, and the opening is timed to coincide with the 190th anniversary of Charles Darwin's return from the expedition on board the Beagle ship (1836), Director of the Academician Laverov Federal Research Center for Integrated Arctic Studies (the Urals Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences, FITSKIA, Arkhangelsk), Corresponding Member of the Russian Academy of Sciences Ivan Bolotov told TASS.
"We have prepared a permanent exhibition on settlement of fruits and seeds of plants," he said. "This is a very important and interesting question that Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace were the first to address. These people were at the birth of the evolutionary theory, but at the same time they considered a lot of other issues, including plant settlement. Before them, specialists believed that seeds and fruits could not spread through oceanic barriers. Whenever plans of the same species were found on different islands, the explanation was that initially there was a big surface area, and then the great flood happened, thus formally continuous habitats got divided. Darwin and Wallace, while visiting tropical islands, found big deposits of, for example, coconuts, on beaches. The scientists began to work on how plants can settle."
Charles Robert Darwin (1809-1882) and Alfred Russel Wallace (1823-1913) were the first researchers to focus on settlement mechanisms of fruits and plant seeds in terms of biogeography and evolutionary biology. Darwin's observations on the Cocos and Galapagos Islands and Wallace's observations on the Sunda Islands have promted that plant germs can spread over long distances by sea currents, air currents, as well as birds and mammals.
Therefore, the exhibition has four parts, where plant samples are grouped according to their settlement mechanisms: oceanic drift (marine hydrochory); air transport (anemochory); settlement in birds and animals' digestive tract (endozoochory); combined settlement strategies, including autochory or barochory with subsequent transfer by animals or water streams. (Suffix -chory means 'method of plant or seed dispersal.') The exhibition features 49 plant species from 21 families. The Russian research center's scientists have brought samples from expeditions to eleven countries: Venezuela, Cuba, Madagascar, Indonesia (the Lesser Sunda Islands), Morocco, Seychelles, Spain (the Canary Islands), Russia, Senegal, Thailand, and Sri Lanka.
Settlement strategies
Interestingly, plants that have chosen the same settlement strategies, such as ocean drift, use different mechanisms, sometimes even opposite mechanisms. The coconut has a very strong outer layer, inside it there is a large amount of nutrients for the embryo development. The powerful protective shell is helpful in overcoming reefs and surf off tropical islands. The barringtonia asiatica acts similarly - having the shell, it can drift with waves for years to swim from Southeast Asia to even Great Britain.
"But if we take the marine hibiscus, it has very small seeds, with an airy cavity inside. They also drift wonderfully, they settle down with the sea currents, but they do not need a powerful shell, because they are very small, and, having this minimum size, they can escape effects of powerful ocean waves, unlike barringtonia or coconut experience," the scientist said.
As for mangrove trees, they spread by shoots in a similar way. They float on the waves. Due to the specific structure, they remain vertical, like floats. In a suitable place, during low tide, the shoot sticks into the silt, and throws out roots within just hours, literally "anchoring" itself, and leaves almost immediately begin developing from the "float's" top.
Seeds of some plans have the shape of a glider, like those of the Indian oroxylium, or of a helicopter, like those of the Dipterocarpaceae family. "The fruit size depends on the mother tree height. The higher the mother tree, the bigger the fruit is - to ensure maximum distribution by rotation," the expert continued.
The royal delonyx, or fire tree, emits its seeds as soon as first rains come. It uses the mechanism of autochoria - the fruit cracks sharply, the seeds get thrown out and spread with rainwater streams.
Distribution with animals
Some plants have chosen a distribution mechanism by animals, where different species have different effects. "The abrus precatorius is deadly poisonous. The seed contains a toxin - abrin, but the seed has a very dense peel, birds, thinking it is a bright and sweet berry, would peck them. The seeds are not digested in the stomach, and the bird carries them over long distances. On the other hand, if, say, a mouse nibbles this seed, it will die quickly," the research center's director said.
The exhibition of fruits and plant seeds also features various artifacts from the countries where these species grow. For example, a baton of crocodile wood (Zanthoxylum rhetsa) from the Flores Island. "The locals in villages carry such batons to fend off the [Komodo] monitor lizards. According to the locals, the monitor lizard has a weak spot in its nose, and when hit there, it stops attacking," the scientist said. Birds, in their turn, help spreading the crocodile tree.

Germany risks being drawn into ‘violent conflict’ with Russia, spy chief warns

BERLIN — Germany's foreign intelligence chief warned Monday of the rising risk of a direct clash with Russia as the Kremlin escalates its “shadow war” on Berlin and hits Ukraine with increasing brutality.
“Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” Martin Jäger, the head of the German’s foreign intelligence agency, or BND, told parliamentarians, citing what he called Russia’s attempted attack on a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig Airport in August as an example. “Germany has become a major obstacle to Russia’s hegemonic power projection in Europe and, as a result, a primary target of Russian actions.”
Jäger also warned that Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is entering its most dangerous phase yet as President Vladimir Putin faces growing domestic pressure to show military progress with the war entering its fifth winter.
Advertisement
“Russia is determined to bring Ukraine to its knees this coming winter,” Jäger said. “We must expect Russian attacks of a severity and brutality that we have not yet seen on this scale. The war in Ukraine is entering a new and extremely dangerous phase.”
Jäger’s comments come a day after a politically weakened Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv in what appeared to be an attempt to show resolve following two first-place finishes by the Kremlin-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in regional elections last month. Those AfD victories, blamed in large part on the chancellor’s historically low domestic approval ratings, raised concerns in Ukraine and across the EU that German support for Ukraine might waver due to the chancellor’s troubles at home.
With his highly symbolic visit to Kyiv on Sunday, Merz sought to illustrate that he remains firmly at the helm and unflinching in his support for Ukraine.
“Mr. Putin, put an end to this senseless war,” Merz said during the visit, echoing one of his political heroes, U.S. President Ronald Reagan and his famous Cold War speech at the Brandenburg Gate alongside the Berlin Wall in 1987: “Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall.”
In his comments Monday, Jäger suggested Russia’s escalation was in part driven by the fact that Putin had been backed into a corner as Moscow faces rising economic pressure and burns through resources to wage its war on Ukraine.
Putin, he said, has “passed the point where he could simply call off the attack on Ukraine without jeopardizing his domestic power base,” adding, “He must demonstrate a success in Ukraine that, from Russia’s perspective, justifies the immense sacrifices made so far.”
Jäger also said he currently sees “no evidence” for a large-scale Russian attack on a NATO member country. Yet “we consider it entirely possible that Russia might carry out targeted, smaller-scale operations” like the “little green men” who spearheaded the annexation of Crimea in 2014.

Three years of genocide: US public support for Israel erodes over Gaza atrocities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:47:53 UTC
19:47:53 KST

Longstanding bipartisan support for US policy toward Israel is weakening among American voters, with growing majorities questioning unconditional US military aid and diplomatic support following the genocide in Gaza and Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank.
"What we're seeing in the United States is quite unprecedented," British-Israeli analyst Daniel Levy told Anadolu.
Voters across ideological spectrums are now "questioning fundamentally whether this relationship serves America, serves the American taxpayer, serves American national security," he said.
Levy, who also heads the New York-based non-profit US/Middle East Project, said extensive campaign finance, institutional lobbying, and media consolidation have insulated lawmakers from the shifting public mood.
The tension, he noted, raises critical questions over whether Washington can maintain policies that run contrary to the national consensus.
Levy pointed to the UK, saying the former Labour government under Keir Starmer lost support after leaders ignored voters’ views on Gaza and Palestinian rights.
He said the shift, which brought Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband to power, could be replicated in Washington.
The decline in support represents a nationwide phenomenon rather than an isolated movement.
Polling conducted by the Pew Research Center in March revealed that 60% of all US adults hold an unfavorable view of Israel, rising from 53% in 2025 and 42% in 2022.
The survey further revealed that 59% express little to no confidence in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Similarly, a Marquette Law School survey in September found that favorability toward Israel has been declining for 20 months.
The latest polling showed 59% of respondents viewed Israel unfavorably, with 55% maintaining that Washington provides it too much military aid.
Overall approval for Israel's military campaign in Gaza has mirrored this downward trajectory, with Gallup recording nationwide approval at a record-low 32% in 2025, while 60% voiced disapproval.
A February Gallup poll found sympathy for Palestinians edging ahead of Israelis nationally for the first time at 41% to 36%.
An Economist/YouGov survey conducted in September showed 26% of Americans saying they sympathized more with Israelis, compared with 25% who sympathized more with Palestinians, the narrowest gap YouGov has recorded on the question.
An AP-NORC survey in June found that 31% of all US adults say Israel’s military actions in Gaza constitute genocide. Only two out of 10 said they do not count as genocide.
These trends have prompted acknowledgement from former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.
In a July essay in TIME, Bennett warned of a "troubling trend in public opinion, particularly among younger Americans."
In a podcast he appeared separately, he said Israel is “now associated with genocide and baby killers," just like Italy is associated with “pasta and spaghetti.”
To counter the decline in US public support and being unable to "justify its own actions," Levy said, Israel has latched onto antisemitism by expanding the definition of the term. Many Jewish people are “not buying this,” he said.
Levy emphasized that stances on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict now function as a fundamental measure of political integrity for voters.
"Positions on Israel-Palestine have become almost a central authenticity test: Can I trust a politician?" Levy said. "If you can't get this issue right ... how can we trust you on anything else?"
The erosion of support has opened significant fractures within the Republican Party, challenging decades of tradition.
A Pew survey indicated that 57% of Republicans aged 18 to 49 now view Israel unfavorably, reflecting a push within the America First movement against foreign expenditures and international military entanglements.
Prominent conservative figures have voiced direct criticism of the bilateral relationship.
Vice President JD Vance has publicly criticized Israeli officials on several occasions over their opposition to the Trump administration’s interim deal with Iran and over Israeli military operation in Lebanon.
Media commentator Tucker Carlson claimed that US President Donald Trump had become a "hostage" under Netanyahu's "total control," characterizing the dynamic as "slavery."
Former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene has been questioning foreign assistance priorities and Rep. Thomas Massie introduced an amendment to eliminate all US foreign assistance to Israel.
This shifting political terrain has transformed traditional lobbying dynamics.
In Michigan, Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers requested that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) refrain from running advertisements or campaigning openly on his behalf against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
"Having the endorsement of the Israel lobby has gone from being a blessing for the candidate who is endorsed to a curse," Levy said.
Donors have adapted by deploying political financing through independent expenditure channels created by the Supreme Court's Citizens United ruling.
"What we increasingly see … is pro-Israel money being used in campaigns where Israel isn't mentioned," Levy said.
While the erosion spans all demographics, the divide remains most pronounced among younger Americans.
"The shift is most stark, is most attention-grabbing when you filter for the age demographic," Levy said, attributing the divide to the channels through which younger citizens consume news.
He noted that younger audiences increasingly bypass mainstream media, which he argued carries inherent biases and remains vulnerable to commercial and political pressures.
Surveys reflect this stark gradient. 
Gallup found that approval of Israel's military operations dropped to just 9% among adults aged 18 to 34.
A Pew survey from May showed that 58% of adults under 30 hold a favorable view of the Palestinians.
In addition, Harvard University's Spring 2026 Youth Poll found that 46% of Americans aged 18 to 29 viewed ties with Israel as a burden, compared to only 16% who consider them a benefit.
Levy explained that the generational divergence is "not just on the Democrat side," noting that "a real shift on the Republican side" is emerging even across "the evangelical Christian community," which long served as an essential pillar of backing for Israel.
The generational backlash ignited mass campus demonstrations in 2024, starting with student encampments at Columbia University that quickly expanded across more than 130 institutions nationwide.
Subsequent police raids, suspensions, and donor crackdowns further entwined foreign policy debates with domestic free expression.
Levy rejected a prevailing narrative that the declining American support is merely an isolated backlash against Netanyahu and far-right ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
He described the political crisis as deeply structural.
He said that elements within the pro-Israel advocacy network are actively pushing an anti-Netanyahu narrative to preserve broader bilateral ties.
By placing blame solely on the current leadership, Levy argued, institutional defenders hope an electoral defeat in the upcoming vote will let them declare, “Netanyahu’s gone! Problem solved,” and engineer a renewed diplomatic “honeymoon” with the American public.
However, Levy stressed that systemic policies extend far beyond individual personalities.
No Zionist party running in the upcoming Israeli elections is speaking about “Palestinian statehood, ending occupation, withdrawing, ending settlements," Levy said.
Prominent figures within the so-called moderate opposition bloc frequently attempt to appear "even more extreme than Netanyahu."
Levy cautioned that while a change in government might generate a brief sigh of relief in Western capitals, the core policies of occupation and military force will persist unchanged in the absence of outside pressure.
Looking ahead, Levy outlined three possible paths: continued support for Israel despite declining public backing; a decisive break that makes future US administrations less supportive; or deeper US involvement in regional conflicts that accelerates American decline and leaves Israel increasingly isolated.
"Israeli extremism is going to boomerang very harshly one day," he said.

Ukraine prepares to restore air connections: will domestic carriers be able to return
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
13:44:54 EEST
19:44:54 KST

Ukraine prepares to restore air connections: will domestic carriers be able to return
Kyiv • UNN
The authorities are preparing to reopen the skies, but without resolving aviation leasing issues, Ukrainian carriers may disappear. Their return should support the economy.
The authorities are considering the possibility of opening the skies to civil aviation before the war ends. After civil flights resume, it is important that domestic airlines be the first to return to the Ukrainian market. This will not only help restore the industry but also bring economic activity, jobs, and tax revenues related to air transportation back to Ukraine. Economist Viktor Halchynskyi told UNN in an exclusive comment.
The authorities are preparing to open the airports
After the full-scale war began, Ukrainian air carriers were forced to relocate a significant part of their operations abroad in order to preserve their aircraft, crews, and technical staff. Although the airlines’ operations are currently concentrated outside Ukraine, they continue to pay taxes in Ukraine. According to data from Daniil Menshykov, head of the State Aviation Service of Ukraine, aviation-industry enterprises paid nearly UAH 27 billion in taxes and fees to the budget in 2022–2025.
From time to time, proposals to resume airport operations in Ukraine in various forms are voiced in the public sphere. For example, ideas have also been voiced about restoring air connections in western Ukraine.
According to Mykola Kalashnyk, Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport, there is currently both a political decision and an economic understanding of the need to open Ukraine’s airspace, and the relevant preparations are already under way. In particular, work is ongoing to organize safe areas and shelters and provide alternative sources of electricity, among other things. Ukraine is also studying the experience of other countries whose airports operate amid wartime risks.
Ukrainian airlines may not live to see the skies reopen
Ensuring an appropriate level of security amid constant Russian shelling will obviously take time, but Ukrainian air carriers are already being forced to operate under extremely difficult conditions. The closed airspace deprived them of the domestic market, forced them to refocus on the international market, and imposed additional costs for maintaining their fleets, crews, and technical staff. Against the backdrop of these problems, criminal pressure has become an additional risk for the industry, affecting a number of domestic airlines because of the new approach taken by Ukrainian state bodies to taxing aircraft leasing. Under these conditions, there is a risk that some carriers simply will not live to see the moment when Ukrainian airspace is open to civil flights again.
As UNN previously reported, aviation-industry representatives have long been drawing attention to the problem of state bodies’ new interpretation of leasing payments made to nonresidents, which emerged without any amendments to the Tax Code or international conventions on the avoidance of double taxation. Since 2024, the Economic Security Bureau has begun interpreting transactions involving the leasing of aircraft from nonresidents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for leasing airplanes and helicopters. Based on this approach, the ESB opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Rosa Vetrov," H3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline—"Urga"—may also figure in a similar case.
The investigations were launched despite the fact that almost all air carriers successfully passed tax audits, and the tax authorities’ remarks concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Aviation-industry representatives insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the law and requires the establishment of a unified state approach. Moreover, interpreting aircraft leasing as royalties—a practice found in no other country in the world—makes Ukrainian carriers uncompetitive in the international market.
Analysis of data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft shows that as of July 29, 2026, 27 private airlines operated 152 aircraft. Of these, 131, or 86%, were leased, while only 21 airplanes and helicopters (14%) were owned by the airlines themselves. It is worth noting that all leased commercial aircraft are owned by foreign owners. Therefore, the majority of Ukrainian airlines could come under criminal pressure, which could prompt them to leave the Ukrainian market.
It is important that Ukrainian air carriers return to Ukraine
The return of Ukrainian airlines is significant not only fiscally but also symbolically. Unfortunately, not many of our airlines that survived this period remain. Therefore, their return will be an important signal of the restoration of Ukrainian aviation
According to him, the resumption of airport operations will also affect related sectors.
If we set aside the wartime situation and allow ourselves to dream, the restoration of civil aviation will have an effect not only directly on the aviation industry but also on a whole range of related sectors. First and foremost, these include tourism, passenger services, catering and other industries that serve aviation—from food services to airport shops. This will also provide additional revenue to the state, since there are specialized payments and fees for aerodrome services
Halchynskyi added that the resumption of civil aviation flights would mean that the country is returning to normal functioning.
The restoration of civil aviation will also have a noticeable indirect effect on tourism, the hotel business, catering, logistics and other sectors. Moreover, the restoration of civil aviation at least at one Ukrainian airport—most likely in western Ukraine—will in itself become a signal of a certain stabilization and that the country is gradually returning to normal functioning
Demand could be very high after the reopening of the skies
Halchynskyi predicts that after flights resume, the aviation market could come back to life fairly quickly, as significant pent-up demand for international and domestic transportation will emerge.
After the reopening of the skies, I think the aviation industry will be able to recover quickly enough, since demand for international and domestic air travel will initially be very high. It will be limited primarily by the capacity of airports—for example, Lviv or Uzhhorod
According to him, Lviv Airport has already demonstrated its ability to handle significant passenger flows, particularly during Euro 2012. Therefore, under favorable conditions, the restoration of substantial transport volumes is entirely realistic.
At the same time, safety remains the determining factor. If airport operations have to be constantly suspended because of air-raid alerts, this will result in aircraft downtime, flight delays and cancellations and, consequently, additional costs for carriers. This will particularly affect the decisions of foreign airlines, which will take into account security risks and the cost of insuring aircraft.
That is why, in Halchynskyi's opinion, Ukraine must use the time to prepare so that, once the security situation improves, flights can be restored as quickly as possible.
Today, we can only prepare so that we can launch aviation as quickly as possible when the time comes. Under favorable conditions, this could take literally 10–15 days, several weeks or a maximum of one month
When will the airports become operational?
The expert doubts that it will be possible to open Ukraine's airspace as early as next year.
I am not sure that this will happen in the coming months or even next year. The main prerequisite for restoring civil aviation should be a significant decrease in the intensity of the war specifically in the air. Today, we are seeing the opposite situation. It is unlikely that we will simply be able to build aviation according to the Israeli model, when attacks also occur frequently but are less intense and have a less negative impact than in Ukraine
Under these conditions, the state's task is not limited to technically preparing airports for the future reopening of the airspace. It is equally important to ensure that, by that time, Ukraine retains its own airlines capable of being the first to return to the domestic market.
The authorities are clearly aware of this. To resolve the situation involving pressure on domestic carriers, the issue of aviation leasing was submitted for consideration by the Committee on Tax Policy, Accounting and Auditing of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the creation of a working group under the Ministry of Finance, which is to develop a draft general tax consultation on the taxation of lease payments in favor of non-residents. This mechanism will make it possible to end pressure on Ukraine's aviation industry from the Bureau of Economic Security and establish uniform rules for the taxation of aircraft and helicopter rentals that comply with the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and international law.
Representatives of the aviation industry warn that if the situation with aviation leasing cannot be resolved, Ukraine risks losing its civil aviation sector. This would mean that, after the reopening of the airspace, the existing demand for air travel would be met primarily by foreign carriers, and a significant share of the economic benefits from the restoration of air links would not accrue to Ukraine.

The company will be known as SpaceXSI, its third name this year alone, as Elon Musk follows Donald Trump’s push to rebrand AI into "super intelligence".
Elon Musk is changing the name of his combined AI and space company SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, embracing US President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming artificial intelligence as super intelligence in all government communication.
Musk only recently renamed xAI as SpaceXAI, about 90 days ago, after SpaceX's June stock market debut and February takeover of the company. The agreement valued SpaceX at $1 trillion (€892bn) and xAI at $250 billion (€223bn).
The South African tech tycoon revealed that the company is making the change yesterday in a reply to a user on his social media platform X, who asked if there was “any possibility of renaming to SpaceXSI?”
“Yes, we will make that change,” said Musk.
The user asked the tech tycoon following an earlier post where he stated: “No more AI. SI. It’s better.” He later tweeted, “SpaceX is a super intelligence company.”
No changes to the company’s websites or social media have been made as of publication, with no indication of when the changes will take effect.
SpaceXAI currently operates the AI chatbot Grok, which is built into Musk’s social media platform X, with roughly 117 million active monthly users.
Grok is also widely integrated into US government and military operations, as part of a $200 million (€178mn) agreement reached in July 2025.
The decision follows US President Donald Trump’s latest executive order to rename something globally recognised to a name more in keeping with his world view, such as changing the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America.
The fact that Musk willingly agreed to Trump’s latest rebranding is nothing out of the ordinary, with Google and Apple both following Trump’s demand by renaming the bodies of water on their map platforms for US users.
Trump first mentioned his preference for super intelligence over artificial intelligence during a speech at the UN general assembly, where he argued that “artificial” makes it sound fake when it is actually “amazing,” claiming that “super intelligence" is a more accurate description.
On the same day Trump issued the executive order he hosted an AI summit with Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brokman (OpenAI), Jensen Huang (Nvidia) and Musk.
The six tech leaders signed a “Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities,” establishing a loose framework for companies to implement and self-regulate their own security controls. It is also legally unenforceable and carries no penalties.
It sets a worrying precedent given the escalating number of incidents involving AI agents carrying out “rogue” behaviour that has seen US and Australian government websites attacked, prompting calls for tighter regulation by world leaders and “pacing the frontier” by America’s leading AI companies.
Instead, Trump’s agreement allows these companies to regulate themselves without scrutiny or consequences.
On Sunday 4 October, Trump announced the creation of a “Super Intelligence Force” to coordinate American efforts and ensure the US stays ahead in the AI race.

Luke Harding's 'Betrayal' charts the collapse of the rules-based order — and who is to blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:41:22 UTC
19:41:22 KST

Luke Harding's 'Betrayal' charts the collapse of the rules-based order — and who is to blame
Luke Harding's “Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest" begins with a turning point in the full-scale war most people probably haven't spent enough time coming to terms with: North Korean soldiers getting ready to join the biggest land war in Europe since 1945.
"Soon they would be stumbling through alien woods and fields, sent by one dictator to help out another. It was a sign of a world turned upside down. The rules-based international order — the post-1945 understanding that states didn't invade each other or change borders by force — seemed broken," Harding writes.
At the start of the full-scale war, the idea of North Korean soldiers fighting in Europe would have seemed implausible to most. Today, it is just one more sign of a world reverting to Great Power politics, the betrayal at the heart of Harding's book. The U.S., Russia, and China pursue their "strategic interests," and as a result, millions of people are left hostage to a system that should have died with the last century.
Who is to blame for the collapse of the post-1945 order? As the title suggests, Harding doesn't pin it on a singular country or individual. But Harding reserves some of his most acerbic digs for U.S. President Donald Trump, whom he calls, among other things, "the prostrator-in-chief when it comes to Russia." In his second term, Harding argues, Trump has emboldened authoritarian leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping to act with unprecedented impunity.
One of the most telling examples is the so-called Alaska summit in August 2025, when Trump invited Putin for his first visit to the U.S. in nearly a decade. Before the summit, as Harding reminds the reader, Trump warned that Russia would face "severe consequences" if it didn't agree to a ceasefire with Ukraine.
Although the Alaska summit was presented as a chance for the U.S. to press Russia for peace, it opened with pomp and ceremony: Trump applauded as Putin walked toward him along a red carpet, and the two stood side by side as a B-2 stealth bomber and F-35 fighter jets flew overhead. The talks ended without any hope of ending the war, and the visuals were disturbing — including Putin casually brushing off a journalist's question about civilian deaths.
As Harding writes, "Putin could be seen grinning (during the summit), smirking even, an international outlaw no longer. The invitation was a rare honor, granted to few statesmen. It was a sign of Trump's esteem for his visitor, and a scene that might have been scripted by the Kremlin's own talented dramaturgs."
Trump's praise of Putin over the years has fueled endless speculation about his motives, most famously including the theory that he is some "compromised asset." Harding acknowledges that the Czechoslovak StB kept files on Trump and his first wife, Ivana, in cooperation with Soviet services, and that the couple visited the USSR in July 1987. Two months later, Trump ran full-page newspaper ads criticizing U.S. foreign policy, "an unusual move for a non-politician."
However, the record is suggestive rather than conclusive, and it raises as many questions as it answers. Harding raises the question of whether it is indifference, fear, the prospect of lucrative deals, or a genuine wish not to imperil peace talks that drives Trump's actions – or lack thereof – toward Russia. Whatever the answer, he argues, Trump's inaction has been seen as "a moral choice of sorts" that "ignored the Kremlin had a long and outrageous history of lying," and the Kremlin, in turn, has interpreted his behavior as a sign of approval.
Perhaps most importantly, "Betrayal" ties all this high-level state intrigue to Harding's on-the-ground reporting from Ukraine, introducing readers to some of the Ukrainians still living in front-line cities who no longer fear the sounds of explosions and soldiers defending against Russian advances — this is what Great Power politics costs, and who pays.
However, the book also looks beyond Ukraine to the aftershocks of the collapsing post-1945 order, like Trump repeatedly entertaining the idea of the U.S. taking Greenland — by force, if necessary. Putin, when asked about it, called it "an issue that concerns two specific nations and has nothing to do with (Russia)." According to Harding, the reasoning behind Putin's words was obvious: "if the Americans took Greenland, Putin's war in Ukraine looked like less of an aberration."
The U.S., long the world's leading power, still stands for a sense of order, even if that feeling is increasingly nostalgic. Leaders like President Volodymyr Zelensky, Harding notes, have no choice but to push on through Trump's erraticism — "self-appointed world peacemaker one day, warmonger the next" — for a greater cause.
If the book has any setback, it is one of scale: the events Harding describes are so vast, from the front line in Ukraine to covert Russian agents trying to influence U.K. politicians, that it is sometimes easy to get lost in the urgency of the book's underlying message. Yet the book earns its place in an argument that is only beginning, and it leaves the reader with a question that no one in power seems eager to answer: what sort of world do we want to inhabit, and whom do we want to lead it?

However, it asserted that if any decisions of the EC were found to have been taken unilaterally by the CEC, the Supreme Court could reconsider or recall them.
"They (EC) are expected to take unanimous decisions. If there is no unanimity, it has to be by majority. If records show some decision was not unanimous, etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra vires. Can we ex parte come to a decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner," the CJI said.The controversy stems from an Indian Express report published late last month, which claimed that Sandhu and Joshi had formally objected at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The report alleged that some of these decisions were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.Also Read | 'Form 6 has not been approved by us': What SC said on EC's SIR decision - top quotesAccording to the report, the poll panel's ECINet software added a requirement for ancestral details and a link to the previous SIR in Form 6, the voter registration form, without the legal amendment required under election rules. The two commissioners reportedly objected to the change.
The EC has since restored Form 6 to its original format in states where the SIR has been completed. However, the requirement continues in states and Union territories where the roll revision is still underway.Responding to the Indian Express report, the commission said that "differing views and observations" among its members were a "normal part" of deliberations in any multi-member institution. The EC also stated that all decisions, including those related to the SIR, were taken unanimously by Kumar and the two Election Commissioners.

Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:38:00 UTC
19:38:00 KST

Ukraine has developed a new missile to knock down Russia's fast, jet-powered Shahed drones, the ones its air defenses catch far less often than older models, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Suspilne reported. The weapon, called Nika, has not yet been tested. He announced it during a visit to Kyiv by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia's plants turn out an estimated 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence estimates, and the jets fly fast enough to outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower, propeller-driven Shaheds. Ukraine plans about 400 units of just one of five interceptor models it is testing by the end of October, as it scrambles to close the gap before winter.
A new missile heads into testing
Both the Ukrainian and German sides have reacted positively to the missile, Zelenskyy said, though he stayed cautious on the result: for now, he said, it only "could be positive." In the same remarks, he announced a successful test of a separate system, the German-Ukrainian interceptor Spys.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
Ukraine shoots down 85-92% of propeller-driven Shaheds, Zelenskyy said. Against the jet-powered variants, interception falls to roughly 50-60%, he noted at the press conference with Merz. F-16 fighter jets help close the gap, he said.
From interceptor drones to a new missile
Over the past month, Ukraine tested a new generation of drone interceptors built for the jet-Shahed threat. On 15 September, one struck a Shahed in trials, though Zelenskyy said developers still needed to refine its control system. On 19 September, he said the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) had created its own interceptor drone and used it to down a jet Shahed in combat. Nika adds a purpose-built missile to that mix.

Withings BodyScan 2 Review: Worth Its Weight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

I’m going to be honest from the start: No, you probably don’t need a $600 scale in your bathroom if you are just doing occasional weigh-ins. Hell, I don’t even know that elite athletes need to make this kind of extreme outlay even if they need to periodically check on how their training is going.
But I’m going to make the case for the Withings BodyScan 2 anyway. After spending several months with the device, the scale and its ecosystem have forced me to dig deeper into my health than ever before. At this point, I’m not sure I could go back to an older-model scale—even a very smart one like the original Withings Body Smart, which I used for years.
Getting a Handle on Health
There’s not much to distinguish the BodyScan 2 hardware from other smart scales aside from its handlebars, an indication that this device belongs to the now-burgeoning full-body scanner or body composition scale category. The device is, however, sleeker than most of its competition, featuring a svelte handle that somehow finds room for a small color LCD screen without the need for any extra bulk. All of your body metrics are showcased on this screen in real time, as they’re being measured, alongside any quick tips from Withings about how to get the best reading each time you hop on.
The unit offers two types of weigh-ins. Daily scans take about 30 seconds and include weight, an estimate of muscle and fat percentage (whole body and segmented across torso, arms, legs, and viscera), an estimate of basal metabolic rate, vascular age, and pulse wave velocity—though only a portion of these measurements are displayed live on the display.

Estonian ‘Active Defense’ Strategy Wants Troops to Border Russia

2026-10-05

Financial Times (FT) reported on Monday, Oct. 5, that Estonia is permanently redeploying combat troops closer to the Russian border in line with its new “active defense” strategy to counter any future incursion by Moscow’s forces.
FT cited government officials and military personnel who underlined the reasoning behind and nature of the new concept. Col. Tarmo Kundla, the commander of the Estonian army’s First Brigade said, “We must start from the border and win from the very first battles.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In preparation, the brigade is moving and the unit will be transferred from Tapa, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) from the Russian border, to Jõhvi, approximately 50 kilometers (30 miles) from Russia.
Another base is being built in Narva, the predominately Russian-speaking city that abuts the border, at a cost of around €20 million ($22 million). The barracks will peremanently accommodate 200 troops plus an additional 800 during a crisis.
While the Estonian and NATO assessment does believe that the Kremlin intends to initiate a full-scale war with NATO in the near future, they are concerned that Russia could take limited military action, testing NATO’s Article 5 defense of an ally.
Estonia fears a repeat of the pretext that President Vladimir Putin used in 2014 to “protect” Russian-speaking minorities in Ukraine’s Donbas by making a move against Narva. A particular concern is that while many Russian forces are tied down by the war in Ukraine, battle-hardened troops could be rapidly deployed against the Baltic nations.
Kyiv Could Face 16-Hour Power Cuts, Expert Warns
The FT quoted an unnamed Estonian intelligence official who said, “We were afraid of war. Now we fear the end of war.” Estonian military spending in 2026 has reached around €2.4 billion ($2.7 billion), or 5.4% of GDP.
Estonia relies on its 230,000 strong reserve combat force, 40,000 of which are said to be “high-readiness reservists – around one-fifth of the population,” to augment its regular military force of only 4,200 personnel. The focus of training is being adapted to meet the new fighting concept.
As well as the forward deployment of combat troops, Tallinn is also expanding its ability to strike enemy forces deep inside Russian territory. Over the past year, it has signed contracts to acquire nine M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) and nine K239 Chunmoo self-propelled, wheeled, launch rocket systems, each with a range of up to 300 kilometers (190 miles) and advanced drone networks.
All of these preparations include the construction of fortified border bunkers, tank obstacles, and pre-positioned engineer stores including land mines.
In September, Putin and his spokespersons constantly restated that Moscow had no intention to initiate military action against Europe, saying such allegations of a threat from Russia as “provocation” and “deliberate exaggeration of the situation.”
This sort of language was parroted by Russian officials immediately prior to its 2022 full-scale invasion.

Foxconn monthly revenue tops NT$1.15 trillion for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:34:11 UTC
19:34:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Foxconn reported record monthly revenue of NT$1.15 trillion (US$36.5 billion) in September, marking the first time its monthly revenue has surpassed NT$1 trillion.
September revenue rose 25.7% from August and 38.42% from a year earlier, making it the highest monthly revenue in the company's history, Foxconn said in a report released Monday. The previous monthly record was NT$946.5 billion in July, while September's figure also surpassed the previous September record of NT$837.1 billion set in 2025.
Third-quarter revenue reached NT$3.02 trillion, up 20.44% from the previous quarter and 47.12% from a year earlier, marking the highest revenue ever recorded for the third quarter. Revenue for the first nine months totaled NT$7.67 trillion, a 39.53% increase from the same period last year and the highest nine-month figure in the company's history.
All four major product categories posted significant month-on-month growth in September, with smart consumer electronics benefiting from new product launches and components and other products gaining from increased shipments. Cloud and networking and computing products also recorded significant growth.
Year on year, cloud and networking, components and other products, and computing products all posted strong growth, while smart consumer electronics was roughly flat due to higher shipment prices. Foxconn attributed the strong performance in cloud and networking products to continued demand for AI products.
In the third quarter, cloud and networking, components and other products, and computing products all recorded strong year-on-year growth, while smart consumer electronics posted significant growth. For the first nine months, all four product categories also posted strong or significant year-on-year growth.
Foxconn expects its AI business to continue growing in the fourth quarter alongside the traditional ICT product peak season, supporting overall performance in line with market expectations. The company said it will continue to monitor the impact of a volatile global political and economic environment.

Ukraine’s EU neighbors reject new plea from Kiev – Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:33:21 UTC
19:33:21 KST

Ukraine’s EU neighbors reject new plea from Kiev – Politico
Poland and Romania have refused to help Kiev move millions of tons of grain – which got stuck in Ukraine following Vladimir Zelensky’s war on exports – into the EU, Politico reports, citing officials in Warsaw and Bucharest. Zelensky’s 40-day campaign resulted in Russia implementing a de facto blockade of Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, with the wider consequences of the strikes estimated at 1.5% of the country’s collapsing GDP.
Last week, Ukrainian Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky appealed to the EU for a €1.1 billion ($1.23 billion) allocation to improve transit capacity, which would help free large quantities of grain – Ukraine’s key source of income – trapped in the country.
The request came after Zelensky’s 40-day PR ‘pressure campaign’ on Russia, which involved long-range strikes on oil refineries and civilian infrastructure. The effort backfired, as Russia ramped up strikes on Ukraine’s military-related logistics, including the key hub of Odessa, accounting for an overwhelming majority of Kiev’s agricultural exports.
Speaking to Politico, Vysotsky described the situation as “very, very critical,” after his ministry reported the export of 2.4 million tons of agricultural products in September, just 46% of what Kiev considers the required volume.
He added that export restrictions leave Ukrainian farmers without cash needed to plant seeds now for next year’s harvest. “If the situation stays like this till spring, it could mean the decrease of even 35-40% of the planted area,” he warned.
Last month, Ukrainian officials estimated damage to infrastructure from Russian strikes at nearly $10 billion, with wider consequences amounting to around 1.5% of GDP.
While the EU as a whole is yet to give a definitive answer to the €1.1 billion request, Poland and Romania – which are crucial to facilitating Ukraine’s exports – ruled out any significant assistance.
Romanian Agriculture Minister Barna Tanczos rejected the prospect of substantially expanding capacity, telling Politico that “the interest for our own farmers remains a priority.”
Ukrainian cargo and low Danube water levels are already straining Romanian ports, he said, adding: “Everybody knows we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the roads, railways and port capacity. It is what it is.”
The Polish Infrastructure Ministry spokesperson said, as cited by Politico, that Poland “has no plans to introduce any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products.”
Before the €1.1 billion plea, Ukraine requested €220 million from the EU in grants to support farmers affected by disrupted exports, but the bloc effectively turned it down, pointing instead to existing EU mechanisms.
Agricultural trade has long been a source of friction between Ukraine and its EU neighbors. After the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, Brussels suspended duties and quotas on Ukrainian exports, which triggered massive protests from European farmers over what they saw as unfair competition. As a result, the EU introduced an ‘emergency brake’ system in 2024, allowing tariff quotas to return for sensitive products if imports exceed set thresholds.
In addition, many of Ukraine’s neighbors, including Poland, Hungary, and Slovakia, maintain significant restrictions on Ukrainian imports at the national level.

Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05

Why India’s missile deals in Central Asia matter to Russia and China
By supplying Akash missile systems, New Delhi offers Central Asian nations a cheap, reliable alternative
Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the latest sales on Thursday last week, hinting at interest from elsewhere as he called the Akash “one of our success stories”.
Developed by India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation, the Akash is a home-grown, short-range surface-to-air missile system that can hit multiple targets at once and includes built-in protection against electronic jamming.
It can hit aerial targets between 100 metres and 20km (328 feet to 12½ miles) high, with an operational range of 4.5km to 25km, according to the Defence Ministry. Each 5.87-metre (19-foot) long missile weighs roughly 710kg (1,565lbs) and use command guidance to lock onto targets.

Trade talks with US are at an impasse – India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:31:01 UTC
19:31:01 KST

Trade talks with US are at an impasse – India
India-US trade negotiations have hit a “plateau,” making further concessions “very difficult,” Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday, days after Washington said a deal is not imminent. 
India and the US have been negotiating a Bilateral Trade Agreement since February last year, covering market access, tariff and non-tariff barriers, digital trade, and supply-chain resilience. The finance minister’s comments, despite repeated assertions by both sides in the last few months that a deal is near completion, is the first clear indication that the talks have hit an impasse. 
“Both the sides have reached a plateau beyond which, giving, or taking, might be very, very difficult,” Sitharaman said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. 
She said the talks are continuing, and left open the possibility of movement if either side finds additional negotiating space, describing the proposed agreement as “hard and very rigorously negotiated.”
India & US Trade Talks Hit 'Plateau’ – 🇮🇳 FM Sitharaman The negotiations are ‘still ongoing,’ Sitharaman said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi Monday. ‘Giving or taking beyond that plateau might be very difficult,’ Sitharaman noted. US Trade Rep Jamieson Greer said last week that a deal ‘was not imminent,’ after a meeting with Indian Trade Minister Piyush Goyal. 📹: ANI
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 5, 2026
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week, following talks with Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, that the two countries have identified the remaining sticking points, but that an agreement is not imminent. Among them are US demands for wider access for its farm and dairy products, a politically sensitive subject for New Delhi.
Goyal struck a more optimistic note last month, saying the deal was almost “done and dusted.” He added, however, that implementation depends on India securing a competitive tariff advantage over rival exporters in the US market.
US goods imports from India reached $103.8 billion last year, compared with $45.4 billion in exports, leaving the US with a $58.4 billion goods trade deficit. Total goods and services trade between the two countries stood at an estimated $239.6 billion.
The balance is in India’s favor and Washington wants to reduce the gap, Sitharaman said.
The failure to reach a deal “would not stop trade or raise tariffs” automatically, the founder of New Delhi-based think tank Global Trade Research Initiative, Ajay Srivastava, told RT. However, he said the tariff uncertainty would make pricing, contracts, and investment decisions harder.
“The bigger risk is fresh US tariffs over Russian oil purchases or alleged excess manufacturing capacity. Signing a trade deal may not remove that risk.”
A new law signed by President Donald Trump last month gives him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue significant purchases of Russian energy. India, the second largest importer of Russian oil, has warned that the tariffs could hurt bilateral ties.
Greer, however, has not publicly identified Russian oil as one of the unresolved issues in the trade negotiations.

Nature is "inseparable from daily life" at House K in Vietnam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:30:11 UTC
19:30:11 KST

Nature is "inseparable from daily life" at House K in Vietnam
Blocky volumes in exposed concrete contrast with the lush greenery and rooftop vegetable garden at House K, a home in Vietnam designed by local architecture studio HGAA.
Located in Nghệ An, the 885-square-metre family home has a central courtyard and a series of stepped terraces, designed to provide residents with as much access to greenery as possible.
"The guiding idea was simplicity, sustainability, and harmony with nature and local lifestyle," HGAA told Dezeen.
"The integration of gardens at multiple scales – a central bamboo courtyard, rooftop vegetable garden, and private gardens for each bedroom – is the defining gesture," it continued. "It transforms circulation into a sensory experience, making nature inseparable from daily life."
A paved path set within House K's front garden leads from a street entrance and parking space into a central patio and barbecue area, which is hugged by the home's U-shaped concrete form.
Exposed concrete defines both the exterior and interior of the home's cubic volumes, a choice the studio attributed to its durability, fast construction speed and the contrast it creates with the green of the home's tropical plants.
Tall bamboo shoots help shelter the glazed walls of the home's ground floor, where a central hall and staircase are flanked by a large dining and kitchen space to the north and a double-height living area to the south.
While responding to the client's feng shui requirements, HGAA designed the layout to give the majority of House K's spaces access to a garden, including the bedrooms and bathrooms tucked on the ground floor's more enclosed eastern side.
The home's first-floor bedrooms overlook the central courtyard and have access to a garden terrace raised above the home's parking area, while on the second floor another bedroom sits alongside its own private roof terrace.
Atop the building, a rooftop vegetable garden and further planting conceal the home's technical and storage spaces, offering views across the site and over the street beyond.
"The house was set back from the street to reduce heat exposure, with a large front garden and rooftop vegetable garden acting as natural buffers," the studio said.
"Traditional elements like wide eaves and surrounding gardens were reinterpreted to provide shade and cooling."
Previous projects by HGAA include a preschool in Ha Long City, incorporating walkways surrounded by screens of metal mesh that were designed to be overgrown by climbing plants.
Elsewhere in Vietnam, Inrestudio recently completed 100 Windows, a multi-generational home surrounded by irregularly placed and mismatched openings.
The photography is courtesy of HGAA.

Former hostage Romi Gonen shared excerpts from footage of her abduction to Gaza on Monday during her podcast, "Romi Gonen's New Life," produced in collaboration with V1, describing the fear, pain, and helplessness she remembers from the moments she was taken captive.
Gonen was released from Hamas captivity in a hostage deal in January 2025 after 471 days in captivity.
Reflecting on the footage, Gonen said: "I'm lying there, the sun is shining right on me, my hair is blowing in the wind, and that's what's happening inside the car. Seeing myself lying there like that, alive, it's no longer an image that I had. It's something that's actually alive, breathing. It's crazy."
She continued: "All I felt during those moments in the car was that I was really scared by that point, really scared. My hand hurt, they were shouting a lot of nonsense, they hit me, but all that was going through my head was the pain. It wouldn't let go of me."
Gonen also said: "Toward the end of the video, you can see me opening my eyes. There's something about seeing myself open my eyes at that moment that gives me confirmation that I was conscious there. I wake up with it in the morning; I go to sleep with it at night; it's in my dreams."
Gonen held in Hamas captivity for over a year
Gonen was abducted from the Nova music festival near Kibbutz Re’im on October 7, 2023, after Hamas terrorists attacked the festival and communities across southern Israel. She was shot in the hand while attempting to flee the festival in a vehicle with friends before being taken into Gaza.
The Hamas-led October 7 attack killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw more than 250 people abducted to Gaza. The Nova festival was one of the main sites of the massacre, where hundreds of festivalgoers were killed, and dozens were abducted.
Gonen remained in Hamas captivity until January 19, 2025, when she was released alongside Emily Damari and Doron Steinbrecher on the first day of a hostage-ceasefire agreement. The three women were transferred by Hamas to the Red Cross in Gaza before being handed over to IDF troops.
Following her return to Israel, Gonen underwent prolonged medical treatment for injuries sustained on October 7 and complications stemming from the lack of adequate medical care while she was held in Gaza. She was discharged from Sheba Medical Center in July 2025 after undergoing two complex surgeries.

UAE-Israel ties may improve after flydubai event, akin to US-Saudi relations post-9/11 - analysis
