New molecule restores memory in animals with Alzheimer's' disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:40:25 UTC
18:40:25 KST

The molecule RSQ-020 targets the Tau protein, which, when it folds incorrectly and forms clumps, is implicated in many severe neurodegenerative diseases.
A Greek research team led by Giorgos Skretas has developed an innovative pharmaceutical molecule that, in preclinical tests, restored learning and memory capacity in animal models with characteristics of Alzheimer’s disease.
The discovery is the result of collaboration between scientists at the Alexander Fleming Biomedical Sciences Research Centre, the National Hellenic Research Foundation and the spin-off company ResQ Biotech. The molecule, RSQ-020, acts by targeting the Tau protein which, when it folds abnormally and forms aggregates, is linked to the onset and progression of serious neurodegenerative disorders.
The development of RSQ-020 relied on a new technological platform created by the same research group. The method uses modified bacteria which can produce an enormous number of different candidate molecules while simultaneously indicating which of them have genuine biological activity. The aim is to pinpoint substances capable of repairing the malfunction of proteins that have lost their normal structure.
This approach differs markedly from the traditional route to drug discovery, said Giorgos Skretas, director of the Institute of Bioinnovation at the Alexander Fleming Biomedical Sciences Research Centre and collaborating researcher at the Institute of Chemical Biology of the National Hellenic Research Foundation.
According to him, classical drug development is based on finding a molecule that “fits” a specific protein target, like a key in a lock. However, the proteins involved in misfolding diseases do not have a stable shape but change constantly, which makes it particularly difficult to develop effective treatments.
“Instead of simply looking for a molecule that will bind to a specific site on the protein, we look directly for one that delivers the desired effect. Our technology allows us to see when a faulty protein is restored, because the bacteria we use emit a green signal when that happens,” the researcher said.
How it works in practice
In practical terms, the scientists inserted a human protein they are studying into a bacterium and programmed it to light up only when this protein returns to a more normal state. At the same time, the same cells produce billions of different small molecules, each representing a potential solution to the misfolding problem.
When a bacterium emits light, this is a sign that it contains a molecule which has achieved the desired objective.
In this way, instead of relying on lengthy tests carried out exclusively under laboratory conditions, researchers can, within a short period of time, identify molecules that are already working inside living cells – an environment that more closely mirrors the real conditions of a human disease.
The technology was initially developed with a focus on amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and the SOD1 protein, but its potential applications extend to many other neurodegenerative conditions. Protein misfolding is a common hallmark of diseases such as Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and other serious disorders of the nervous system.

In the 2026 Shanghai Ranking, a leading international ranking of research universities, Hebrew University places 89th and the Weizmann Institute of Science 71st. Both are among the ranking's top 100 institutions worldwide. The Technion, ranked 97th last year, has slipped into the 101-150 band.

﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? | Michael Jacobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:39:04 UTC
18:39:04 KST

Among the many crucial decisions Andy Burnham has to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year.
Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities.
The last time the UK chaired the forum was in 2009, when Gordon Brown presided over the rescue of the global economy after the financial crash. Before the London summit in April 2009, the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, had wrung his hands, saying that “none of us has a plan”. Barack Obama had a quick response to this: “Gordon has a plan.”
He did. Brown got the G20 to agree to a $5tn fiscal stimulus among its member states, increase International Monetary Fund lending to developing countries and create a new global coordinator for financial regulation, the Financial Stability Board.
But 2009 was a rare year for the G20, in that it actually achieved something. In general, the long communiques issued at its annual leaders’ summits reflect only the lowest-common-denominator agreement on broad principles. The G20 rarely commits its members to doing anything they were not planning to do anyway, and only occasionally makes genuinely collective decisions. One of the most consequential was the suspension of developing countries’ debt during the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the subsequent establishment of a “common framework” for debt treatment.
Indeed, for what is meant to be the effective executive committee of the global economy, the G20 is an oddly weak institution. Its 19 members (plus the EU and the African Union) have no HQ or staff and do not even have a standing website: if you want to know what the G20 has agreed over the past 20 years you need to go to a set of unofficial webpages hosted by some enterprising academics at the University of Toronto.
For most countries, hosting the G20 summit is a chance to impress its domestic audience by showing that its head of government bestrides the world stage. Last year Donald Trump boycotted it; the South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, was glad simply to get any kind of agreed communique. This year, the US is the host, with one of Trump’s own properties near Miami the summit venue in December: expect a show of personal and US power and very little attempt to achieve anything by way of multilateral cooperation.
But that makes Burnham’s task next year even more critical. The UK needs to show that it is still possible for the world’s leading nations – including the US and China – to work together to meet the key challenges facing the world.
So what should the UK’s presidency priorities be?
First, agreement on the need for, and a process towards, a global treaty on the regulation of artificial intelligence. After the recent alarm over the existential risks of AI, the UK has a chance to lead the world towards a global agreement on its control. Even if Trump is unwilling to sign up, getting the rest of the world to do so, seeking a form of global “technological security”, would be a vital achievement. A future US president might well wish to accede later.
Second, acknowledgment of the growing risk to food security and a plan to deal with it. The incoming “supersized” El Niño weather pattern is combining with the climate crisis, soil and biodiversity loss, and the impact of the war in the Middle East on diesel and fertiliser costs to create a perfect storm for the world’s food system. Agricultural yields are falling and food prices rising, leaving millions of people at risk of hunger. The G20 needs to act to prevent it.
Third, acknowledgment of accelerating climate insecurity – the severe risks posed by the climate emergency to all countries’ economies and societies – and agreement on coordinated measures to improve climate resilience. Though the Trump administration does not support emissions reduction, it does accept the need to adapt to climate change, and this year’s extreme weather events have impressed on all governments how urgent this is. The G20 should agree to provide more support to the most vulnerable countries.
Fourth, agreement on a debt restructuring programme for low- and middle-income economies whose debt – through no fault of their own, but because of rising global interest rates – has now become unsustainable. For too many countries the compounding of debt burdens with rising energy and food prices has made sustainable economic growth all but impossible.
What connects these issues is that all are global problems that can only be tackled through international cooperation. They each address aspects of national and global security – technological, food, climate and economic. Importantly, the first three address problems that are highly visible and politically salient to the British public, enabling the government to demonstrate how international action benefits people at home. (And the fourth represents a vital contribution to global economic growth.) And all have a good chance of being agreed in the G20, despite the conflicts and tensions that in other areas divide the world’s leaders.
G20 host countries always invent a slogan to express their presidency ambitions. In other contexts Burnham has said he wants to give people a sense of hope. That is something people all over the world need. For the G20 he might wish to try “national security through international cooperation”. It would not be a bad legacy to aim for.
- Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime minister

Yemen war escalates: What’s the latest, as government forces claim gains?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:38:26 UTC
18:38:26 KST

Yemen war: What’s the latest, as government forces claim advances?
After launching major military offensive to reclaim Houthi-held areas, Yemen’s government says it has taken key district
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has announced a major military campaign to retake all territory controlled by the Houthis, marking a new escalation in a civil war that had largely been frozen for several years before intensified battles in recent weeks.
The announcement by Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), the executive body of the Yemeni government, comes after weeks of heavy fighting and major Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important city of Taiz.
On Monday, Yemeni government forces said that they were launching a “strategic” offensive on the country’s capital Sanaa, which the Houthis have held since 2014.
Earlier in the day, the Yemeni forces — who are backed by Saudi Arabia — said they had regained control of the Dhubab district on the country’s west coast near the Bab al-Mandab strait, though the Houthis denied the announcement.
The fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Yemeni government forces has expanded since a fragile 2022 truce collapsed in July, displacing more than 100,000 people since then.
Last month, the Houthis launched a rapid offensive that captured about 150km (93 miles) of Red Sea coastline and areas around Bab al-Mandeb, the narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which is a critical route for international shipping.
On Monday, the foreign minister of Yemen’s internationally recognised government requested more support from the international community to defeat the Houthis, saying it’s “in the world’s interest” for the country to be stable.
“We call upon our brothers, friends and the international community to support the Yemeni people, their state, and their national institutions in confronting the terrorist Houthi militia, which seizes their will by force of arms and lays waste to the lives of their sons – after exhausting all opportunities for de-escalation and peace,” Afrah Al-Zouba said in a post on X.
So what is the latest on the fighting, and what does Yemen’s government hope to achieve?
What is the latest on the fighting?
The Yemeni government army said on Monday that 1,747 Houthi fighters had been “neutralised” in 1,122 military operations in the Saada, al-Jawf and Taiz governorates and along Yemen’s western coast.
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili said the attacks targeted artillery and rocket positions, fortifications, supply lines, reinforcements and command centres.
Al-Nuzaili said warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers were involved and 364 military and logistical vehicles had been destroyed or disabled. The casualty and equipment figures have not been independently verified.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government also announced that its forces had taken control of the Dhubab district on the Red Sea, and were launching a major offensive on Sanaa.
Elsewhere, the front line in Marib governorate in northeastern Yemen witnessed an escalation in fighting on Monday.
A military source told Al Jazeera that government forces launched an attack on Houthi positions on the Ragwan front in the north of the governorate, coinciding with air strikes targeting Houthi positions and reinforcements.
The source said the raids targeted Houthi positions near Mount Helan as well as an arms depot and military reinforcements northwest of Marib.
On Sunday, a Saudi-led coalition said its forces carried out 97 attacks against Houthi reinforcements around Taiz and the Tor al-Baha front using warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and snipers.
On the developments in Taiz, Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau chief, Saeed Thabet, said Houthi operations in the rural areas around the strategic city are based on guerrilla tactics aimed at easing pressure on the coastal front and tightening the blockade of the road to Aden.
What has Yemen’s government announced?
Al-Alimi said on Sunday that government forces have been ordered to launch military operations to regain Houthi-controlled territory and restore state authority across Yemen.
“We have instructed the armed forces, security forces and all military formations to begin carrying out their assigned tasks under an approved plan until the country is liberated from the Houthis,” al-Alimi said.
Military sources told the Reuters news agency that over the previous 48 hours, the Houthis advanced against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Taiz, pushing forward along the last remaining road linking the city with Aden on Yemen’s southern coast. The AFP news agency, meanwhile, quoted four security sources as saying the Houthis had cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with Aden, the Yemeni government’s interim capital.
The Houthis have controlled Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, and much of Yemen’s populous northwest since 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened militarily the following year at the head of a coalition supporting the internationally recognised government but failed to dislodge the group.
A United Nations-brokered truce in 2022 brought several years of relative calm before fighting intensified again this year. The latest round of fighting has focused heavily on the Red Sea coast and Taiz.
Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemeni defence analyst, said he believes Yemen’s government and its allies face a formidable rival in the Houthis.
The missile arsenal of the Houthis, the precision of their drones and their military “capabilities have grown” with support from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), he told Al Jazeera.
And having joined the US-Israel war on Iran on their own timeline, the Houthis have reinforced their place in Tehran’s “axis of resistance” and given the IRGC a way to shift pressure from the Strait of Hormuz to Bab al-Mandeb in the Red Sea, he said.
What has Saudi Arabia said?
Saudi Arabia has pledged continued support for the internationally recognised government.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Malki said Saudi Arabia and its allies would continue supporting Yemen until state institutions were restored and the Houthi threat to shipping in the southern Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb was ended.
Al-Malki also said Saudi Arabia had an “inherent right” to defend its sovereignty and take military measures to deter Houthi attacks, citing attacks in Riyadh, Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, Najran, Taif and Yanbu in recent weeks.

2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded for discoveries in optogenetics
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:38:16 EEST
18:38:16 KST

2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine awarded for discoveries in optogenetics
Kyiv • UNN
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the prize for the discovery of light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics." The Nobel Committee announced this on October 5, UNN reports.
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries that led to the development of optogenetics, which makes it possible to switch the activity of individual nerve cells on or off in the living brain. This method is now used in laboratories around the world to uncover the secrets of the brain
Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel — the 2026 medicine laureates — reportedly discovered the remarkable protein channelrhodopsin in single-celled algae.
"Hegemann wondered how Chlamydomonas, a single-celled alga, is able to swim toward a source of light. In the early 2000s, he and Georg Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, an algal protein with unique properties located on the cell surface. When illuminated with blue light, a channel opens in the protein. Charged ions then enter the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that regardless of which cell they inserted the protein into, those cells became light-sensitive," the statement said.
This year's Nobel Prize in Medicine laureate Karl Deisseroth, as noted, transformed the channelrhodopsin protein into a light-controlled switch for nerve cells.
Deisseroth introduced the channelrhodopsin gene into the nerve cells of rats. By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal. He published this discovery in 2005. Two years later, he made this light-controlled switch for nerve cells work in the brains of living mice.
The 2026 Nobel laureates in Physiology or Medicine have laid the foundation for a new era in neuroscience, the Nobel Committee emphasized.
"Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to identify neural circuits that control certain memories, feelings and behaviors associated with neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using this method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairments," the statement said.
"Optogenetics has fundamentally changed our understanding of how the brain works. Every day brings new discoveries that help unravel one of humanity's greatest mysteries: how our incredible brain works," the statement noted.
For reference
Nobel Week 2026 began on October 5 and will run until October 12. During it, laureates in six categories are announced.

The remains of Czar Samuel, a medieval Bulgarian ruler, were flown to Sofia on Saturday under a military flypast. Honour guards then carried the coffin in a state procession to the Church of St Sophia, where crowds queued to pay their respects.
Samuel spent his reign fighting the Byzantine Empire to expand his kingdom, and he died in 1014. His bones were found in a Greek border area 60 years ago, and Bulgaria has negotiated with Athens for decades to bring them home.

As rising seas threaten low-lying Pacific Islands, regional leaders call on the world to take climate more seriously
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:37:00 UTC
18:37:00 KST

Pacific Islands urge world leaders to take action on climate
October 5, 2026
For Pacific islanders, the ocean is a source of food, livelihoods and cultural identity. But a changing climate is turning that lifeline into a threat, as rising global temperatures drive sea levels higher.
"When there's a low tide, you'll actually see foundations of homes, you see burial grounds of your ancestors...," said Anne Rasmussen, lead climate negotiator for the Association of Small Island States (AOSIS), adding that higher seas are making some land uninhabitable.
This week, a handful of world leaders are in Fiji with ministers and climate negotiators from around 60 countries to discuss the outstanding issues surrounding the UN-led international climate conference that kicks off in Turkey next month.
Pacific leaders see these talks ahead of COP31 as an opportunity to highlight the increasing urgency facing their low-lying islands.
"It's actually to bring the people who are continuing to turn a blind eye and deaf ears to the communities of the vulnerable islands to these effects," Rasmussen told DW, emphasizing the importance of holding these talks in the Pacific.
"It showcases the vulnerability. It showcases the impacts that are already happening. And it also brings the community, the real people at the front line, to participate in these pre-COPs," she added.
On the frontlines of climate change
Leaders attending the event will first travel to the island of Tuvalu, which scientists predict could be one of the first countries to become inhabitable due to rising sea levels caused by human-driven climate change.
At the UN General Assembly last month, Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told delegates that sea level rise is a "present reality."
"Tuvalu's message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come."
At an average of just two meters above sea level, the archipelago has faced more frequent and severe flooding as water levels have risen.
"Having back-to-back hurricanes and storms, having back-to-back significant floods...it really sets back countries and affects communities,” Rasmussen, who comes from the Pacific island of Samoa, told DW. "People are losing their homes."
She also said rising sea levels are contaminating freshwater sources with salt, which threatens crops. In addition, hotter oceans mean corals lose the algae they rely on to survive, causing them to bleach and become less able to accommodate the diverse marine life that local populations rely on for their income.
Overshooting agreed limits on temperature rise
Although only few leaders from outside the region are expected at the conference, negotiators from countries including Germany, Mexico and South Korea will be present. Efforts to limit planetary heating are expected to be high on the agenda.
Pacific leaders are pushing for a renewed commitment to keep global temperature rise capped to 1.5 degrees (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a limit that was agreed on by world leaders at the Paris climate conference in 2015.
A UN report released in September said under a best-case scenario, temperatures were likely to reach at least 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels. The study added that it is still possible to "bring temperatures down".
Natasha Green, Australia country lead for climate think-tank E3G , said small island and least developing states are calling for countries to work together to enable vulnerable nations to "adapt and build resilience to the worsening impacts of climate change".
Tricky questions of climate finance
A key issue at this week's talks will be climate finance. Poorer nations, which have done little to contribute to rising global temperatures, yet are feeling some of the worst impacts, have long called on richer, higher-emitting countries to provide more money to help them adapt to a hotter world.
Laura Schäfer, international climate policy head of division at environment and human rights nonprofit, Germanwatch, said she would like to see Australia, who holds the COP presidency, "address tricky questions." 
Such as "how to include carbon majors, including the big fossil [fuel] industry in paying for climate damages like the ones we have just seen in Nepal." 
Also on the agenda will be a the non-use of fossil fuels for creating energy. At the 2023 climate conference, countries agreed for the first time to move towards a future that doesn’t rely on oil, gas and coal. Since then, however, there has been little progress.
Earlier this year just under 60 states took part in the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.
Scientists say an end to burning these polluting sources of energy is the only way to bring global temperature levels back under agreed limits. And thereby prevent some of the worst impacts of climate change — like the rising sea levels affecting island states and coastline communities.
"It's really important that the COPs continue to progress and elevate the commitment [...] to transition away from fossil fuels," said Green.
Edited by: Tamsin Walker

German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:37:00 UTC
18:37:00 KST

German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine
October 5, 2026
The Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has gone to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, the academy announced on Monday.
The trio won the award for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, which combines the methods of optics and genetics to create a form of non-invasive stimulation of neurons.
The Nobel Assembly said that optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain, as researchers have been "able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders."
"The impact of optogenetics extends far beyond understanding the healthy brain, it has also helped revealed how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia," Abdel El Manira, Nobel committee member and professor of neuroscience, said after the announcement was made.
In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. Researchers hope that the field could lead to treatments for neurological and sensory disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
Who are the winners?
Hegemann is considered to be the leading expert in photobiology and one of the founding fathers of optogenetics. He is a professor of neuroscience at the Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany.
Georg Nagel is a biophysicist and professor at of neurophysiology at the University of Würzburg, Germany. Karl Deisseroth is a professor of bioengineering and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University in the US.
The trio came togther as Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae could swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.
Deisseroth then joined in to work with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
Medicine is the first of Nobels announced this week
The award for medicine is the first Nobel prize to be awarded this week, with laureates set to be named in physics, chemistry, literature and peace in the days up to Friday.
Last year's prize was awarded jointly to Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell of the United States and Shimun Sakaguchi of Japan for "for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance."
The prizes will be presented at ceremonies in Stockholm, Sweden on December 10.
Each prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.

====================================================================================================

SC seeks EC response on changes during SIR: Why has Form 6 become a flashpoint — explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:34:32 UTC
18:34:32 KST

Chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar with election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi.
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday raised questions over changes made to Form 6, the application used for registering a voter, during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The issue came up while the court was hearing petitions alleging that several decisions linked to the SIR exercise were taken without the approval of all three election commissioners, particularly Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, who were at odds with poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar on multiple occasions.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana sought responses from the Election Commission, the Centre, the CEC and the other two election commissioners before examining whether the poll panel's statutory procedure was followed.The bench, however, refused to pass an immediate order seeking the suspension of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, while considering the controversy over Form 6, which was one of the central issues raised in the petitions.
What is Form 6
Form 6 is the application through which an eligible person seeks inclusion of their name in the electoral roll. The Election Commission's guidelines states the application is addressed to the Electoral Registration Officer of the constituency where the applicant ordinarily resides.
The form requires basic details such as the applicant's name, details of a relative, Aadhaar information, gender, date of birth and present ordinary residence. Applicants are also required to complete a declaration, with the guidelines warning that making a false statement in it is punishable under Section 31 of the Representation of the People Act, 1950.The Election Commission's instructions also mandates that an applicant can fill the form either in English or in the official language of the state. Also, an applicant who does not know the number or name of the relevant constituency cannot have the application rejected merely for that reason.For age verification, applicants can submit a self-attested copy of one of the documents specified in the form. The guidelines also provide for verification by the Electoral Registration Officer in cases where the prescribed documents are unavailable.
The Form 6
The dispute over Form 6
The petitions allege that additional requirements connected with the SIR were introduced into Form 6 through the Election Commission's software.One of the allegations is that details concerning an applicant's ancestry (details of father or grandfather) and a link to the previous SIR were incorporated into the process without an amendment to the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.The petitioners have further alleged that Election Commissioner Vivek Joshi objected to the modification and that Election Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu subsequently endorsed the objection. Therefore, the issue therefore goes beyond the information sought from voters.
Chagnes were made to Form 6 without amending the electoral rules.
At the heart of the dispute is whether the Election Commission could alter the form and introduce SIR-linked requirements through its software without following the legal process required for changing the relevant electoral rules. During the hearing, the CJI specifically flagged the question of who authorised the modification.“Any modified Form 6 has not been approved by us. Let's be clear. When record has produced, we would like to see who has modified. But, your prayers appear jumbled up,” the CJI noted, as quoted by LiveLaw.The court, however, did not accept the petitioners' allegations as established facts at this stage as Justice Bagchi said the court would first need responses from the concerned authorities and records before deciding whether any decision was taken contrary to the statutory framework.Also Read | 'Form 6 has not been approved by us': What SC said on EC's SIR decision - top quotes"If records show some decision was not unanimous etc., we will injunct those decisions and say they are ultra-vires. Can we ex-parte come to decision that all decisions were unilateral? We expect them to respond in a clear, transparent manner," Justice Bagchi added.
EC retracts on From 6
Amid the raging controvery, the Election Commission withdrew the additional SIR-related declaration from Form 6 in states where the electoral roll revision exercise had been completed.In states where the SIR was concluded, the EC removed additional declaration from the ECINET app and portal, as well as the respective Chief Electoral Officer portals. This meant that applicants in states where SIR is over will only need to fill the regular statutory Form 6 to enrol as voters.Just days before this action and as the controvery over dissent in the poll body emerged, the EC in a press note had, however, said that "the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. For non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used."
The larger SIR controversy
The Form 6 dispute forms part of a broader challenge to how the Election Commission has allegedly handled the SIR exercise. The petitions rely on claims that the two other Election Commissioners formally raised objections on at least 14 occasions over several months to decisions and orders concerning the revision of electoral rolls.The allegations include changes to electoral-roll software, communications issued in the name of the Election Commission and other decisions allegedly taken without the approval of all members of the multi-member poll panel.The petitioners have invoked Section 18 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023. The provision states that the Commission's business should, as far as possible, be transacted unanimously and that where the members differ, the matter is to be decided according to the majority view.The pleas argue that this framework means powers vested in the Election Commission cannot be exercised individually by the CEC where the law requires the Commission to act collectively.The petitioners have sought several forms of relief, including suspension of Gyanesh Kumar as CEC until the matter is decided, preservation of electoral-roll data and audit trails, and restrictions on further substantive changes to Form 6.
Another plea has sought criminal proceedings against the CEC and other officials and argued that decisions, guidelines and software changes allegedly made without the full Commission's agreement should be declared unconstitutional, ultra vires and void ab initio.The Supreme Court has therefore, at this stage, not ruled on whether the alleged changes to Form 6 or other SIR-related decisions were unlawful. The immediate question before the court is whether the Election Commission followed the statutory decision-making process.The court will consider the records and responses of the respondents before deciding whether any particular decision can be struck down.
Rajeev Singh is a Digital Content Producer with The Times of India. He covers politics, policies, defence, and conflicts for readers curious to know their implications. He loves digging into legal maxims and political trivia. On off days, when not turning pages or learning русский, he lives in the reverie of “what ifs” and “how abouts.”

Israeli lecturer indicted for planning mass terror attack against Palestinians, Arab Israelis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:33:11 UTC
18:33:11 KST

The State Attorney’s Office on Monday indicted a mathematics lecturer at Bar-Ilan University for allegedly planning a series of mass terrorist attacks, motivated by nationalist ideology, against hundreds of Arab citizens of Israel and Palestinians.
The defendant, a Petah Tikva resident in his 60s, cannot be named under a court-issued publication ban.
The goal, according to the prosecution, was forced mass transfer. The defendant called the plan “AY”T,” a Hebrew acronym for “Am Ya’aseh Transfer,” which roughly translates to, “the people will carry out transfer.”
He was charged in the Central District Court in Lod with preparing to commit an act of terrorism under the Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats, and obstruction of justice. Prosecutors also asked the court to keep him in custody until the conclusion of the legal proceedings against him.
According to the indictment, he developed the plan from early February 2023 until his arrest about two weeks ago. The prosecution said it was initially fueled by the May 2021 riots during Operation Guardian of the Walls and intensified after the outbreak of the Swords of Iron war.
The idea was to activate different terrorist cells simultaneously in different locations. The prosecution said the defendant also conducted a reconnaissance tour around Tuba-Zanghariya to examine possible access and attack routes.
The alleged plan envisioned 72 Jewish attackers, including the defendant, at least half of whom would have firearms licenses. They were to be divided into 12 cells of six people each and use a variety of weapons, including handguns, rifles, axes, and hammers.
The intended targets were mixed cities and Arab communities throughout Israel, including Tuba-Zanghariya in the North, which the indictment describes as a primary target.
The plan further called for the terrorist cells to receive assistance and support coordinated in advance with subversive elements who would be recruited from within the IDF, including the bombardment of Arab population centers by the Air Force, Artillery Corps, and Armored Corps.
According to the indictment, the practical section of the plan instructed members of the public to join in “carrying out mass killings and rapidly seizing areas of friction, roads, entrances to and exits from Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals… Do not show mercy even to the women or their cruel and repulsive children; do not stop in the face of pleas; harden your hearts. Any pause will lead to an intolerable state of chaos, followed by the massacre of Jews.”
The simultaneous mass terrorist attacks, amplified and publicized on social media in real time, were intended to cause all Arab citizens of Israel, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians living in east Jerusalem and the West Bank, to flee or be permanently expelled to Jordan, Lebanon, and the Gaza Strip, according to the indictment.
Attempted recruitment of Moshe Feiglin
The defendant tried for about a year and a half to recruit supporters to join him, but none agreed, the indictment states.
In particular, he allegedly sought to recruit Zehut chairman Moshe Feiglin, who is No. 2 on the joint Religious Zionist Party-Zehut electoral list. He intended to enlist Feiglin and, with his help, recruit additional activists to take part in the plan.
The defendant attended two of Feiglin’s public events and tried to arrange a meeting with him and give him a summary of the plan, but Feiglin did not respond to any of his approaches, according to the indictment.
About a month ago, the defendant allegedly wrote a letter addressed to Feiglin in which he threatened to distribute it and, in his view, damage Feiglin’s public standing ahead of the election unless Feiglin cooperated and helped advance the plan.
About two days later, he allegedly went to Feiglin’s home, gave the letter to a passing neighbor, and asked her to deliver it. He later attended a Zehut event at Jerusalem’s Mahane Yehuda market and, through another woman, delivered several copies of the letter and a second letter containing a similar threat to the party’s director-general.
Feiglin's team said it filed a police complaint as soon as the letter was received.
The indictment further alleges that the defendant tried to conceal his activities and prevent the plan from being discovered. Among other measures, he allegedly wrote his documents by hand rather than on a computer, wore a protective mask, hat, and sunglasses when meeting prospective recruits, used a false name, and borrowed passersby’s phones to contact others.
Bar-Ilan said in response that it “condemns in the strongest possible terms and is deeply appalled” by the attributed acts to the lecturer. The university also called on authorities to “pursue the matter to the fullest extent of the law, should the allegations be substantiated.”
It added, “The university has, and will continue to have, zero tolerance for conduct of this nature – conduct that is fundamentally incompatible with the values we share as Jews, as Israelis, and as human beings, and that stands in clear opposition to the values of Bar-Ilan University.”
It concluded, “The lecturer will be suspended from his duties with immediate effect, pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings.”

IDF killed two-thirds of terrorists who invaded Israel on October 7, intel chief tells cabinet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:32:18 UTC
18:32:18 KST

Of the 6,000 people who crossed the border from Gaza and infiltrated Israel on October 7, 4,000 have been killed, an Israeli source told The Jerusalem Post on Monday, citing data shared by Maj.-Gen. Shlomi Binder, head of the IDF's Military Intelligence, during a security cabinet meeting on Sunday evening.
"There are 2,000 remaining, and we will get to every last one of them," Binder said.
In the latest strike on Sunday, the IDF announced that it had killed Saqr Nabil Musa Qaisi, a Nukhba terrorist from Hamas who was posing as the director of a humanitarian aid organization called Deniz Feneri.
Earlier on Friday, the military killed Ibrahim Mustafa Suleiman Abu Oweimer, a Nukhba platoon commander in Hamas’ military wing and one of the terrorists who infiltrated Israel on October 7.
During the weekend, the military killed two Islamic Jihad rocket array commanders and reportedly attempted to kill Ali al-Amoudi, Yahya Sinwar’s successor as Hamas’s leader in the Gaza Strip.
There was no confirmation by the IDF that Amoudi was killed in the strike, with conflicting reports in Israeli media about his status.
The Post learned in July that the military had killed at least 420 Hamas terrorists since the 2025 ceasefire was established, while it has continued to target Hamas commanders ever since.
According to these estimates, from October 2025 til July 2026, Hamas reportedly has killed dozens or more of its own population since the ceasefire in order to retake control of all areas of the Gaza Strip where the Palestinian population lives.
UN estimates that around 1,000 Gazans have been killed during this time, meaning that, since the ceasefire, the percentage of Gazans killed by the IDF has likely been less than 50% civilians.
Defense Ministry says 1,318 Israeli security personnel killed since October 7
Since the start of the Israel-Hamas War on October 7, 2023, 1,318 members of Israel's security forces have fallen in the conflict, according to data published by the Families, Commemoration, and Heritage Department of the Defense Ministry on Sunday.
The number includes fallen personnel from the IDF, Israel Police, Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Fire and Rescue Services, security coordinators, and local response team members.
The numbers account for the fallen across all fronts, including the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and the West Bank.
More than 7,150 people have been officially recognized as relatives who lost someone in service since the start of the war, including 2,143 bereaved parents, 355 widows, and 880 orphans. 3,772 people lost a sibling in the war.
Despite the ceasefire that took effect in the Gaza Strip on October 10, 2025, a number of Israeli soldiers have been killed in incidents along the Yellow Line that delineates the buffer zone within the strip.
Yonah Jeremy Bob, Amir Bohbot, and The Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
12:31:00 EEST
18:31:00 KST

German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has stated that he sees the danger of a violent conflict with Russia, noting that the confrontation between the countries has acquired a "new, dangerous quality".
Source: European Pravda, citing Jäger's remarks during a hearing in the Bundestag, quoted by Die Welt
Details: The German intelligence head warned that the war in Ukraine, marked by increasingly brutal Russian attacks, is entering a "new, very dangerous phase", while the threat of hybrid attacks against Germany remains real.
Jäger stated that the risk involves Germany being dragged into a conflict with Russia.
The intelligence head emphasised that Russia is visibly escalating the conflict in Ukraine and continues to step up pressure on Europe and Germany. The confrontation Germany is in with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous character. The country risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia.
As an example of this escalation, he cited the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, responsibility for which Berlin attributed to Russia.
Jäger noted that no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany. Germany did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on the country, seeing it as its main adversary because Germany does not tolerate Russia's revisionist, expansionist policy and its war of aggression against Ukraine.
According to Jäger, the Russian leadership seeks to "ensure for the future that no political decisions directed against Moscow are made in Berlin or other European capitals". The consequence of this is "increasingly aggressive actions by Russian intelligence services" against Germany and other states.
Jäger stated that Russia is waging a shadow war against Germany. This undeclared war cannot be characterised using traditional military or legal categories. Germany is not in a state of defence, yet they are still under attack – that is precisely what a shadow war is.
The intelligence head added that Russia sought to undermine Europe's political support for Ukraine and emphasised that they had to be prepared for intimidation attempts and further interference. He noted that nuclear threats would likely be voiced again.
However, according to Jäger, at this time the intelligence agency sees no signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory. Nevertheless, "Russian military actions on a limited scale" are possible, particularly in the Baltic states, specified the head of German intelligence.
Background:
- Chancellor of Germany Friedrich Merz declared that his country is "preparing for major hybrid attacks, including severe ones" and will respond to them "swiftly and very clearly".
- German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt planned a package of measures covering protection against drones and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

Hackers access data of 8.8 million people in Denmark in 'extremely serious' breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:27:14 UTC
18:27:14 KST

A major cybersecurity breach has exposed the personal data of 8.8 million people in Denmark.
Denmark has suffered a major data breach after hackers broke into the country's national population registry and accessed the personal information of millions of people.
The country's digital affairs minister announced the data breach on Monday, calling it "an extremely serious incident" that affected 8.8 million people.
"Unauthorised individuals obtained illegal access" to the names, addresses and CPR, including those who have died or emigrated, the ministry said in a press release, referring to Denmark’s social security numbers.
“This is an extremely serious incident,” Christina Egelund, digital affairs minister, was quoted as saying in the press release.
“Together with all the relevant authorities, we are in the process of mapping out the full extent of the incident,” she added.
Denmark has a population of around six million, but the national registry has information on 11 million, including data on those deceased and people who have emigrated from the country.
An investigation has now been launched into the incident. Authorities said they have no information on who carried out the breach.
They broke into the national registry by hacking into a Danish company that legally had access to it, the government said, adding that the access has not been revoked.

Development Road Project could generate $80 billion annually as energy corridor, minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:27:05 UTC
18:27:05 KST

Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar (AA Photo)
The Development Road Project could generate around $80 billion in annual economic value if it is developed into an energy corridor carrying oil, natural gas and electricity, according to Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar.
The project is designed to connect the Persian Gulf to Türkiye and Europe through road and railway links while strengthening energy ties between Türkiye and Iraq and creating a major international trade corridor.
Speaking after a visit to Ankara by Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudhair, Bayraktar said the project should be viewed as more than a transportation link. Türkiye is determined to develop it as a strategic energy route supported by oil, natural gas and electricity transmission infrastructure along the corridor, he said.
Bayraktar noted that the route could eventually handle up to 2.5 million barrels of oil per day. He said Iraq currently produces around 4 million barrels per day, while Kuwait has production capacity of roughly 2 million barrels per day, creating significant potential for regional crude flows to be redirected through the corridor.
According to Bayraktar, transporting 2.5 million barrels of oil per day through the route could create annual economic value of approximately $65 billion-$70 billion.
He also highlighted the project’s natural gas potential, saying it could provide an alternative route for Qatari gas exports to reach Europe via Iraq and Türkiye. Qatar currently depends largely on LNG shipments and the Strait of Hormuz for its gas exports, he noted.
“If Qatari gas is transported through Iraq and the Development Road, with part of the gas remaining in Türkiye and part exported to Europe, the combined oil and natural gas trade could generate an annual economic value of around $80 billion,” Bayraktar said.

Nolo becomes typhoon after crossing International Date Line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:25:05 UTC
18:25:05 KST

Merve Berker
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Nolo, which has been active for nearly three weeks, has changed from a hurricane to a typhoon after crossing the International Date Line in the Pacific Ocean, media reports said Sunday.
Nolo was a Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph (185 kph) Sunday morning Hawaii time before crossing the date line, according to NBC News.
By Monday morning Japan time, Typhoon Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 100 mph (161 kph) and was moving west at 19 mph (31 kph), according to the Japan Meteorological Agency.
"The good news is there's a large, vast ocean, so even though it is still going to be strong, it's not near any land," NBC quoted John Cangialosi, a senior hurricane specialist with the US National Hurricane Center, as saying.
Nolo is forecast to continue moving west while gradually weakening.
The storm skirted Hawaii as a hurricane a week ago before weakening into a tropical storm and regaining hurricane strength Friday.
Tropical cyclones with winds exceeding 74 mph are called hurricanes in the northern Atlantic and central and eastern Pacific, but are known as typhoons in the North Pacific.

2026-10-05

18:24:55 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Istanbul Airport remained Europe’s busiest airport, averaging 1,587 daily flights during Sept. 21-27, according to the European Organization for the Safety of Air Navigation (EUROCONTROL).
The organization’s latest European Aviation Overview showed Istanbul Airport leading the region in combined arrivals and departures.
Amsterdam Schiphol followed with 1,423 daily flights, ahead of Paris Charles de Gaulle with 1,384, Frankfurt with 1,359 and London Heathrow with 1,324.
Istanbul Airport’s traffic declined 1% from the previous week due to weaker domestic activity, while remaining broadly unchanged from the corresponding period of 2025.
Türkiye’s Transport and Infrastructure Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu highlighted the ranking in a social media post Monday, saying Istanbul Airport continued to maintain its leading position in Europe.
He said Türkiye was continuing to strengthen the infrastructure that positions Istanbul as one of the world’s key air transport hubs.
The report also ranked Istanbul Airport seventh globally by average daily departures, while Amsterdam placed 10th.
Across the European network, daily flights averaged 35,279 during the reporting period, down 1.1% from the previous week but up 2.9% year-on-year.

Student protests continue across France as up to 500 high schools close
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:23:59 UTC
18:23:59 KST

Melike Pala
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Student protests continued across France on Monday, with classes fully or partially suspended at between 400 and 500 high schools amid demonstrations over education conditions and a rise in related incidents, according to broadcaster BFMTV.
The figure represents roughly 10% to 13% of France’s 3,700 high schools, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said, citing safety concerns at the affected institutions.
The protests, which began in the Paris region in mid-September, intensified last week as students demanded more resources, better-maintained school buildings, smaller classes and measures to address staff shortages.
In the Ile-de-France region surrounding Paris, more than 160 high schools were expected to be closed Monday, according to regional authorities.
The mobilization was accompanied by several incidents in Paris.
At Vauquelin High School in the capital, authorities reported three fires near the entrance Monday morning.
The school’s headteacher alerted police after the first fire was reported at around 7.50 am local time (0550GMT), prompting firefighters to intervene and students and staff to be confined inside the building.
Around 100 students were reportedly evacuated from the school following the incident.
Meanwhile, students began blocking Turgot High School in Paris early Monday, using bins, fences and signs to obstruct access.
The Interior Ministry and Education Ministry have reported a significant rise in arrests and injuries since the mobilization began.
Authorities said around 5,000 people had been arrested since the start of the movement, about 85% of them minors in the Ile-de-France region.
Twenty-four schools have been “burned or ransacked,” while 78 Education Ministry staff members and around 600 police officers and gendarmes have been injured, according to the education minister.
The minister also said 170 students had been injured since the protests began.
Five investigations have been opened by France’s General Inspectorate of the National Police into incidents linked to the mobilization.
Prime Minister Francois Bayrou is seeking to ease the crisis by putting forward five proposals and has called for decisions to be reached before the end of October.

The agency said the epidemiological situation in Irkutsk and the nearby city of Shelekhov remained stable.
Local media and Telegram channels on Friday claimed that the 28-year-old woman had died of plague following an alleged laboratory accident in Shelekhov.

Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said an emergency regional sanitary commission had met after reports of a suspected “highly dangerous infectious” disease case. He said all identified contacts had been placed under medical observation, with no symptoms reported and laboratory tests returning “negative.”

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Monday that India and Switzerland would work together for global peace and stability amid the US-Iran and Ukraine wars.
The remarks came as Modi hosted Swiss President Guy Parmelin, who is on an official visit to the South Asian nation.
Modi and Parmelin held “wide-ranging discussions” in New Delhi hours after the Swiss president arrived in India, Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal wrote on US social media platform X.
Noting that India and Switzerland believe in “democratic values, rule of law, dialogue and diplomacy,” Modi said: “We will work together for global peace and stability.”
Modi said whether it is Ukraine or the Middle East, India “continues to support every effort towards peace.”
“We also agree that reforms in global institutions are necessary to address the increasing global challenges,” he said.
The Indian prime minister also said the two countries would “develop trusted supply chains and reliable solutions for the entire world.”
“Today we recognized the new possibilities of cooperation in military exchange and defense production. We also agreed to promote cooperation in nuclear energy,” he said.
The Indian Ministry of External Affairs said key outcomes from Monday’s talks included new agreements on “transport, mobility and infrastructure, migration and mobility, and young professionals, alongside new joint research in health, clean energy and space.”
India, which established relations with Switzerland in 1948, recorded bilateral trade of approximately $23.35 billion in 2024-25.

13th-century Christ mural in Ghent’s St Nicholas Church to undergo extensive restoration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:21:51 UTC
18:21:51 KST

A 13th-century mural of Christ in the St Nicholas Church in Ghent is undergoing a thorough restoration. The painting depicts Christ on a throne, surrounded by kneeling figures. The work was discovered by chance in the late 1990s, by which time it was already in a poor state of repair.
13th-century Christ mural in Ghent’s St Nicholas Church to undergo extensive restoration
The mural came to light in 1998 when the Baroque altar of the Chapel of the Sweet Name of Jesus in the lower church was dismantled. Christ suddenly appeared on a throne, surrounded by kneeling figures. The mural was in a pitiful state.
“The condition of the mural was a cause for concern,” city authorities say. “The underlying layers of plaster were crumbling and showed cracks. That is why, immediately after its discovery, the work was given a protective layer of Japanese paper.”
Some of the Japanese paper has already been removed for preliminary investigations. The restorers will remove all the paper in the spring. In doing so, there is a chance that further parts of the work will come to light. The actual restoration is scheduled for the spring of 2027.
Organ restoration too
Bressers Architecten is overseeing the restoration of the mural in the St Nicholas Church. Further restoration work in the church in the centre of city is planned over the coming years. The 19th-century organ, built by the French organ builder Aristide Cavaillé-Coll, is also due for a refurbishment.
The instrument dates from the 19th century and has not been played for 60 years. The Flemish Government has earmarked around 1.94 million euros for the restoration work, alongside restoration work at St James’s Church in Ghent.

Kyiv • UNN
Drone operators of the 423rd Separate Regiment "Scythian Griffins" gathered the first autumn "harvest".
September proved "fruitful" for the soldiers of the 423rd Separate UAS Regiment "Scythian Griffins." The total number of targets hit increased by 12% and reached 1,318 verified enemy targets, the regiment’s press service reports , writes UNN.
In particular, September saw a notable increase in the number of enemy personnel hit (+30), artillery systems (+30%), energy facilities (+40%), telecommunications equipment (+34%), and ammunition and fuel depots (+40%). In total, during the past month, the regiment’s soldiers hit: 307 enemy personnel, 480 shelters and fortifications, 252 heavy vehicles, 12 artillery systems, 2 tanks, and 53 fixed-wing and copter-type UAVs. The destroyed targets also began to include the first enemy UGVs, which had not previously been actively used in the Zaporizhzhia area.
Every year, the same pattern is observed in our area of operations—the enemy becomes more active before winter arrives and tries to take advantage of worsening weather conditions to conduct mechanized assaults. The number of targets destroyed from September through November always increases noticeably, and this year the history will repeat itself. For the terror against the civilian population and civilian infrastructure in our rear, we will give the enemy a truly hellish autumn in the Dnipro steppes

Yemeni government forces seize district by Bab el-Mandeb, military sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:18:58 UTC
18:18:58 KST

Yemeni government forces seize district by Bab el-Mandeb, military sources say
RIYADH, Oct 5 - Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces seized key positions on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Monday, military and government sources said, as they fought to reverse last month's advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and drive them from the vital waterway.
The government forces have taken large parts of Dhubab district, which overlooks Bab el-Mandeb, and are asserting full control over the area with heavy air support from a Saudi-led coalition, three military sources and one government source told Reuters.
Houthi-aligned media had earlier denied that government forces had made advances in the area.
Fighting has raged along several frontlines in Yemen for weeks after a dormant civil war erupted in a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, with the Houthis seeking to control the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait and firing missiles and drones at Saudi cities and infrastructure.
With Gulf energy exports already restricted by Iran's closure of the Hormuz Strait, the fighting in Yemen has threatened another major oil export route, pushing up global prices and raising new risks in a region already aflame.
The internationally recognised Yemeni government announced on Sunday the launch of its offensive to recapture territory, with President Rashad al-Alimi swearing to fight "until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia".
SAUDI ARABIA BACKS OFFENSIVE TO RETAKE TERRITORY
Saudi Arabia, which arms and trains Yemeni government forces, is backing the military campaign with air power and has sought logistical help from allies to push back the Houthis, restore free traffic in the Red Sea, and end the group's attacks on its territory.
While the war has raged on several frontlines in Yemen, the heaviest fighting has been in the southwest, both in the coastal area near the strait and in the hills around the city of Taiz, where the Houthis are trying to surround government forces.
A Houthi-run news agency on Monday cited a military source as saying that the group had driven government forces from the al-Mawasit district of Taiz province, reaching the home of Alimi, head of Yemen's interim presidential council.
The mountainous district sits close to the main road running from Taiz to Aden, the last route that government forces have had into the city, which has been on the frontlines since early in the civil war.
Yemen's conflict began after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in the following year with an air campaign aimed at restoring the government and ousting the Iran-backed group.
The fighting quickly ground to a bloody stalemate, with most frontlines stalled, leading to a major humanitarian crisis in what was already the poorest Arab state, until a ceasefire was agreed in 2022 that held until this summer. REUTERS

US withdraws all bomber aircraft from UK airbase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:15:39 UTC
18:15:39 KST

A U.S. Air Force B-1 Lancer bomber is pictured on the tarmac at RAF Fairford base in Fairford, south-west England on September 27, 2026. (AFP File Photo)
The United States confirmed on Oct. 4 that it has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from the British airbase of RAF Fairford, with officials telling U.S. media that the move was linked to “new threats.”
Police were called to the base in southwest England on Sept. 27 after a local farmer reported a group of men with several vans engaged in “suspicious” activity.
The scare prompted a counter-terrorism probe and forced evacuations at 85 homes near the airbase, which was used by the United States to launch strikes on Iran.
Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but “a quantity of petrol was recovered,” according to counter-terrorism police.
A statement from a Pentagon official on Oct. 4 said “we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States.”
The statement noted that “operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time.”
An unidentified U.S. official told CNN that the bombers were moved after “an unspecified new threat,” with the source calling the latest threat a “real world incident.”
Speculation about the motives behind the incident ranged from terror threat to fuel thievery, as energy prices in the U.K. hit record highs this week.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, a charge rejected by Tehran.

Kyiv Rolls Out 12+ .50-Cal Turrets to Hunt Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:15:25 UTC
18:15:25 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Kyiv Rolls Out 12+ .50-Cal Turrets to Hunt Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones
Ukraine has deployed more than 12 automated gun turrets in Kyiv to counter Russian jet-powered drones, with another eight systems set to be installed across the Kyiv region as Russia increasingly uses faster UAVs in attacks on the country.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the deployment on October 4 during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
“We have started installing turrets. More than 12 have already been installed in the capital, and now another eight ‘fifties’ will additionally be installed in the Kyiv region,” Zelenskyy said. The systems are automated combat modules designed for .50-caliber machine guns.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine is developing a combined approach to air defense as Russia adjusts its strike tactics and increases the use of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles alongside conventional Shahed-type UAVs.
According to the Ukrainian president, Ukrainian forces currently intercept approximately 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed-type drones. The interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is lower, at roughly 50% to 70%.
Aircraft are also being used against the faster drones, including Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets, Zelenskyy said. Ukraine is currently working to secure additional weapons suitable for those interception missions.
Jet-powered drones pose a different challenge from propeller-driven Shahed-type UAVs because of their higher speed, reducing the time available for detection, tracking, and engagement.
The announcement came during Merz’s visit to Kyiv on October 4. During the visit, Germany also announced a new support package for Ukraine worth more than €1.3 billion, including funding for weapons and energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

Russia Builds Giant Hangars Near Moscow. Here’s What They Could Hide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:15:16 UTC
18:15:16 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Builds Giant Hangars Near Moscow. Here’s What They Could Hide
Russia is nearing completion of several large aircraft hangars at the Ramenskoye airfield near Moscow, with their dimensions and location suggesting they could support testing, maintenance, or modernization of Russia’s Tu-160, Tu-95, and Tu-22M3 strategic bombers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
New satellite imagery published by the AviVector analytical group on October 4 shows significant progress on several large aircraft hangars under construction at the Ramenskoye airfield near Moscow. The structures were first identified under construction in March 2026.
The largest building measures approximately 100 by 230 meters (328 by 755 feet) and stands about 33 meters (108 feet) high. It is divided into three hangar sections, each roughly 77 meters (253 feet) wide. An adjoining structure measures about 17 by 220 meters (56 by 722 feet), while a second major building covers approximately 90 by 220 meters (295 by 722 feet).
The scale of the main structure exceeds what would normally be required simply to shelter aircraft. Each of its three sections is around 21 meters (69 feet) wider than the maximum wingspan of a Tu-160, Russia’s largest operational bomber, while the building’s depth exceeds the aircraft’s length by roughly 46 meters (151 feet).
The 33-meter height is also about 2.5 times the height of the Tu-160, potentially providing sufficient space for cranes, elevated work platforms, and other equipment used during aircraft maintenance, testing, or modernization.
The construction site is connected by road to the Gromov Flight Research Institute, although satellite imagery currently shows no direct taxiway linking the new buildings to the airfield’s runway.
The imagery also shows lighter metal-framed hangars nearby. Unlike reinforced aircraft shelters, these structures would provide little protection against potential drone or missile strikes.
Ramenskoye, located in Zhukovsky in the Moscow region, is part of the Gromov Flight Research Institute’s aviation testing complex and hosts experimental, state, and civilian aviation operations. Zhukovsky International Airport, which opened in 2016, operates from the same airfield.
The site is also used by Russian aircraft manufacturers for flight-testing programs. Sukhoi facilities at Zhukovsky have supported testing of the Su-57 fighter, while Yakovlev uses the complex for certification work involving the MC-21 airliner and the Russian-built version of the Superjet.
Tupolev also maintains testing and research facilities at the site. Its programs include experimental and upgraded versions of the Tu-160M, Tu-95MS, and Tu-22M3—the same bomber families that the dimensions of the new hangars could accommodate.
However, the buildings’ purpose has not been independently confirmed. Another possibility is that the construction is connected to the expansion of the permanent exhibition complex previously used for the MAKS International Aviation and Space Salon.
The MAKS exhibition grounds are located immediately next to the construction site. The complex covers more than 42 hectares, including over 40,000 square meters of indoor exhibition space and more than 45,000 square meters dedicated to outdoor aircraft displays.
The proximity of the new buildings to those facilities leaves both aviation testing and exhibition-related use as possible explanations for the construction. Satellite imagery alone does not establish the final purpose of the structures.
Earlier, Russian Tu-160, Tu-95MS, and Tu-22M3 strategic bombers were spotted at Ramenskoye alongside major new construction, with the activity assessed at the time as more likely linked to testing, modernization, and exhibition preparations than to a permanent bomber deployment.

18:14:36 KST

A Milan court on Monday rejected a
second petition against an order for the furnaces of the
troubled former ILVA steelworks in Taranto to be shut down by
the end of this month.
                                    
The government-appointed administrators of the plant and AdI
S.p.A., the company that owns it, had requested a suspension
pending a decision by the supreme the Court of Cassation on the
appeal against the closure of the facility's hot area.
                                    
The Cassation is set to hold a hearing on the case on October
20.
                                    
The original decision was made in July, when a Milan court
upheld a motion presented on health grounds by members of a
parents' association and a child with a rare genetic mutation
and said that activity at the hot area must stop within three
months unless all the asbestos on the site is removed and
measures to bring particulate emissions within safe limits are
taken.
                                    
The ruling ramped up existing uncertainty about the future of
the plant and implementation of a plan to decarbonize it and
make it electric, with fears thousands of jobs could be lost.
                                    
Italy's steel federation Federacciai said in August that its
board has tasked its president, Antonio Gozzi, to express an
interest in taking over the former ILVA steelworks with the
authorities on behalf of a consortium of Italian companies.
                                    
Premier Giorgia Meloni's government has not ruled out State
involvement.
                                    
Indian group Jindal, Czech group CE industries, and US-based
private investment group Flacks have also expressed interest in
buying the plant.
                                    
The Taranto factory, once Europe's biggest steelworks, has been
dogged by economic problems in recent years and linked to high
cancer rates in the Puglia port city.
                                    
ADI was put into State-controlled administration early in 2024
after ArcelorMittal's ownership of the group ended
acrimoniously.

German spy chief warns of violent conflict risk with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:14:27 UTC
18:14:27 KST

Ayhan Simsek
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Germany is in danger of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia, the head of the country’s foreign intelligence service warned Monday, saying Moscow now treats Berlin as a main adversary.
 
Martin Jaeger, president of the Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, told parliament’s intelligence committee that the confrontation with Russia has taken on a new and more dangerous quality.
 
“Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia. The attempted attack in Leipzig is only one example of that,” he said, referring to an attempted drone strike on a Ukrainian cargo plane in August.
 
“No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany,” Jaeger said. “We did not seek this confrontation. Russia is forcing it upon us and sees us as a main adversary, because we refuse to accept its revisionist, expansionist policies and its war of aggression against Ukraine.”
 
His remarks came a day after Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv and announced new measures to support Ukraine. Only hours before that trip, Russia’s Foreign Ministry had urged foreign diplomats and other visitors to stay clear of the Ukrainian capital, above all military sites and government buildings. Drone attacks on Kyiv continued during the visit.
 
Russia’s ‘shadow war’ against Germany
 
Jaeger told lawmakers that, according to the BND’s assessment, Germany has become a main obstacle to “Russian hegemonic power projection in Europe” and therefore a prime target for Russian operations.
 
He accused Moscow of stepping up increasingly aggressive covert activities by its services in and against Germany.
 
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us,” Jaeger said, referring to sabotage attempts and other hybrid attacks. “This undeclared war cannot be grasped in conventional military or legal categories. Germany has not declared a constitutional state of defense, and yet we are under attack.”
 
Jaeger said the intelligence services need new powers, and that a government draft law would strengthen the BND as Germany’s first line of defense.
 
“Russian intelligence agencies operate with a high degree of professionalism and ruthlessness,” he said. “The threat of attacks against targets in Germany remains real and present. We must counter this. That also requires a fundamental change in the Federal Intelligence Service.”
 
Russia has not issued an immediate statement in response to the BND chief’s warnings. Moscow has in the past dismissed allegations of hybrid attacks in Europe as baseless, accusing Western governments of using such claims to justify higher military spending and sustain support for Ukraine.

South Korea says North deliberately planted mines in demilitarized zone that wounded 3 soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:12:18 UTC
18:12:18 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
South Korea said Monday that North Korea had "deliberately planted" two mines inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that exploded last month and wounded three South Korean soldiers, reiterating its demand for an apology from Pyongyang.
Pyongyang has denied involvement in the Sept. 21 incident and slammed Seoul over what it called “cheap tricks,” urging South Korea to stop attempts to “tarnish the image” of North Korea.
“The military strongly calls on North Korea to offer a sincere apology to the South Korean soldiers injured in the mine blast and immediately remove the mines it planted in violation of the armistice agreement,” Lt. Gen. Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of the South Korean Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), told a news conference.
The Korean Peninsula has remained divided since the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty, leaving the two Koreas technically at war.
The JCS said a joint operation with the UN Command (UNC) successfully removed additional mines planted near the blast site.
It added that the mines involved in the explosion “contained TNT and thermosetting resin components consistent with North Korean mines” and that fragments “recovered from the injured soldiers have also been found to be identical to North Korean plastic antipersonnel mines previously recovered from the Imjin River.”
The JCS said the mines were discovered about 10 meters (33 feet) south of the Military Demarcation Line, suggesting they had been “planted” there rather than swept into the area, Yonhap News reported.
