Spain's prime minister has called early elections amid the housing crisis
Kyiv • UNN
Pedro Sánchez has called early elections in Spain for November 29 following protests over the housing crisis. Polls predict an advantage for the center-right.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced early elections for November 29 on Monday. The vote could mark the end of the last major socialist government in the EU and remove one of U.S. President Donald Trump’s leading European critics from the political forefront. Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Sánchez was prompted to call early elections by the housing crisis, which sparked nationwide protests after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in Madrid from the apartment where she had lived since 1956. On Friday, lawmakers rejected two bills intended to resolve the problem.
Sánchez’s standing had already been weakened by corruption scandals that undermined the position of his Socialist Party. This summer, the prime minister faced harsh criticism over the migration crisis in the enclave of Ceuta.
According to polls, Spaniards may elect a government led by the center-right People’s Party, which is currently supported by 34% of voters, compared with 26% for the Socialist Party. The People’s Party will likely be forced to form a coalition with the far-right Vox party, which, according to the publication, could win 18% of the vote.
In his address to the nation, Sánchez warned about the growing popularity of far-right forces.
You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you want to play in this era and what role Spain should play. You must decide whether to join the far-right wave, which leads to regression everywhere it comes to power, or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice and environmental responsibility
Over the past year, Sánchez has gained recognition on the international stage as one of the Western leaders who most strongly criticized U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over their policies regarding the conflicts in Gaza and Iran.

Spanish PM calls early election after housing crisis defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:10:48 UTC
18:10:48 KST

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez arrives to attend the EU Summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, on June 18, 2026. (AFP File Photo)
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Oct. 5 called a snap election for Nov. 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his minority government.
The defeat on Oct. 2 was just the latest political setback for the Socialist premier, one of the few European prime ministers from the left still in power.
“To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people,” Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was “to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament.”
Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Oct. 3 to demand affordable housing.
The government’s proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties in Spain’s parliament.
The defeat infuriated those protesting the country’s increasingly expensive housing market and underscored the difficulties his minority coalition government faces in passing legislation.
Spain has been operating under its 2023 budget, the last national spending plan passed by Sanchez’s government, for several years.
The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid flat where she had lived for decades.
Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up more than a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP) ahead of the Socialists.
Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the European Union.
Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent, according to real estate website Idealista.
Abascal’s eviction catalyzed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.
The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 percent, say housing campaigners.
The backlash led the new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.
The housing bills Sanchez’s leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts, on whose support the government relies, voted against them, arguing they were hastily drawn up and would make the housing crisis worse.
Sanchez defended his government’s record in his address, pointing out that under his leadership Spain’s economy has grown faster than those of its main European peers.
But after eight years in power, Sanchez is also under pressure from corruption scandals involving people close to him, including his wife and top figures in his Socialist Party.
While polls put the PP ahead, they suggest the party would fall short of an absolute majority in parliament and would need the support of far-right Vox to govern.

'New pace, new height': PM Modi-Parmelin talks put India-Switzerland ties on fast track
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:06:29 UTC
18:06:29 KST

File photo: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss President Guy Parmelin at Hyderabad House for bilateral talks, in New Delhi on Monday
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Swiss Confederation president Guy Parmelin held wide-ranging talks in New Delhi on Monday, with the two sides discussing ways to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, mobility, infrastructure, defence, nuclear energy and critical technologies.The talks came as India and Switzerland seek to build on the India-EFTA Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement (TEPA), which entered into force last October and is set to complete a year of implementation this week.Addressing a joint press statement after the talks, PM Modi said the relationship between India and Switzerland had gained fresh momentum and highlighted the two countries' cooperation in innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology.“India-Switzerland friendship is centuries-old... Innovation, infrastructure and advanced technology are strong pillars of our foundation today. With the Summit today, we are going to give a new pace and height to our partnership,” PM Modi said.
India eyes $100 billion investment under TEPA
PM Modi said TEPA was an ambitious blueprint for investment, innovation, jobs and shared prosperity and set out a target of attracting $100 billion in investment into India and creating 1 million direct jobs over the next 15 years.
“I am very happy to welcome the president of Switzerland to India. First of all, I would like to appreciate his commitment to India-Switzerland relations. With his personal support, last October we implemented a historic Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement between India and the European Free Trade Association, or EFTA, countries,” PM Modi said.
“This is India's first FTA with any economic bloc in Europe,” he added.The Prime Minister said India and Switzerland had also taken decisions to increase market access for Indian exports to Switzerland and facilitate investment between the two countries.He said the measures would support exports of Indian agricultural products, pharmaceuticals, textiles and engineering goods, while encouraging Swiss investment in sectors including biotechnology, life sciences, banking, insurance, food processing and sustainability.
Defence, nuclear energy and infrastructure on agenda
The talks also expanded beyond trade and investment, with PM Modi saying the two countries had identified new opportunities for military exchanges and defence production cooperation.“We also agreed to further deepen nuclear energy cooperation,” he said.PM Modi pointed to projects such as the Varanasi ropeway, Noida's Jewar airport and railway and tunnelling projects in mountainous regions as examples of India-Switzerland infrastructure cooperation.The two sides also signed an agreement covering transport, mobility and infrastructure, with PM Modi inviting Swiss infrastructure companies to increase investment in India and participate in capacity-building, design and manufacturing.People-to-people ties were another focus of the discussions. PM Modi said the Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement and Young Professionals Agreement signed during the visit would create new opportunities in Switzerland for Indian students, researchers, professionals and young people.
Parmelin calls visit a ‘stepping stone’
Parmelin, who is on a three-day State visit to India, described the trip as an opportunity to further strengthen the long-standing relationship between the two countries.He said India and Switzerland shared democratic values as well as trust and mutual respect, and described his visit as a “stepping stone” towards deepening their partnership.The Swiss president's visit is also significant for TEPA, which was signed in March 2024 after nearly 16 years of negotiations and came into force in October 2025. The EFTA countries — Switzerland, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway — have committed to investing $100 billion in India over 15 years under the agreement.Parmelin is scheduled to attend the second India-EFTA Prosperity Summit on October 7, marking the first anniversary of TEPA's implementation.
Swiss business delegation accompanies Parmelin
Parmelin arrived in New Delhi earlier on Monday and was accorded a ceremonial reception at Rashtrapati Bhavan before visiting Rajghat to pay tribute to Mahatma Gandhi. He was accompanied by a delegation of senior officials and business representatives.External affairs minister S Jaishankar also met Parmelin and said he appreciated the Swiss president's commitment to deepening the India-Switzerland partnership and building on the promise of TEPA.
According to the ministry of external aaffairs, Switzerland is India's largest trade and investment partner among the four EFTA countries.More than 330 Swiss companies currently operate in India across sectors including engineering, services, precision instruments, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, while Indian companies in Switzerland have a presence in areas including IT, pharmaceuticals and machinery.Parmelin will also meet President Droupadi Murmu, who is scheduled to host a banquet in his honour. The visit is his first State visit to India and his second trip to the country this year, after his participation in the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February.

Brent and WTI prices declined due to increased exports and the G7 decision to release oil from reserves. Geopolitical risks remain.
Oil prices fell on Monday, October 5, as rising oil exports from the Middle East and the release of oil reserves by G7 countries increased supply, offsetting concerns about further damage to oil infrastructure in the Persian Gulf as the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran drags on. UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Brent crude futures fell 72 cents, or 0.71%, to $101.59 per barrel at 06:34 GMT (09:34 Kyiv time), while the price of U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude stood at $90.05 per barrel, down $1.05, or 1.2%.
The price of Brent crude lost most of its gains last week, while WTI fell 1.6% after G7 countries agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel fuel and oil from emergency reserves and pledged to refrain from restricting energy exports under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump ruled out a U.S. ban on diesel exports following the G7 decision03.10.26, 14:37 • 8566 views
According to shipping data, as of Monday, this release will increase oil exports from the Middle East, which exceeded pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September despite attacks on vessels passing through the Strait of Hormuz.
ICE gasoil futures rose more than 2% to $1,390.25 per barrel on Monday.
Experts' opinion
"The G7 decision to use strategic reserves partially removes the immediate supply anxiety from the price, while the view is growing that Saudi Arabia's export volumes are returning to pre-war levels, even if those barrels are still being transported at higher costs and via less efficient routes," said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.
"This combination is enough to contain prices for now, even if the risks of further damage to energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf region have not disappeared," he noted.
The Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in response to 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen over the past 12 hours. There was no confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
On Sunday, the Saudi-backed and internationally recognized Yemeni government said it was launching a large-scale military campaign to retake all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis. Meanwhile, Aramco unexpectedly cut November oil prices for Asia to a six-year low.
Brent prices continue to remain above $100 per barrel amid persistent geopolitical tensions and an increase in attacks on commercial vessels in the Persian Gulf, according to a note from ING analysts.

Qatar partners with Euroclear to widen foreign access to government debt market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:05:03 UTC
18:05:03 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
Qatar’s central bank and Euroclear, a Brussels-based provider of securities settlement and custody services, announced Monday a collaboration to establish an international settlement link aimed at widening foreign investor access to the country’s domestic government debt market.
The initiative will allow international investors to access Qatari government bonds and sukuk, or Islamic bonds, through Euroclear’s infrastructure, while giving issuers access to a broader and more diversified pool of capital.
The collaboration is expected to boost liquidity, improve market efficiency and deepen international capital flows into Qatar. It aligns with the country’s Third Financial Sector Strategy and Third National Development Strategy for 2024-2030.
The link will cover eligible Qatari riyal-denominated conventional government bonds and sukuk.
Euroclear Bank will act as the issuer central securities depository, while Edaa, Qatar’s central securities depository, will serve as the investor depository for local investors. Qatar Central Bank will act as issuer and paying agent.
Euroclear Chief Executive Valerie Urbain said the collaboration would “simplify market access, enhance liquidity and strengthen Qatar’s appeal to global investors.”

Ministry of Defence Sanctuary Awards
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:04:41 BST
18:04:41 KST

Ministry of Defence Sanctuary Awards
The annual Sanctuary Awards recognise outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the Ministry of Defence (MOD) estate.
The Sanctuary Awards have been recognising outstanding conservation and sustainability efforts across the MOD estate since 1991.
The awards celebrate and encourage group and individual efforts that benefit sustainable development, environmental and heritage conservation, utilities and resource-saving measures, sustainable construction and procurement or community awareness on land or property that the MOD owns or uses in the UK and overseas.
35th Sanctuary Awards 2026: Shortlisted entries
Winners will be announced on 17 November 2026. You can sign up for the free Sanctuary Awards 2026 live feed online.
Many congratulations to the 14 projects that have been shortlisted for the 35th Sanctuary Awards 2026:
- 507 Specialist Team Royal Engineers – A1 Steam trust, Darlington Railhead Construction Project (A1 Steam Locomotive Trust, Darlington)
- AA Wick Marsh Ranges (AA (Wick Marsh) Ranges, Fingringhoe, Colchester)
- Aldershot’s Training Area – sustaining military capability (Aldershot Military Fieldcraft Training Areas)
- Barton Stacey Flyfishing Club (Barton Stacey Training Area)
- Beckingham Cadet Training Centre – sustainable construction (Army HQ, Andover)
- Devonport Open Days (HMNB Devonport)
- Group Captain Maurice Dixon (RAF Leeming and RAF High Wycombe)
- Sq Ldr Don Earl (RAF High Wycombe)
- Exercise Druid Sacrifice (RAF Valley)
- Find it in Plymouth – supply chain resilience at Devonport (HMNB Devonport)
- FuelActive – cleaner fuel for Team Leidos’ fleet (Defence Fulfilment Centre, DM Beith, MOD Bicester, JHC FS Aldergrove, MOD Kineton, MOD Longtown, DM Gosport, HMNB Portsmouth)
- Lydd Ranges Sea Defence Project (Lydd Ranges)
- Project Life (National Armaments Director Group Bicester)
- SPINNERET – microgrids for operational energy (MOD Bovington Camp)
Nominations were sought in the following categories:
- Climate Change Resilience Award – projects or activities focused on taking action to enhance climate resilience through adaption.
- Energy Award – for energy of fuel projects that decrease energy demand, increase energy efficiency and/or increase energy resilience through sustainability.
- Environmental Enhancement Award – projects focused on wildlife, biodiversity, environmental research, or tackling pollution or contamination issues.
- Heritage Award – projects focused on archaeology, historic buildings, historic parks or gardens, landscape preservation, museum collections, or heritage education or public engagement.
- Individual Achievement Award – any individual who has made a significant personal contribution to MOD’s sustainability or conservation ambitions.
- Social Impact Award – grass-roots sustainability projects focusing on community engagement, green spaces, wellbeing or facilitating public access.
- Sustainability Improvement Award – for projects that demonstrate sustainability improvements through implementation of circular economy principles (including reducing resource consumption or waste and recycling), sustainable procurement, sustainable construction or refurbishment projects, and improvements in equipment or systems through eco design.
The Operational Capability Award will be chosen from the shortlisted nominations and awarded to the project which best delivers enhanced operational capability through sustainability and climate considerations.
And the Silver Otter Trophy will be chosen from the category winners and awarded to the best Establishment, Conservation Group or community led project or individual conservation effort on the MOD estate.
For queries please email: DIO-Sanctuary@mod.gov.uk

Wahab, however, is not taking this for granted, having won her latest race by a small margin after a series of attack ads funded by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee helped narrow her previous double-digit lead.

Swiss government backs VAT increase to fund 13th pension

Swiss government backs VAT increase to fund 13th pension
The Swiss government has supported an increase in Value-Added Tax (VAT) to pay for the 13th payment of the Swiss old-age and survivors' (AHV/AVS) pension.
On Monday, the government advocated a rise of 0.4 percentage points, from 8.1% to 8.5%, ahead of the referendum on November 29. A double majority will be required for the vote.
To fund the 13th AHV/AVS pension, which will be paid from December 1, CHF4.2 billion ($5.06 billion) will be required in 2026. This figure is expected to rise to around CHF4.5 billion in 2030 and CHF5.4 billion in 2040.
Parliament has opted for funding solely through VAT, rejecting a parallel 0.2-point increase in employees’ contributions. The 0.4-point rise in VAT will generate CHF1.5 billion per year.
+ Swiss Senate backs mixed financing for 13th pension
The reduced rate will remain at 2.6%. The VAT increase for the accommodation sector will be 0.2 percentage points, rising from 3.8% to 4%.
This change will not be sufficient in the long term. In its AHV2030 reform proposal, the government has included a scenario for additional funding for the 13th pension. Both the left and the right have voiced criticism.

Staples Print and Marketing Services Review: Fast Holiday Gifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

I print all the time, and not just because I test printers, but because I like paper. It doesn't matter if they're documents, photos, posters, or banners; I like artifacts—everything is better in physical form. And it's not just dinosaurs like me; while eschewing digital media, Gen Z is embracing printed matter, too (see, the kids are alright).
I've lost track of how many photo books I've printed over the years—mostly one-offs of little projects, fun things for friends, and maybe five copies at most. I'm not a photographer anymore, but old habits die hard, especially when you see the way people react to paper books. The response to a book, versus showing someone your latest Instagram post, is not even comparable.
With the holiday season kicking off, it seems apropos to point out that photo books make great gifts, as do mugs, prints, and my personal favorite for kids: photo puzzles. I've tested dozens of printing services over the years, and one of my favorites for holiday gifts is Staples.
You can order Staples prints online through the company's website, which features a variety of tools to help you design your photo gift, be it a mug, print, or puzzle. The print quality is great, and the online tools are well done and easy to use. But while ordering online is convenient, it's not why I like Staples for printing. It's because I can go to my local store and talk to actual human beings about my printing needs.
Printing can be tricky, and preparing your digital files exactly how the printer wants them isn't always easy. Best practice is to provide a high-res, flattened PDF file in CMYK color, but if you don't know what that means or how to get your file into the right format, fear not. The best way to print, even if you do know how to format it accurately, is to bring the file to your local Staples and talk to the print and marketing specialists there. They can catch potential issues before you print, and in most cases they can print a proof (sometimes at a reduced size, but still a proof) so you can see what you're getting beforehand. This is one advantage over online-only services.
Another big advantage is that you can get your gifts the same day if you pick up in-store. If you're in a rush this holiday season, remember that tip. You can even order online and pick up in-store to save yourself a trip.
Want to really step up your game? Here's my pro tip. Head to your local Staples to place your order, but have them print it at a Staples production center. Tell the store to have the production center send proofs for you to approve in person. This eliminates the same-day advantage, as it will likely take several days—sometimes as much as two weeks—but the printing quality will be better.
What's the quality like? I printed a couple of 11-ounce mugs—other options include a 15-ounce mug and a 17-ounce travel mug—and the results were on par with other services I've tested. I happen to like the shape of the Staples mugs a little more than what I got from others, but that's more personal preference than anything. For the design, you can choose a premade template and upload a photo of your choice, or you can start from scratch and design your own mug. As with all Staples printing services, you can choose same-day pickup if you want five or fewer. For larger orders, you'll need to get them delivered.
The photo options, like mounted prints, are nice. The print quality here lags behind dedicated photo services like our top picks, Mpix and Printique, but for the price it's quite good (both Mpix and Printique are more expensive). They offer canvas prints, metal prints, foam-backed prints, and posters up to 36 by 48 inches.
Staples is also a great place for business printing. I'm in the process of transitioning back to running a business, and the first thing I did wasn't setting up an Instagram account or doing anything with social media. The first thing I did was print business cards. Staples online business card maker is fantastic. And if I had a physical presence for my business, I'd have printed banners and posters and signs and everything else. Because we live in the real world, and if you want your business to succeed offline, you're going to need to print.

No plane, no gain: US aviation sanctions ground ordinary Iranians while missing the regime
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

No plane, no gain: US aviation sanctions ground ordinary Iranians while missing the regime
Borzou Daragahi for The Straits Times
- The US sanctions on Iran's aviation sector have severely restricted travel and commerce, causing cancellations and complicating access to medicines and essential goods.
- These sanctions mainly hurt ordinary Iranians, increasing economic hardship with soaring inflation, job scarcity, and disrupted education and migration plans.
- Experts doubt sanctions will force regime change, warning they may strengthen Iran's leadership while lacking a clear, cohesive US strategy.
AI generated
ISTANBUL – Hossein-Reza’s plans to leave Iran for a trip to see friends and family in the Netherlands in October were waylaid by the US’ imposition of sanctions on the country’s aviation sector in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast – Washington’s attempt to isolate Iran economically.
Would he be able to secure a ticket to Amsterdam, he wondered? Would he be forced to travel by road to neighbouring Turkey or Armenia?
While some respond to such uncertainty with anxiety or even dread, Hossein-Reza, a 40-something documentarist, was relaxed.
After a year in Iran that included chaos and gunfire in the streets, warfare in the skies, internet blockages and economic devastation, as well as questions about the country’s very future, he is taking the travel hiccup in his stride.
“I never even try to book a ticket until a day or two before I have to leave,” he said in an interview, on the condition that his full name not be published.
The Iranians who spoke to the press did so under heavy risk, withholding their full names for fear of official reprisals for communicating with foreign journalists.
The US has placed some of the toughest financial restrictions on Iran ever imposed on an adversary – and the sanctions continue to intensify as the conflict drags on.
The pressure campaign has gone far beyond travel bans on targeted individuals or sanctions on the weapons trade or dual-use goods to include, since September, punishments of third-country companies that do business with 27 airlines and companies in Iran’s civilian airline sector and restrictions on the country’s auto and rail industries.
The result has complicated the supply of some crucial medicines into the country as well as any travel and commerce. Flights to a number of neighbouring countries – including Iraq, Azerbaijan and Oman – have been cancelled.
However, air travel to Russia and China has not been affected, and sporadic flights to the major air hubs of Istanbul and Dubai continue.
A video posted on social media platform X on Sept 24 showed a flight crew aboard an Iranian Varesh Airlines flight from Tehran to the Tajikistan capital of Dushanbe returning home after its route through Azerbaijani airspace was denied.
The severe sanctions on aviation add to what many describe as growing despair and malaise among many ordinary Iranians.
“Iranians will be resilient as long as there is hope,” said one Western diplomat who recently left Tehran, speaking on condition of anonymity as he was not authorised to speak to the media. “But if there’s no light at the end of the tunnel, there is less reason to stay steadfast.”
Hamidreza Ahmadi, a Tehran tech entrepreneur, described growing frustration among ordinary Iranians as they struggle to understand the uncertainties the conflict has thrust upon their lives.
He described frustration over contradictory statements and goals by US President Donald Trump – from regime change, to a peace deal, to halting a nuclear programme supposedly destroyed in 2025, to reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which was already open before the war began.
“Geopolitically, everyone’s very, very confused,” he said. “Like, what do you mean America’s almost out of munitions? How could that be? They see Iran is getting weaker. They feel that. But they also see a bunch of Iranian missiles and a bunch of drones landing.”
Iranians describe difficulties in securing jobs, with youth unemployment rates estimated to be as high as 50%, a freezing of investment and business expansions, as well as price increases, including for subsidised fuel and petroleum products that are the lifeblood of the Iranian economy. Prices for some drugs have tripled, according to local reports, while food prices have soared.
Iran’s year-on-year inflation reached 84% in August.
“Sanctions are something that, wherever you are on the political spectrum, affect you on a daily basis, and nobody can see a way out of it,” Ahmadi said in an interview.
In theory, sanctions are supposed to punish the regime rather than ordinary people. But compliance experts say companies effectively refrain from doing even non-restricted commerce with entities linked to a country as heavily sanctioned as Iran.
Brett Erickson, founder of Obsidian Risk Advisors, a US consultancy focused on international crime and due diligence, told The Straits Times: “Most companies are going to de-risk and just not assume the legal hurdles that need to be jumped through.
“And that’s something we see with Gaza and Yemen and so many countries where technically, it is allowed. But in reality, we see huge shortfalls as a result of companies not wanting to assume the risk.”
Pharmaceuticals and foods are specifically excluded from sanctions, but companies often refrain just to avoid the hassles and hurdles of any trade with Iran.
Trump administration officials and their supporters know that the sanctions hurt ordinary Iranians. But this is precisely the goal – raise public frustrations to a level where the people turn on the regime. Beyond sanctions, the US has very few options, experts said.
“The problem with sanctions is we’ve plucked all the low-hanging fruit,” Alan Eyre, a former US State Department official who was part of the team that negotiated the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran, said in an interview.
“We’ve plucked all the high-hanging fruit. We’ve cut the tree down. So it’s not as if there are a lot of super-duper effective sanctions that we haven’t used.”
The latest round of sanctions significantly differs from previous rounds because they focus on an entire sector of the economy, regardless of whether an individual or company is involved in any activity deemed harmful by the US.
Erickson said: “It essentially just cuts off the entire industry, regardless of whether it has a nexus to someone who is sanctioned by the US.
“It is a very significant measure. And again, it does need to be understood that the overwhelming hardship will be shouldered by the civilian population. Obviously, things can be transshipped into Russia and China and other countries that refuse to play ball, and that will be significant for the Iranian government.”
Observers are closely watching how aggressively Washington attempts to enforce sanctions on third countries such as Turkey or the United Arab Emirates, as well as China, which has vowed to ignore them. But the sanctions may be the most severe that Iranians have faced, and potentially the hardest to circumvent.
Ali Ahmadi (no relation to Hamidreza Ahmadi), a fellow at the Switzerland-based Geneva Centre for Security Policy who regularly travels between Iran and the West, said: “They figure out how to operate within the parameters of the sanctions.”
Ali Ahmadi was recently in Tehran and booked a flight on an obscure airline, which was cancelled at the last minute, but he managed to rebook on a different airline. “When I called the website I was buying the tickets from, they said, pick one of the more reputable, bigger names because they already know how to get through the sanctions,” he recalled.
Others have found the new restrictions more challenging.
Maziar, a 42-year-old in Tehran, is struggling to bring his frail 86-year-old father home from a trip to visit relatives in California.
“I’ve been trying to figure out the least exhausting path for my dad to get back to Iran,” he said, asking that his family name not be disclosed.
“We were hoping to use the Dubai route. But that’s no longer an option. We’re going to wait it out a bit longer and hope for a better option, and if the situation doesn’t change, we’ll have to use the land border crossing via Turkey.”
Even Iranians sympathetic to the US are angered by the latest US sanctions.
One impact of the latest round of restrictions has been the cancellation of the English-language proficiency tests required for overseas employment or education because the companies running the paid exams fear the wrath of the US Treasury Department.
Iranians who spent years on plans to study or move abroad have suddenly found their dreams thwarted. “On paper, sanctions are supposed to make the government weaker, but how is cancelling tests making the government weaker?” said one Tehran resident, who asked that her name not be published.
Even as prices of food and medicine in Iran increase, there have been no reported shortages of luxury goods – another sign that the sanctions are mostly squeezing the poor.
Observers have criticised the US strategy as rudderless, aimed more at satisfying Washington hawks’ demands for action rather than part of a cohesive strategy.
Ahmadi from the Geneva Centre said: “Within the context of US policy as a whole, pressure for pressure’s sake has become ossified. Like you’ve got to do something. What’s the next measure? Do that. Istanbul Airport is probably kind of vulnerable to US sanctions. Okay, we’ll threaten to sanction them. There’s no strategy here.”
Iran experts, including former US officials, have publicly voiced doubt that ratcheting up economic pressure will convince the Iranian government to give in to US demands – in fact, it could have the opposite effect.
Eyre, the former State Department official, said: “The people running Iran think that if they just show any weakness in the face of all this pressure, it’s going to lead to them being swept out of power. That’s why sanctions are unlikely to work.”

France becomes Europe’s ‘weakest link’ under Macron’s leadership — news agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:59:26 UTC
17:59:26 KST

NEW YORK, October 5. /TASS/. Nearly 10 years of President Emmanuel Macron’s rule have turned France into Europe’s "weakest link," Bloomberg reported.
Macron came to power in 2017 as a business-oriented politician who sought to bring about an "economic and political revolution" in France. However, the president’s political movement will "be effectively over" after he leaves office in 2027, and the promised "revolution" never led to a change in France’s economic policy, in which government spending plays a significant role compared to other Western countries, the article noted.
"After a decade of political missteps and global cataclysms that made government spending his (Macron’s - TASS) go-to solution, popular anger is rising, growth is sinking, debt is soaring and investors are dumping French assets in a global bond market rout that has made it the euro area’s weakest economic link," William Horobin, the article’s author, pointed out.
According to him, the final battle to preserve the legacy of "Macronomics" will be the passage of next year’s French budget in parliament. Even if the minority government puts together a credible budget proposal, Macron’s potential successors, opposition leaders Marine Le Pen Le Pen and Jean-Luc, who are leading in the polls, could roll back all of his reforms. "The messy end" to a decade in power contrasts with the proclaimed vision of making France "the powerhouse of a retooled Europe with the heft to stand for itself as [US President] Donald Trump undermines NATO from within," the author stressed. The conflict in Ukraine and the difficulty of balancing relations between the US and China only increase the likelihood that populist political forces will come to power in France, which "threatens to overtake what’s left of the post-World War II order," he argued.
According to Horobin, key moments of Macron’s presidency include the attempt to reform fossil fuel taxation in 2018, which led to mass protests by the Yellow Vest movement, a radical increase in government spending following the pandemic and energy crisis, costing the treasury approximately 262 billion euros, and the decision to call for early parliamentary elections in 2024. France’s public finances and Macron’s political capital have not recovered since then, the author emphasized.

Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:56:40 UTC
17:56:40 KST

Polymarket goes to court to overturn Dutch gambling ban
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
US prediction platform Polymarket has gone to court in The Hague to overturn a Dutch ban on its services, arguing that it sells financial products, rather than bets.
The company confirmed the case to the Financieele Dagblad. The judges will reportedly be asked to decide whether betting on real-world events counts as gambling, which the Dutch gambling regulator Ksa says that it is.
Polymarket argues that it is more like trading in derivatives, which should be supervised by financial markets regulator AFM.
Polymarket users buy contracts that pay out in USDC, a type of cryptocurrency whose value is equal to the US dollar, if a particular event does or does not happen. The company says this is comparable to futures contracts traded on financial markets.
Fines and bans
The Ksa ordered Polymarket to stop serving Dutch users in an order dated January 20 and made public on February 17. It said the platform was offering games of chance without a licence and threatened a penalty of €420,000 a week, up to a maximum of €840,000.
Polymarket stopped Dutch users from placing bets later in February, but the regulator ruled it had acted too late and in May demanded €420,000, and rejected the company’s objection in June.
The platform drew widespread attention in the Netherlands after users staked millions of dollars on the outcome of the October 2025 general election.
Only sport
According to the Ksa, Dutch law only allows betting on sport, so a licence would not be an option for Polymarket either.
“Prediction markets are on the rise, in the Netherlands too,” Ksa director Ella Seijsener said in a statement in February. “These types of companies offer bets which are not allowed on our market under any circumstances, not even by licence holders.”
Last week, MPs voted down a motion from the far-right Forum for Democracy (FvD) asking the government to look into regulating prediction markets as a separate category within gambling law.
Gambling lawyer Micha Schimmel told the FD he gives Polymarket’s case little chance. He pointed to a 2015 ruling which found that a service can be a financial product and still count as gambling. Polymarket is also banned in France and Germany.

VKG pushes back cellulose plant timeline as search for investors continues

VKG pushes back cellulose plant timeline as search for investors continues
The company has yet to find a way to build its bioproducts plant in Europe at a low enough cost to compete on the global market.
When VKG unveiled plans to build a cellulose plant in summer 2021, the company hoped to open the facility in Ida-Viru County five years later. Instead of opening the plant, however, the company is still searching for potential investors this year.
This year, VKG also relinquished a 10-year long-term contract with the State Forest Management Center (RMK) for the purchase of raw materials.
According to VKG CEO Ahti Asmann, the company is looking for ways to make the project more profitable.
"The situation with the bioproducts plant is complicated. We have indeed been in talks with investors and we have come to understand that using a conventional European approach and European prices may make it difficult to compete globally," Asmann said.
After the designated spatial plan was established in spring last year, the company's CEO hoped investors could be found within a year. Under current plans, the company aims to reach an investment decision by the first quarter of 2028. If it has not found an investor by then, the company will assess whether it makes sense to proceed with the planned plant in Lüganuse Municipality.
"We are currently looking for a way to structure the project so that it is competitive and so that the investment can be made at a more reasonable cost," Asmann said.
If the company finds an investor by 2028, the plant is currently expected to begin operations in 2030, four years later than originally planned.
The estimated cost of the plant has risen by 50 percent from the original estimate, from €800 million to €1.2 billion. VKG has invested €2 million in the project to date.
VKG plans to use low-value wood at the plant to produce cellulose, dissolving pulp and biochemicals, with end products used in the textile and biochemical industries, as well as in the paint, food and pharmaceutical industries.
As a byproduct, the bioproducts plant would generate 800 gigawatt-hours of electricity per year. That would amount to around 10 percent of Estonia's current annual electricity consumption.

UK Green Party votes to equate Zionism with racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:55:56 UTC
17:55:56 KST

On the 4th of October, the UK Green Party voted to classify Zionism as a form of racism, sparking condemnation from British Jews and anger from the Israeli government—which stated it now views the party as an organization that supports terrorism, reports Reuters.
The party, which garnered 6% of the vote in the 2024 parliamentary elections, stated that it regards Zionism as an ethno-nationalist political project and reiterated its call for the UK Labour government to end arms sales to Israel. Zionism is a religious-nationalist political movement advocating for the gathering of all Jews in their historical homeland, the re-establishment and strengthening of a Jewish state, Jewish immigration to Israel, and the displacement of Arabs from the region.
In its statement, the Green Party also noted that the proposal underscores the party's support for the right to self-determination and calls for the creation of a single democratic state within the territory of historic Palestine.
The definition of Zionism—which inspired the founding of the modern State of Israel and addresses the rights of other peoples within Israel and adjacent territories—is a subject of controversy. Jewish groups sometimes describe this as the right to self-determination.
Despite objections from several high-ranking representatives, the Green Party's proposal received majority support within the party:
 1,022 members voted in favor, while 813 voted against. Party leader Zack Polanski did not participate in the vote.
Several British Jewish groups have already condemned the vote. The Progressive Judaism movement stated that the Green Party has made antisemitism part of its policy and has become a racist party. The movement added that the fact that some Jews supported the proposal does not mean it will not be used against others.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar has decided to ban Polanski from entering Israel. The ministry stated that, according to the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's definition, the party's proposal constitutes antisemitic rhetoric because it denies Jews the right to self-determination.
On the 3rd of October, Green Party Deputy Leader Mohtin Ali—a supporter of the proposal—told Sky News that the main driving force behind it was the high number of Palestinian casualties in Israel's war against the terrorist group Hamas. He pointed out that the proposal clearly defines Zionism, describing it as an ethno-nationalist movement, ethnic cleansing, and genocide.
The British government regards the actions of Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank as ethnic cleansing,
 though it has noted that the question of whether Israel is committing genocide is a matter for the courts to decide. Israel—which denies both ethnic cleansing and the commission of genocide—called on other British political parties on the 4th of October to condemn the Green Party's vote, stating that the Green Party had adopted not only the color green from Hamas but also an ideology calling for the destruction of the State of Israel through armed struggle.
Polanski and other Green Party representatives said they would continue to speak out against the heinous crimes of Benjamin Netanyahu's government, emphasizing that there is no contradiction in supporting the rights of both Palestinians and Jews.

17:54:25 KST

Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
- Published
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, Sánchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".
Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for Sánchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.
"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," Sánchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
Sánchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
Sánchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
Sánchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".
The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It was later lowered to €1,650 - still €300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home, but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".
Sánchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife Begoña Gómez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by Sánchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.
In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.
And in June, Sánchez's former transport minister, José Luis Ábalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

‘Iran-linked terror plot’ behind US bomber evacuation – NYT
The US has rushed to withdraw bombers from an air base in the UK after receiving new threat information about an alleged terrorist plot against the facility, the New York Times reports, citing sources.
The announcement cited by the NYT comes a week after five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in what was trumped as a high-level security operation which hosts US bombers used in the war against Iran. However after an hysterical media reaction in the UK, the five, all British citizens in their early 20s, were released on bail the following day.
Days later, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham claimed that London had "strong indications" that Iran could have been behind the incident, which only came to life after a local farmer called the police, having seen a group of men run from their white vans on a country road when caught in the headlights of her car.
All 12 US Air Force B-1 bombers were withdrawn over the weekend, allegedly after commanders received new warnings concerning a possible Iranian-backed plot against the base, two anonymous US officials told the NYT on Sunday.
Some aircraft had reportedly only arrived the week before as part of a routine rotation. According to teh NYT's sources the withdrawal was deemed so urgent that several bombers took off without aerial refueling support. At least three bombers reached their home base in South Dakota by Sunday, the officials said.
According to one source, the information was connected to threat warnings that surfaced three weeks earlier, but new details received over the preceding 24 hours alarmed commanders and increased the urgency of withdrawing the bombers. The details were not disclosed.
The Pentagon’s European Command confirmed that the aircraft left England but declined to comment on any new warnings.
“We can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford are redeploying to their home stations in the United States,” the command said in a statement. “US Air Force bombers routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.”
The episode in September prompted media speculation about possible Iranian or Russian involvement or links to Islamist extremists.
The incident unfolded after a local resident reported three vans blocking a road after midnight and hooded men running from her car headlights. Police initially suspected the vans could contain explosives, but none were found, although gasoline was recovered.
The suspects, all London residents aged 23-25, were later detained on suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack. A sixth man, a dual British-Iranian national arrested in London on October 1 on the same suspicion, has also been released on bail.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there are “strong indications” that Iran played a part.
US President Donald Trump criticized the suspects’ release, saying the US and UK authorities knew about them and that they “were looking to do big damage to our fort.”
Iran has denied having any involvement. The embassy in London accused Britain of promoting “Iranophobia.” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi rejected Burnham’s allegation, saying he is “barking up the wrong tree.”

Ukraine faces US$8bn loss due to closure of ports

Unknown Publisher

11:53:00 EEST

Ukraine faces US$8bn loss due to closure of ports
Ukraine risks losing at least US$8 billion in export revenue from June 2026 to June 2027 if its Black Sea ports remain closed.
Source: The Financial Times, citing an estimate by Ukraine's Minister of Agrarian Policy Taras Vysotskyi
Details: According to Vysotskyi, such a shortfall would equal approximately 20% of Ukraine's total export revenue for the past year. This represents a forecast based on a prolonged port shutdown, rather than already recorded losses.
Ukraine had planned to export 64 million tonnes of agricultural products this year. However, without the resumption of maritime shipping, Vysotskyi estimates that at best only half of this volume will be successfully exported.
As the FT reports, Russian attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have effectively halted operations along the primary maritime export route. Road transport is significantly more expensive and cannot compensate for its loss.
Even a resumption of shipping would not mean a return to previous volumes. Shota Khajishvili, owner of the Risoil terminal in Chornomorsk, told the publication that following the attacks, the company could operate at only 30% capacity – loading two vessels simultaneously instead of five.
Background: The European Commission proposes to significantly restrict Ukraine's access to the EU agricultural market and agricultural subsidies even after accession.

Israel's mental health crisis in the wake of Oct. 7 attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Israel's mental health crisis in the wake of Oct. 7 attacks
October 5, 2026
Warning: This article contains references to death by suicide that some readers may find disturbing.
As October 7's third anniversary approaches, Ronen Shalev's body tells him something's coming.
"You start shivering," he tells DW. "It's not just one day and you move on. We have many graves to visit, many families to meet. It's a difficult time and you feel it in your body."
Both of his children attended the Nova Party in Israel's south, where almost 400 people were killed in a terrorist attack carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates in Gaza. In total, roughly 1,200 people were killed in the attack and around 250 were taken hostage.
The attack triggered the war in Gaza, during which Israel has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced much of the territory's population.
Shalev's son, Roee, was shot and hospitalized, but he survived. Roee's partner, Mapal Adam, was killed in front of his eyes. Shalev's daughter, Lior, also made it out.
Shortly after that day, Shalev's wife Gavriela went missing, before her body was found in a burned car with a goodbye letter. "She couldn't handle the sorrow from that day," Shalev says.
At the same time, his son Roee's post-traumatic symptoms started emerging, mostly in the form of extreme mood swings. "He went to treatment to please me, but he didn't really believe in it. He thought he was OK, that he was strong," Shalev remembers.
Two years after Gavriela's death, Roee couldn't take it anymore, either.
"I'm alive, but I'm dead within," Roee wrote in his goodbye message, which he posted on his Instagram account. "I'm sorry."
A country in post-traumatic state
Since October 2023, Israel has been grappling with a mental health crisis of unprecedented scale.
According to a report by Israel's State Comptroller from February 2025, some 39% of the Israeli public reported suffering from post-traumatic symptoms, depression, anxiety or a combination of the three, on a medium or severe level.
This amounts to some 3 million people, 600,000 of whom could suffer severely. However, the report also found that the number of people receiving mental health treatment had only risen by 1% since October 7, 2023, a difference of around 60,000 people.
Among the affected groups are survivors of the attack, as well as people evacuated from their homes in Israel's south and north due to the war.
Noga Dagan-Buzaglo is a researcher with the Adva Center, a think tank focusing on inequality in Israeli society. She wrote an extensive paper about Israel's mental health system and its challenges post-October 7.
She tells DW that while the country's mental health budget did increase due to the war, it was too little, too late, as the health system faced an ongoing crisis that was not handled properly.
"The biggest challenge is convincing people to work in Israel's public mental health system, both due to lower wages in comparison to the private sector and due to an overload of work," she says.
Sedatives often the go-to solution
The current situation affects mental health professionals, too. Research by the University of Haifa found that 84% of the therapists who treated people affected by the October 7 attack showed traumatic symptoms themselves, and some 45% of them said they feel mentally exhausted.
Israel's Health Ministry has repeatedly said it has increased funding and job openings for the country's public mental health system, but staffing shortages remain, especially in peripheral regions in the far north and south.
Because of these issues, the report said waiting times for treatment through Israel's public healthcare system were longer than six months. In some cases, Dagan-Buzaglo says, patients had to wait more than a year before receiving help.
Mental health NGOs and volunteers try to fill the gaps, often struggling themselves under the workload. This also leads to an increased use of prescription medications. Some people turn to substances like alcohol and drugs.
The Israeli Ministry of Health said earlier this year that it had registered a rise of between 13% and 17% in the prescription of sedatives, sleep aids and antidepressants.
Those who suffer from the situation the most are the ones who cannot afford to pay a private therapist. Dagan-Buzaglo labels the Israeli public health system's response to the situation as "simply bad."
Soldiers at risk
Combat soldiers have received a special focus when it comes to Israel's mental health crisis.
Statistics published by the Israeli parliament and the IDF suggest a sharp rise of suicide cases among reservists: from a maximum of one annual case in the six years preceding the war to 11 cases in 2024, as well as nine cases investigated as suspected suicides in 2025. This does not include ex-soldiers who committed suicide due to trauma after the end of their service.
Dagan-Buzaglo, a researcher at the Adva Center, says that while professionals receive better pay and conditions working for the army, the lack of personnel is still apparent. "In the army, too, the length and quality of treatment are by far not at an adequate level."
To start solving the problem for both civilians and soldiers, she believes the system needs more support. "We have to acknowledge the fact that trauma is not over after a year. This means investing money."
Breaking the taboo
Ronen Shalev holds regular lectures and talks about the importance of mental health, often to groups of soldiers. He believes this is the best way to continue his son's legacy of fighting to live on.
Shalev, who himself was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), says he made a choice to live his life to its fullest.
His message: The taboo regarding suicidality — which still exists across Israeli society — needs to be broken. "This is especially true regarding those who say they are strong. They're the scary ones as they're less likely to receive treatment."
For Shalev, speaking publicly about his family's experience has become part of his own recovery — and a way to encourage others to seek help before they reach a crisis point.
"Life, with all its pain, is still worth deciding in favor of," he said.
If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://befrienders.org/
Edited by: Andreas Illmer

Israel bars UK Green leader after party votes to define Zionism as racism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:51:14 UTC
17:51:14 KST

UK Jewish groups say the motion stokes hatred after a string of attacks on their community, while the government and other parties have condemned a policy that even at least three out of five Green MPs opposed.
Israel has barred the leader of Britain's Green Party Zack Polanski from entering the country after the party's members voted to define Zionism as racism.
Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar took the decision on Sunday evening, hours after the vote at the left-wing party's annual conference, Israel's foreign ministry said. It called the resolution "a clear antisemitic text" and described the ban on Polanski as a "first step".
"The Greens have adopted not only the green of Hamas, but also its ideology: the elimination of the State of Israel through armed struggle," the ministry said.
Israel's president, Isaac Herzog, called the party's decision "a disgrace".
"Zionism is the national liberation movement of the Jewish people, and it forms the basis for the Jewish people's right to a state and a national home in the Land of Israel," Herzog said on X.
The motion passed by 1,022 votes to 813. It states that Zionism will be "treated as any other form of racism" and commits the party to supporting a "single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine".
Jewish groups warn over safety
The vote comes at a time of heightened fear among British Jews. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said the motion stoked "anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed".
Two worshippers were killed in an attack on a Manchester synagogue on Yom Kippur last year. In March, ambulances run by a Jewish volunteer service were set alight in Golders Green, north London, the first in a string of arson attacks on synagogues and other Jewish sites in the capital. Two Jewish men were stabbed in the same neighbourhood in April.
Last week, two Iranian nationals were charged over an alleged plot to carry out an attack in Manchester around this year's Yom Kippur.
The Community Security Trust, which monitors antisemitism, recorded 1,926 incidents in the first half of 2026, its second-highest half-year total, including a record 135 assaults.
Ahead of the Green Party vote, the heads of the Board of Deputies, the Community Security Trust and the Jewish Leadership Council wrote to the party.
"This motion would make the Green Party the first electorally significant UK political party in living memory to adopt what appears to be an overtly antisemitic political platform," they said.
UK parties condemn vote
Bridget Phillipson, chair of the ruling Labour Party and minister for women and equalities, condemned the decision.
"It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she said in a party statement.
The opposition Conservatives described the Greens as "toxic to its core".
"British Jews should not have to disclaim a belief in Jewish self-determination and the existence of Israel in order to be accepted by a British political party," said Chris Philp, the party's shadow home secretary.
Divisions in the party
"This has been a serious and deeply felt debate within our membership," a Green spokesperson said.
In a joint statement, Polanski and the party's MPs said there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".
The motion exposed divisions in the party. At least three of its five MPs opposed it, and Polanski, who is running to become an MP in former prime minister Keir Starmer's London constituency, skipped the vote.
He said earlier this week that the "displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people" was "clearly racism".
United Nations investigators have accused Israel of committing "genocide" in the war in Gaza, a finding that Israel has rejected.
The Greens, who hold five of the 650 seats in Britain's parliament, have surged in popularity under Polanski, attracting voters dissatisfied with the centre-left Labour government's stance on the Israel-Hamas war. Polls show his popularity has taken a hit in recent months following several missteps.

Hackers get personal information on 8.8 million people in Denmark government data leak
- Hackers illegally accessed Denmark's national registry, stealing personal data of around 8.8 million people, including names, addresses and social security numbers.
- The breach affected data beyond Denmark's six million population, including deceased and emigrated individuals, raising serious concerns.
- The authorities are investigating the incident, which involved hacking a company with legal registry access; the hackers remain unidentified and access has not yet been revoked.
AI generated
COPENHAGEN – Hackers broke into Denmark’s national registry and gained access to personal information on millions of people, the digital affairs ministry said on Oct 5.
“The administration of the national registry (Central Person Register) has found that unauthorised individuals obtained illegal access in particular to the names, addresses and CPR numbers of around 8.8 million registered people”, including those who have died or emigrated, the ministry said in a press statement, referring to Denmark’s social security numbers.
“This is an extremely serious incident,” Christina Egelund, digital affairs minister said in the statement.
“Together with all the relevant authorities, we are in the process of mapping out the full extent of the incident,” she added.
Denmark has a population of around six million, but the national registry has information on 11 million, including data of those who have died and people who have emigrated from the country.
An investigation has been launched into the incident, with the hackers not yet identified, the statement said.
They broke into the national registry by hacking into a Danish company that legally had access to it, the government said, adding that the access has not been revoked. AFP

Budget 2027: Accounting Chamber identified risks related to UAH 1.5 trillion in loans and defense spending
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:50:22 EEST
17:50:22 KST

Budget 2027: Accounting Chamber identified risks related to UAH 1.5 trillion in loans and defense spending
Kyiv • UNN
The 2027 Budget includes more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external loans without identified creditors. The Accounting Chamber considers the forecast overly optimistic.
The draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 includes more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external loans, but potential lenders have not yet been identified. The Accounting Chamber of Ukraine reported this, pointing out the risks and analyzing defense expenditures, UNN reports.
Details
"The draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027 provides for attracting more than UAH 1.5 trillion in external loans, while the potential lenders for these loans remain unidentified. Another UAH 131.3 billion in revenue depends on the planned tax changes coming into force. According to the Accounting Chamber's assessment, this creates risks of insufficient funds being received to finance state needs," the post says.
The total amount of financial resources in the state budget for 2027 is reportedly planned at UAH 8.03 trillion, "which is 12.9% more than the amount approved for 2026." "More than half of these resources — UAH 4.32 trillion, or 53.7% — is planned to be received in the form of grants and loans from international partners," the post says.
At the same time, auditors noted that the timely and complete receipt of these funds will determine the possibilities for financing the planned state expenditures. Of these funds, UAH 1 trillion 822.9 billion constitutes external borrowing, the Accounting Chamber stated.
"The forecast regarding the feasibility of attracting foreign funds in precisely these amounts is assessed by the Accounting Chamber as overly optimistic. After all, potential lenders for UAH 1.5 trillion — 88.8% of external borrowing to the general fund — have not yet been identified. Therefore, the failure to receive the necessary amount of financial support from international partners will be the key risk to the financing of the state budget in 2027," said Accounting Chamber Chairwoman Olha Pishchanska.
Expenditures: the main priority is security and defense
State budget expenditures for 2027 are planned at UAH 7.3 trillion.
Budget expenditures on security and defense are planned at UAH 4.855 trillion, or 66.8% of all expenditures. Of this amount, UAH 1.5 trillion is allocated for payroll, including servicemen's monetary allowances. Another UAH 264.9 billion constitutes a reserve for the security and defense sector. State guarantees of up to UAH 30 billion are also provided.
"At the same time, if hostilities intensify or the prices of fuel, weapons, and imported components rise, the need for funds may increase. Even taking the allocated reserve into account, there may be a need for additional funds, primarily for the procurement and repair of weapons and military equipment. Therefore, the Accounting Chamber emphasizes the need for a more detailed assessment of the planned expenditures in this area," the Accounting Chamber's statement says.
The budget also provides UAH 570.9 billion for social protection and social security. In particular, UAH 292.8 billion is allocated for pensions, UAH 42.3 billion for housing subsidies and benefits, and UAH 38.1 billion for support for families with children.
The Accounting Chamber separately drew attention to the significant difference in approaches to remuneration in state bodies.
In particular, it is proposed that a reference amount of UAH 2,331 be applied to employees of certain state bodies whose remuneration is regulated by special laws, as well as to employees of tax and customs authorities. By contrast, the subsistence minimum for able-bodied persons, amounting to UAH 3,691, is proposed for determining the basic amount of judges' official salaries. This approach increases the planned amount of payroll expenditures in the judicial system.
The state budget deficit and debt burden
The state budget deficit for 2027 is planned at UAH 1.67 trillion, or 15% of GDP. The total amount of state borrowing will be UAH 2.37 trillion.
At the end of 2027, state and state-guaranteed debt is projected at UAH 12.7 trillion. Its ratio to GDP will increase from 105% to 113.9%.
Debt repayment and servicing are allocated 15.1% of all state budget expenditures — UAH 1.2 trillion. As of July 2026, nearly 80% of the debt was denominated in foreign currency. The depreciation of the hryvnia beyond the projected level creates a risk of an increase in the debt and the costs of its repayment and servicing.
Recommendations of the Accounting Chamber
Based on the results of its examination of the 2027 State Budget, the Accounting Chamber recommends that, during the finalization of the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027:
-  clarify and provide additional justification for the sources of budget financing, in particular external borrowing; 
-  take into account the existing reserves for increasing certain state budget revenues; 
-  assess the adequacy of the expenditures envisaged for the security and defense sector; 
-  eliminate legal inconsistencies. 
The conclusions and proposals of the Accounting Chamber, as noted, have been submitted to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine for consideration during the review of the draft Law of Ukraine "On the State Budget of Ukraine for 2027."
We remind you
The 2027 Budget draft envisages a deficit of 15% of GDP and debt exceeding 110% of GDP. UAH 4.885 trillion is planned to be allocated to security and defense.

Farhadi criticizes Hollywood’s perspective at Rio Film Festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:44:43 UTC
17:44:43 KST

Farhadi criticizes Hollywood’s perspective at Rio Film Festival
TEHRAN – Renowned Iranian filmmaker Asghar Farhadi discussed the perceived dominance of American cinema and cautioned against viewing Hollywood as a reliable source for authentic portrayals of foreign cultures.
Farhadi, who is in Brazil for the presentation of his latest film “Parallel Tales” at the Rio Film Festival, made the remarks during a panel, ISNA reported.
The two-time Oscar winner was asked about “Argo” winning Best Picture just a year after “A Separation” won Best International Film at the Oscars. “I watched the film at the time it came out and felt it was a ‘Hollywood thing’,” Farhadi said.
In “Argo,” loosely based on a true story, director Ben Affleck plays a Latino exfiltration specialist who masquerades as a Hollywood producer to rescue six Americans held captive in Tehran during the US hostage crisis in Iran.
“The problem with these kinds of films in Hollywood [and] some people in the United States [is that] they look at the world from up to down,” he added. “Someday you should ask them: Why do you feel you’re up and we’re down? I don’t understand why they have this ego that they’re up.” The Iranian director then said Americans often claim to “have democracy,” but they don’t. “You don’t have democracy. It’s a lie.”
Farhadi then recalled spending time in the US a few years ago when working on a project and, during research, travelling to San Francisco to speak with incarcerated men. “I met some people in prison who are Black, [some who come] from other countries, and the real America was there. But people in the world don’t see that part of the United States.”
“I have this problem when they feel they are up and they think, ‘[others] should be like us,’” he continued. “Even if it’s in a good way and they want to be kind to you, they wish ‘one day you’ll become like us,’ and no, I don’t want to.”
Still on “Argo,” the director said movies like that “are not deep.” “They make these movies for money; it’s a business. And in these films, it’s always a white guy from the United States saving others. My question is: Why? Why does an American go to Cuba or Iran to save people? People understand they can save themselves. Who asked you to come and save us?”
Asked about how he broaches politics in his films, the renowned filmmaker said that, whenever “you talk about society, you are talking about politics.” “Even when you talk about family life, their relationships, their difficulties and problems, indirectly you are talking about politics. In my films, I always try not to talk about politics directly because, to me, that is a bit far from cinema. The cinema that I believe is the kind of cinema that gives space to audiences to discover things about themselves.”
The director then brought up Abbas Kiarostami’s “Fellow Citizen” as Iran’s “most political film.” The 1983 documentary heavily trails drivers across the streets of the Iranian capital. “He made a documentary about car drivers in Tehran, but when you see people, the way they talk to the police, the layers are very political.”
“Media and cinema don’t give you a complete image of people’s ordinary life,” he added. “But the thing about empathy is that, all around the world, people are similar to each other. Cinema is based on hate and love. And [when it comes to] hate and love, everywhere is the same. A love between a mother and child in Brazil and in Tehran is the same. The way they express it is different, but the core is the same.”
Farhadi said that when he watches a Brazilian film, he soon forgets he is watching a story from another place in the world, and feels it is a “film about us” as people. “If one day people can travel to other countries, and if they shake hands, that’s the best way to know people, not through media. I don’t believe media can give us the whole image.”
On this, the filmmaker emphasized how his last two films, “A Hero” and “Parallel Tales,” are about how we see others and how we are seen in return. They are also heavily influenced by “how social media has shaped our lives.”
“When we see something in the media, we should be careful,” he continued, adding that most information replicated by mainstream media about Iran, for example, comes from “very simple knowledge” of real life in the country. When a singular discourse is perpetuated, the director implied, it means people are “ready to accept” when someone says “they are the enemy.” “This is something the media is doing, because the most powerful media belongs to powerful people. This is the problem.”
Farhadi spoke very briefly about his next film, reiterating it will be shot in Persian. Enquired as to whether the film might deal with the current war in Iran and the conflict in Palestine, the director said: “Not directly,” suggesting the current political climate might have an underlying effect on the story despite not being the subject of his project.
“The Salesman” helmer also recalled how “Parallel Tales” was supposed to be shot in the US: “I stayed there for three years, writing, searching, casting. I did casting in the US with American actors, very big names. But every day that I came back to my home, I told myself: I cannot connect with this. Something is wrong. It was a big problem. One night I decided to change.”
SS/SAB
