Three years on: Israel is asphyxiating Gaza and dismantling the means of survival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:41:58 UTC
17:41:58 KST

- Israel is continuing its genocide in Gaza, Palestine, where the space in which people can live is shrinking and the conditions for survival are being systematically destroyed.
- Governments must act now to ensure that Israel stops the destruction and killing, and prevents ethnic cleansing, in Palestine.
Amman / Jerusalem – Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) warns that Israel is progressively asphyxiating Gaza, Palestine, and continuing its genocide: the space in which people can live is vanishing, while the conditions people need to survive are being systematically destroyed through continued violence, the deliberate blockade of essential supplies, and the destruction of healthcare and vital infrastructure.
In the past year, the physical trapping of people in Gaza has been made increasingly definitive by the establishment of Israel’s Yellow Line. Originally presented as a temporary, first-phase military withdrawal position and a key part of maintaining the so-called ceasefire – it is now reinforced by military positions, berms and ongoing demolitions and has continued to move west, squeezing people into a smaller and smaller area. Israeli forces now occupy approximately 65 per cent of Gaza, using the line to draw a clear border around this area.
As the Yellow Line moves, the threat to people living nearby becomes increasingly immediate, compounded by the uncertainty of approaching a line that is not clearly or consistently demarcated. People risk being shot by Israeli forces when they approach it, and MSF teams continue to treat people with gunshot wounds sustained nearby. Its encroachment is also disrupting the delivery of essential assistance: MSF water trucking has had to stop when shooting occurs near communities living close to the Yellow Line.
“The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map,” says Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza. “It has become a mechanism of encirclement and ethnic cleansing, while cutting communities off from the infrastructure, healthcare, water and other essentials they need to survive.”
The Yellow Line cannot be treated simply as a line on a map.
Amande Bazerolle, MSF head of emergency response in Gaza
Violence is not confined to the areas around the Yellow Line. In June and July alone, despite a so-called ceasefire, MSF teams treated more than 1,200* cases of violent trauma across Gaza, including blast injuries, burns, gunshot wounds and injuries resulting from physical assault.
Over the past three years, our teams have treated more than 200,000 trauma cases*, including injuries resulting from intentional physical violence, while Israel’s military offensive has killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 20,000 children.
As Israel confines Palestinians into increasingly limited areas, families are being pushed into overcrowded and unlivable conditions, without sufficient access to clean water, sanitation services, shelter, or healthcare. These conditions are contributing to the spread of disease.
MSF teams have treated more than 11,000 cases of skin diseases, such as scabies, this year alone, while seeing more than 1,500 cases of chickenpox in June and July. MSF distributed around 2.1 million litres of drinking water per day in August, yet the scale of need remains far beyond what can be met under these restrictions. 
“Most people have less than six litres of domestic-use water per day and limited access to basic hygiene items such as soap and detergent,” says Dr Murad Asaliyya, medical activities manager in Gaza. “We are treating gastroenteritis, acute respiratory infections, a lot of skin conditions, hepatitis, bacterial skin infections, scabies and lice.”
“At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies,” says Dr Asaliyya. “Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.”
At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies. Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.
Dr Murad Asaliyya, medical activities manager in Gaza
Over the past three years, access to healthcare has deteriorated dramatically, with hospitals increasingly running out of basic supplies and patients unable to access essential medicines and treatment. Restrictions on essential supplies, such as engine oil and spare parts, are also crippling the infrastructure needed to keep hospitals, ambulances and water systems running, with generators already breaking down and water-trucking operations reduced.
The destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system and damage to more than 80 per cent of all structures in the Strip, alongside the lifelong physical and mental health impacts of repeated violence and displacement, will extend far beyond the present and prevent any meaningful recovery for years to come.
Nor is this crisis limited to Gaza. Since 2023, violent settler attacks, military operations and raids on homes, displacement camps and agricultural land, illegal settlement expansion, displacement, home demolitions and movement restrictions have rapidly escalated across the West Bank and East Jerusalem, particularly this year. Patients at MSF clinics tell teams about homes being demolished by Israeli forces, attacks by settlers, and livestock being stolen. The policies of violence, harassment and forced displacement affecting Palestinians extend beyond Gaza, causing further fragmentation of Palestine.
“It will take generations to recover from the harm that has already been done over the past three years, and in the preceding decades, while the excruciating consequences of Israel's ongoing genocide are still being felt every day,” says Bazerolle. 
“Destruction, displacement and deprivation have become normalised — practices Israel is carrying out with impunity,” says Bazerolle. “Governments must act now to ensure Israel stops the destruction and killing, prevents ethnic cleansing, and stops denying Palestinians the means of survival.”
*This refers to cases not patients, including new or follow-up consultations.

Iran says it disabled Starlink terminals during January protests

Sahin Demir

Iran claimed Monday that it had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during nationwide protests in January and has other tools to counter the satellite internet service.
According to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, head of Iran’s National Cyberspace Center, said Tehran had successfully disabled Starlink terminals during the protests.
“For the first time, Iran managed to successfully disable Starlink terminals during the coup in January,” Aghamiri said, using the Iranian authorities’ description of the protests.
He claimed that Western media had also reported at the time that Iran had successfully carried out an operation to disable Starlink terminals.
“That important technical operation, which was completely successful, is one of our tools, and we also have other tools at our disposal to counter Starlink,” he added.
Aghamiri’s comments came in response to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who displayed a Starlink terminal during his address to the UN General Assembly in New York on Sept. 24.
Netanyahu said the device allowed Iranians to access information, accusing Tehran of spending large sums of money on internet censorship.
Iran witnessed widespread anti-government protests in January, with demonstrations intensifying on Jan. 8 and 9 amid clashes between protesters and security forces.
Iranian authorities imposed a nationwide internet blackout on Jan. 8 as the protests intensified.
Starlink remained one of the few ways for Iranians to access the internet during the blackout, although reports at the time indicated that the satellite service was also experiencing significant interference and disruptions.
Aghamiri said the disruptions were caused by an Iranian operation targeting Starlink terminals.
Starlink, operated by US space technology company SpaceX, provides internet connectivity through a network of satellites.

Bar-Ilan lecturer indicted over plot to kill hundreds of Arabs in coordinated attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:39:42 UTC
17:39:42 KST

A mathematics lecturer at Bar-Ilan University has been indicted on allegations that he spent more than three years planning coordinated terrorist attacks intended to kill hundreds of Arab Israelis and Palestinians and drive Arab communities from Israel and the territories.
The defendant, a man in his 60s from Petah Tikva whose name is currently under a court-imposed gag order, called his plan “AIT,” a Hebrew acronym for a phrase meaning “The People Will Carry Out Transfer,” according to an indictment announced Monday by the Central District Attorney’s Office.
Prosecutors charged him with preparing to commit an act of terrorism under Israel’s Counter-Terrorism Law, extortion by threats and obstruction of justice. They have asked the court to keep him in custody until the end of legal proceedings.
According to the indictment, the defendant began developing his plan against the backdrop of the May 2021 intercommunal violence in Israel and intensified his efforts after the outbreak of the war following the Oct. 7 attack.
Prosecutors allege that, motivated by nationalist ideology, he sought to carry out multiple terrorist attacks simultaneously across the country, killing hundreds of Arab Israeli citizens, including Bedouins, as well as Palestinians living in east Jerusalem and the West Bank.
The alleged objective was to cause Arabs to flee or be permanently expelled toward Jordan, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip.
For more than three years, beginning in February 2023 and continuing until his arrest about two weeks ago, prosecutors say the defendant developed what they described as an organized, detailed plan.
His alleged preparations included reconnaissance trips, handwritten documents laying out the proposed operation and its ideological justification, and repeated efforts to recruit participants.
72 attackers divided into 12 cells
Under the plan described in the indictment, 72 Jewish attackers, at least half of them licensed gun owners, would be divided into 12 cells of six people each. The defendant allegedly intended to participate himself.
The groups were to arm themselves with weapons including handguns, rifles, axes and hammers and launch surprise attacks simultaneously in mixed Jewish-Arab cities and Arab communities across Israel.
The indictment further alleges that the defendant envisioned recruiting sympathetic elements within the IDF to provide support for the attacks, including attacks on Arab population centers involving the Air Force, artillery and armored forces.
In a section of his plan titled roughly “How to carry out AIT here and now,” prosecutors say the defendant wrote instructions encouraging participants to conduct mass killings and rapidly seize control of areas of friction, roads, entrances and exits to Arab communities, mixed cities and hospitals.
The document allegedly instructed participants not to show mercy to women or children and warned that stopping the attacks would lead to chaos and the killing of Jews.
According to prosecutors, the defendant believed that simultaneous mass attacks, combined with their real-time dissemination on social media, would prompt Arab citizens of Israel, Bedouins and Palestinians in east Jerusalem and the West Bank to flee beyond Israel’s borders.
Attempts to recruit supporters
Prosecutors say the lecturer spent roughly a year and a half attempting to recruit supporters and partners for the alleged plot, but none agreed to participate.
He also allegedly conducted reconnaissance around the Bedouin community of Tuba-Zangariyye in northern Israel to examine access routes and determine how it could be attacked. Prosecutors say he intended the community to serve as one of the plan’s main targets.
The indictment says the defendant also devised a secret recruitment scheme involving Zehut leader Moshe Feiglin.
According to prosecutors, he planned first to recruit Feiglin and then use his assistance to identify additional participants.
The alleged plan called for selected activists to be invited to a Zehut election event without being told the real purpose of the gathering. During the event, prosecutors say, they would be informed that they were being recruited for a terrorist attack to take place the following day and would receive detailed operational instructions.
The defendant allegedly attended two public events held by Feiglin and attempted to arrange a meeting with him and deliver a summary of his plan.
Feiglin did not respond to any of his approaches, according to the indictment.
Alleged attempt to threaten Feiglin
About a month ago, prosecutors say, as the election approached, the defendant wrote a threatening letter addressed to Feiglin after failing to secure his cooperation.
The letter allegedly criticized and insulted Feiglin over his refusal to cooperate and threatened to make the correspondence public if he did not help advance the plan, in what the defendant believed would cause Feiglin political damage ahead of the election.
About two days later, prosecutors allege, the defendant went to Feiglin’s home and handed the letter to a neighbor, asking her to deliver it to him. She did so.
The defendant later attended a Zehut event at Jerusalem’s Mahane Yehuda market and, through another woman, gave the party’s director-general several copies of the threatening letter along with an additional letter containing a similar threat, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors allege extensive efforts to avoid detection
The indictment says the defendant took numerous precautions throughout the alleged planning process to conceal his identity and prevent authorities from discovering the plot.
He allegedly wrote documents and letters by hand rather than on a computer, drafted instructions explaining how participants could avoid identification and used disguises while meeting people he sought to recruit.
Those measures allegedly included wearing a face mask, hat and sunglasses, using a false name and borrowing the phones of passersby to contact other people.
In its request to keep the defendant in custody until the end of proceedings, the Central District Attorney’s Office said the alleged conduct stretched over several years and reflected an extremist ideology that led him to develop a detailed, multi-stage plan intended to cause large-scale loss of life among Arab Israelis and Palestinians in east Jerusalem and the West Bank.
Prosecutors argued that the defendant’s alleged efforts to advance the plan, combined with its nationalist and ideological motivation and the heightened security tensions during the period in which it was developed, demonstrate that he poses an immediate danger to individuals, the public and the state.
Bar-Ilan University said: “Bar-Ilan University condemns in the strongest possible terms and is deeply appalled by the acts attributed to the lecturer in the indictment. The University’s leadership calls upon the police and the prosecution to pursue the matter to the fullest extent of the law, should the allegations be substantiated.
The University has, and will continue to have, zero tolerance for conduct of this nature—conduct that is fundamentally incompatible with the values we share as Jews, as Israelis, and as human beings, and that stands in clear opposition to the values of Bar-Ilan University.
The lecturer will be suspended from his duties with immediate effect, pending the conclusion of the legal proceedings.”

One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:39:26 UTC
17:39:26 KST

One day behind bars: Students and incarcerated women break prison stigma in Thailand
“Your mind follows the thread, one by one, row by row. You know? It’s like meditation. I don’t like machines.”
Weo, a prisoner at the Central Women’s Correctional Institution in Bangkok, prefers to sew by hand. She tried the sewing machine, but noticed that her mind was calmer when threading with her fingers directly. By not using a machine, she can produce a unique pattern that is hard to find in conventional shops.
She is explaining this to a group of design students who, sketchbooks in hand, are walking through the rows, observing the women who sew.
As time passes, some lose their initial apprehension and sit across from them, picking up fabric samples. Others ask about the products they are making. Some borrow their needles and, with the women’s guidance, try a bit of sewing themselves. A few sit on the floor in the basket-weaving corner with the women who have, by now, mastered the skill.
Today, the students have left the classroom behind to spend their morning at Thailand’s first women’s prison, where approximately 150 women learn weaving, knitting and machine sewing to make marketable products.
The students’ task is to design a product that these women can manufacture during their sentences.
Through the wall
The initiative, launched in November 2025 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) and the Thailand Institute of Justice (TIJ) pairs design students with incarcerated women to create modern, sustainable products that can be sold outside prison.
Earlier this year, 22 students visited the prison and interacted with the women who are now manufacturing new products. Their designs had to appeal to modern consumers, be practical and tell a story linked to rehabilitation that would raise awareness of the critical role vocational training plays in reducing recidivism.
“The stigma surrounding those who have made mistakes has long been a wall in our society. To help them cross that barrier, we must restore their human dignity,” said TIJ’s Chontit Chuenurah.
“By weaving their stories into these products, we use the creativity of the youth to build a bridge between the prison and the outside world, replacing fear with understanding.”
Under the theme Through the Wall, the initiative seeks to dismantle physical and social barriers, helping incarcerated women return successfully to society, she added.
“The project aims to create prison-made goods that appeal to modern consumers while equipping correctional officers with essential marketing skills,” said Aki Okanan, former prison reform expert at UNODC.
The project also raises international awareness of the role of rehabilitation and vocational training in reducing re-offending she added.
Time well spent
A panel of judges evaluated nine projects from 19 students in a competition earlier this year.
The winner was Time-Made, featuring intricately smocked watch straps.
For the students behind the design, time has a two-fold meaning: the sentence that prisoners can reduce by working in prison, and the time that people outside value, a privilege sometimes taken for granted.
“We wanted our product to remind people that we can use time carefully and meaningfully. That we can watch our time,” says Game, 21, co-winner of the competition.
First steps
All designs received support for product development and marketing, and the winning product, together with a selection of others, will be produced in collaboration with partner correctional facilities.
Natty, also 21, has been studying lifestyle products for three years. She had expected the prison to look gloomy and scary and was surprised to find the workroom bright and airy. Still, she noticed that most prisoners used dark colours.
“I want to take the skills they have and show them brighter fabrics and see what happens,” she said.
Sitting by Weo’s side, Ana*, from Latin America, tells the story of how she was caught attempting to smuggle cocaine into Bangkok. After four years in prison, she can produce perfect stuffed animals and is fluent in Thai, although she has never seen Thailand outside prison.
“I heard it’s beautiful here, but it doesn’t matter. After this, when I manage to get back to Brazil, I will start an import business and sell stuffed animals from Thailand. I know how to do it. I have the connections, and I speak the language.”
As the students pass through the gates and security controls to leave, their enthusiasm wanes. Although the prisoners cannot leave, this collaboration connects them to the outside world, the first step in reintegration.

Israel marks October 7 anniversary as national memorial day

Shadow chancellor to address Tory conference as he claims slashing red tape could cut cost of new houses by £50,000 – UK politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:37:01 UTC
17:37:01 KST

Tories accused of copying Reform UK after shadow chancellor says axing red tape could cut cost of new homes by £50k
Good morning. Yesterday Kemi Badenoch published a tract setting out the principles that a Conservative government would follow in office. It was presented as Thatcherism revived for the 21st century, and a key theme was that government should leave wealth creation up to business, and not get in the way with red tape.
Today Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, is presenting a plan that illustrates what this would mean in practice. Normally, at party conference, ministers and shadow ministers put out a press release in advance of their speeches highlighting just one headline policy idea, with perhaps one or two associated policies.
Overnight Griffith has published what is practically a manifesto. The press release alone runs to almost 5,000 words. Jessica Elgot had the task of reading them all for us yesterday and here is her write-up.
She has led her story on the plan to get rid of two environment quangos, the Environment Agency and Natural England.
But there are plenty of other proposals in the package too, including:
-Getting rid of net zero regulations and other planning laws, including section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy, that put up the cost of housebuilding.
-Getting rid of the EPR (extended producer responsibility), a law intended to make producers liable for waste disposal costs. The Tories call it the “grocery tax”.
-Backing a third runway at Heathrow.
-Leaving the Aarhus convention, an international treaty giving the public access to information relating to environmental decision-making. The Tories claim this enables the “lawfare hindering every major infrastructure project in this country”.
-Speeding up the delivery of more nuclear power stations.
-Simplifying the tax code.
The Tories claim the plans relating to housebuilding would “cut up to an estimated £50,000 off the price of a new home”.
There is more detail in what Griffith is proposing, and there is clearly a lot to discuss. Labour and Reform UK have both responded overnight – but taking different lines of attack.
Labour has said that Griffith has no credibility on these topics. In an overnight statement, Bridget Phillipson, the party chair, said:
Trusting the co-author of Liz Truss’ disastrous mini-Budget with Tory plans on the economy and housing is like asking an arsonist to run the fire service. Kemi Badenoch is once again demonstrating her appalling lack of judgement.
The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn.
But Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader and business spokesperson, says that Griffith is copying ideas that his party has already adopted. He says:
Tories pledge to scrap some costs regulations and taxes they put in place!
They are copying Reform policies we announced weeks and months ago!
They are trying to fix problems they created 😡
Never forget
Never forgive
One of the themes emerging at this conference is that, while there is far less talk of some sort of Tory/Reform UK pact than there was a year ago, the policy overlap continues. Yesterday the Conservatives announced two other proposals (excluding foreigners from the student loan scheme, and reducing aid spending to just £1bn a year) that were little more than cut-and-paste versions of Reform UK pledges.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9.45am: Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, speaks at the conference on the main stage (the smaller of the two halls the Tories are using at this conference for speeches). The other main morning speakers are Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, at 10.30am; Damian Hinds, the shadow health secretary, at 11.15am; and Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, and Laura Trott, after 12.15pm.
12.14pm: Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, speaking in the fanzone area on the Conservative’s rural vision.
2pm: Griffith takes part in “meet the team” event in the symphony hall (the conference stage being used for larger events) with Richard Fuller, chief secretary to the Treasury, Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, and Julia Lopez, the acting shadow business secretary.
This is from Vicky Spratt, the journalist and housing specialist, on the Tory proposals to cut building regulations. (See 8.08am.)
Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith has told the Tory conference that he would “scrap unnecessary net-zero housing red tape” and cut the cost of “delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000.”
How would the Tories guarantee that developers pass on these supposed savings to homebuyers?

The pensions triple lock is protected by voter power. That’s how politics works, but it isn’t how democracy should work, and it certainly doesn’t give fairness a chance.
Now the prime minister has touched the third rail of British politics by daring to fix this unfairness, he needs voters on side. Compulsory voting would give Burnham the political cover and popular support to deliver. The people most likely to back reform, including younger voters, would be at the ballot box to reward a government that took on intergenerational inequality. Compulsory voting brings everyone into the decision, those directly affected and those who aren’t, encouraging a more considered response to major policy choices.
Burnham has said that he will set up a commission on electoral reform. He has not explicitly said that he wants it to look at compulsory voting, but there is increasing interest in the idea in progressive circles.

Ideological net zero rules alone have added more than £30,000 to the cost of building a new home. Local Government viability assessments show that Net Zero rules add tens of thousands of pounds to the cost of building a new home. For instance, Birmingham City Council assessed that improved efficiency, heat pumps and solar panels increase the cost of a new detached home by as much as £30,789. The London Borough of Lewisham estimated that these rules would increase build costs by 15 per cent. (Birmingham City Council, Net Zero Plan Supporting Evidence Report, 7 September 2023, link, Lewisham Council, Viability Study 2022, 17 May 2022, link.)
These costs can be even higher as local and regional authorities often gold-plate these rules, imposing extra cost on developers. For instance, Policy SI2 (C) in the London Plan 2021 requires a 35 per cent uplift on energy efficiency beyond the national Building Regulations for major developments. (Mayor of London, The London Plan, March 2021,link.)
Other mandated changes are adding thousands in costs:

Requirements for EV chargers on all new residential buildings are increasing costs by £870 per property. (Home Builders Federation, The Viability Crunch, 1May 2026 link.)
Accessibility standards introduced in 2022 have gold-plated requirements for wider internal staircases and level thresholds for entry to properties in new builds, which are estimated to have added £1,800 to the cost of building a home. (Home Builders Federation, The Viability Crunch, 1May 2026 link.)
Additional Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) rules are adding £5,700 to the cost of construction:
Local authorities are imposing additional local rules significantly exceeding the national 10 per cent target for BNG. For instance:
More than a dozen local authorities require BNG of 20 per cent or more (as of January 2025). (Urbanist Architecture, BNG requirements for planning, 27 January 2025, link.)

Good morning. Yesterday Kemi Badenoch published a tract setting out the principles that a Conservative government would follow in office. It was presented as Thatcherism revived for the 21st century, and a key theme was that government should leave wealth creation up to business, and not get in the way with red tape.
Today Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, is presenting a plan that illustrates what this would mean in practice. Normally, at party conference, ministers and shadow ministers put out a press release in advance of their speeches highlighting just one headline policy idea, with perhaps one or two associated policies.

She has led her story on the plan to get rid of two environment quangos, the Environment Agency and Natural England.
But there are plenty of other proposals in the package too, including:
-Getting rid of net zero regulations and other planning laws, including section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy, that put up the cost of housebuilding.
-Getting rid of the EPR (extended producer responsibility), a law intended to make producers liable for waste disposal costs. The Tories call it the “grocery tax”.
-Backing a third runway at Heathrow.
-Leaving the Aarhus convention, an international treaty giving the public access to information relating to environmental decision-making. The Tories claim this enables the “lawfare hindering every major infrastructure project in this country”.
-Speeding up the delivery of more nuclear power stations.
-Simplifying the tax code.
The Tories claim the plans relating to housebuilding would “cut up to an estimated £50,000 off the price of a new home”.

School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns

School textbooks overpriced and poor quality, watchdog warns
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Consumer watchdog ACM has criticised educational publishers for pricey and poor-quality textbooks, calling on the industry to change its practices.
The ACM says that for the past seven years, prices for educational materials have been rising faster than those of other products and schools say the publications are not meeting their needs.
In a statement, the watchdog said it “calls on educational publishers to stop mandatory tied selling of licences and textbooks, and to better align product supply with demand.”
One major problem the organisation highlighted is that textbooks and the licences for e-materials are bundled together, which drives up costs. The ACM wants them to be sold separately.
The organisation also calls on schools to do more research into the textbooks they purchase.
“Pressure on publishers starts with schools’ willingness to switch to other learning materials,” board member Martijn Snoep said in a statement.
Secondary schools buy around €280 million worth of learning materials every year.

Expert warns of continued ‘earthquake storm’ after tremors hit southern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:35:34 UTC
17:35:34 KST

A potential “earthquake storm” could continue in southern Türkiye, according to an expert, after magnitude 4.9 and 5.2 earthquakes struck Adana and Osmaniye within minutes of each other, causing panic but no reported damage.
The earthquakes occurred on Oct. 4 in the districts of Saimbeyli in Adana and Sumbas in Osmaniye. Türkiye’s Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) said a magnitude 4.8 earthquake struck Saimbeyli at 2:19 p.m., followed by a magnitude 4.9 quake in the same district at 2:36 p.m. and a magnitude 5.2 earthquake in Sumbas at 2:43 p.m. The earthquakes occurred at depths of about 7-9 kilometers.
AFAD’s preliminary assessment of the magnitude 5.2 earthquake recorded at least 16 aftershocks ranging from magnitude 1.0 to 2.4. Overall, 113 earthquakes were recorded in the region during the following 24 hours.
The authority noted that 32 earthquakes of magnitude 4 or greater have occurred in the area since 1900, with the strongest reaching magnitude 5.7.
Seismologist Hasan Sözbilir said the latest activity occurred between the Saimbeyli and Savrun faults, which have been considered areas of accumulated seismic energy following the February 2023 earthquakes.
“Earthquakes of similar magnitude may continue their activity in the form of an earthquake storm at this stage,” Sözbilir said, urging residents not to panic.
Hakan Güneyli, a member of AFAD’s Earthquake Science Board, said the available data indicated that the sequence would gradually weaken.
“Based on the data so far, we can say that these earthquakes will diminish in magnitude and occur at increasingly longer intervals,” Güneyli said. He added that smaller aftershocks could continue for some time.
Güneyli linked the activity to the transfer of elastic deformation energy generated by the February 2023 earthquakes toward the west and southwest. He also warned that seismic activity could continue for years following the 2023 disaster.
He further warned that recent tremors, combined with heavy rainfall and steep terrain, could increase the risk of landslides and rockfalls in the region.

Why protecting home values is Beijing’s new priority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

Why protecting home values is Beijing’s new priority
With resale transactions outpacing new home sales for the first time, stabilising the existing housing stock has become vital
Official figures published by the National Bureau of Statistics in September reveal that secondary market home transactions have surpassed new residential builds in volume. Nationwide registered resales reached 549 million square metres, signalling that housing demand in China has not vanished. Rather, it appears to have structurally migrated.
This marks a departure from the previous growth model. For a quarter of a century, following the end of the old welfare housing system in 1998, China’s property market operated on a high-velocity loop: developers acquired municipal land, pre-sold unfinished apartments, collected buyer cash and funnelled those advances into their next projects. That mechanism turned residential construction into the primary economic engine of the country.
That engine is now losing momentum. What is emerging is not merely a smaller version of the old market but a different market altogether. The centre of gravity is shifting – from developers selling a promise of tomorrow to households trading the homes of today.

Dutch government considers nationwide mobile phone ban in schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:29:52 UTC
17:29:52 KST

Melike Pala
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The Dutch Cabinet has called on primary and secondary schools to ban students from using mobile phones throughout the school day, including during breaks and on school grounds, broadcaster NOS reported Monday.
Under the proposed measure, students would be required to keep their mobile phones away for the duration of the school day, including in classrooms, assembly halls, during breaks and elsewhere on school premises, from Jan. 1, 2027.
The Cabinet currently does not have the legal authority to impose a nationwide ban on mobile phone use in schools but can issue recommendations to the education sector.
The proposal is part of a broader government strategy aimed at protecting children from risks associated with excessive and potentially harmful online activity.
Officials warned that addictive algorithms, autoplaying videos and social media can make it difficult for young people to reduce their screen use.
The government previously reached national agreements in 2024 aimed at restricting mobile phone use during lessons.
The Cabinet is also calling for stronger measures to protect children online, including a possible age limit for access to social media platforms.
The European Commission is considering an age threshold of 13, while the Dutch government has proposed setting the minimum age at 15.
The government is also preparing tighter regulations for family vloggers and child influencers.
Under the proposed rules, online content produced by children under 15 could be classified as child labor and subject to penalties.

Ukraine Hits Russian Buk-M3, Drone Launch Hub, and EW Station in Coordinated Strikes
Ukrainian forces launched retaliatory strikes against Russian military targets on October 3 and overnight into October 4.
A Russian Buk-M3 air defense system, a strike-drone storage and launch site, an electronic warfare station, and several other military facilities were targeted during the operation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on October 4, the Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system was hit near Kuroshany in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.
Ukrainian forces also struck a site near temporarily occupied Donetsk where Russian forces stored, prepared, and launched attack drones.
The General Staff described such facilities as priority targets because of their role in Russian drone operations against Ukraine. “Systematic strikes on such facilities are aimed at reducing the Russian Federation’s ability to use strike drones against Ukraine’s civilian population,” the General Staff said.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian electronic warfare station near Klimovo in Russia’s Bryansk region. Russian telecommunications nodes were also hit near Hirnyk, Yasynuvata, and Donetsk in the Donetsk region, according to the General Staff.
In the temporarily occupied Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces targeted Russian repair units near Vesela Tarasivka and Lysychansk.
Earlier on October 4, drones targeted Russia’s Khanskaya military airfield in the Republic of Adygea, where Su-34 and Su-35 fighter jets are based, with open-source footage showing a fire near the facility.

Germany Unveils €1.35 Billion Ukraine Package as Merz Arrives in Kyiv to Finalize Drone Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:28:48 UTC
17:28:48 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Germany Unveils €1.35 Billion Ukraine Package as Merz Arrives in Kyiv to Finalize Drone Deal
Germany is preparing to provide Ukraine with €1 billion in new military assistance and another €350 million to repair damaged energy infrastructure, as Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv for talks on expanding bilateral defense cooperation.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on October 4, German government officials said Merz is expected to announce the funding package during his visit, while Germany and Ukraine are also set to finalize an agreement covering the joint production of several types of drones.
“I travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said. “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us.”
Reuters reported that Merz traveled to Kyiv alongside German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and a delegation that includes executives from Siemens Energy, Hensoldt, Diehl Defence, Quantum Systems, and other companies. The German chancellor is also expected to discuss reforms requested by Ukraine’s European Union partners, including anti-corruption measures.
A major part of the visit is expected to focus on expanding Ukrainian-German defense production. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week, following a phone call with Merz, that the two countries were preparing to finalize an agreement covering drones, missiles, and related software, Reuters reported.
One of the priorities is the rapid production of interceptor drones designed to counter high-speed jet-powered attack drones. German defense company Quantum Systems has tested technology for this role.
The planned cooperation extends beyond drone interceptors. According to Reuters, Germany and Ukraine are also working on the joint development and production of weapons with ranges exceeding 1,000 kilometers, giving Ukraine additional domestically and jointly produced options for long-range strikes against military targets inside Russia.
Merz arrived as Russia continued large-scale attacks on Kyiv. Air raid alerts and explosions were reported across the Ukrainian capital on October 4, while one Russian strike damaged the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River and nearby infrastructure, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
Germany has significantly expanded its military support for Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The German government says it has provided or committed around €57.6 billion in bilateral military assistance for Ukraine, while Berlin has also financed energy repairs, air defense capabilities, and other infrastructure support.

New Zealand petrol prices hit highest level since Mideast conflict
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
16:28:21 CST
17:28:21 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 5 (Xinhua) -- Petrol prices in New Zealand have risen to their highest level since the start of the Middle East conflict, according to fuel monitoring site Gaspy.
Gaspy on Monday showed the average price of 91-octane unleaded petrol at 3.505 NZ dollars (about 1.96 U.S. dollars) per liter, slightly higher than the 3.502 NZ dollars per liter recorded at the peak of the Middle East conflict in April, Gaspy director Mike Newton told Radio New Zealand (RNZ).
The latest increase followed a sustained period in which the price of Brent crude oil has remained above 100 U.S. dollars a barrel. Brent crude was trading at about 101.5 U.S. dollars a barrel on Monday.
The New Zealand dollar has also fallen sharply over the past two months, dropping about 7 percent since August to around 55.8 U.S. cents, close to a one-year low, RNZ reported.
A weaker New Zealand dollar makes imported fuel more expensive, adding to upward pressure on petrol prices. ■

Ukrenergo: Russian attacks cause new power outages in six regions
According to Ukrinform, the National Electricity Company “Ukrenergo” reported this on Facebook.
“The enemy continues to carry out attacks on Ukraine’s civilian energy infrastructure. As a result of the shelling, as of this morning, there are new power outages in the Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy, Poltava, Odesa, and Kherson regions. Where current security conditions allow, emergency repair work has already begun," the statement reads.
As of 9:30 a.m. on Monday, electricity consumption is 6.2% higher than on the previous business day—Friday, October 2. This is due to cloudy weather in some regions, which reduces the efficiency of residential solar power plants.
Ukrenergo advises shifting peak energy consumption to the period when industrial solar power plants operate most efficiently—from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. At the same time, from 5:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m., energy officials urge residents not to turn on several high-power electrical appliances simultaneously.
“No consumption restriction measures are currently anticipated. However, due to Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, the situation may change in some regions. Stay updated by checking the websites and official social media pages of your distribution system operator (oblenergo)," Ukrenergo added.
As previously reported, in September 2026, contracts worth approximately €25.6 million were signed through the Ukrainian Energy Support Fund for the supply of critically needed equipment.

Yemeni forces seize Dhubab, strategic sites near Bab el-Mandeb, army says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:27:44 UTC
17:27:44 KST

Sahin Demir and Lina Altawell
05 October 2026•Update: 05 October 2026
The Yemeni army said Monday that government forces had seized the Dhubab district and strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait following clashes with the Houthis.
 
Yemen’s official Saba news agency said forces from the Nation’s Shield and the pro-government Southern Giants Brigades, backed by the Popular Resistance, took control of Dhubab in western Taiz province.
 
A military source told Saba that the forces launched a large-scale operation with air support targeting Houthi positions and forces across several areas of the district.
 
The forces advanced and took control of key positions while cutting supply lines and routes leading to Bab el-Mandeb, the source said.
 
The source said an unspecified number of Houthi fighters were killed or injured in the clashes, while several military vehicles and equipment were destroyed or damaged.
 
The Southern Giants Brigades separately announced the launch of what they called a “decisive” military operation against the Houthis in the Bab el-Mandeb area.
 
The Houthi-controlled Saba news agency, however, cited a military source as denying any government advance toward Dhubab, calling the reports “baseless.”
 
Bab el-Mandeb is a strategically important waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Arabian Sea and is a key route for international shipping.

FACTBOX: Incumbent president, senator to advance to runoff in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:26:46 UTC
17:26:46 KST

RIO DE JANEIRO, October 5. /TASS/. Brazil’s first round of the presidential election ends without any candidate receiving the 50% of votes needed to win.
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro will compete in the runoff election on October 25.
TASS summarizes key results.
First-round results
- Official results from the Superior Electoral Court, which serves as Brazil’s election authority, show Senator Flavio Bolsonaro leading the first round with 47.09% of the vote after 99.70% of electronic voting records were processed. More than 56 million votes were cast for him.
- Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva finishes in second with 45.09%, receiving more than 53.6 million votes.
- Bolsonaro leads Lula da Silva by 2 percentage points, a difference of nearly 2.39 million votes.
- The other candidates do not seriously challenge the two frontrunners, dividing the remaining votes among themselves.
- Writer Augusto Cury finishes third with 2.89%, receiving 3.44 million votes.
- Mission movement activist Renan Santos comes in fourth with 2.25%, receiving 2.67 million votes.
- Goias Governor Ronaldo Caiado receives 2.19%, or 2.60 million votes.
- Minas Gerais Governor Romeu Zema wins the support of 0.27% of voters, or 325,900 votes.
- Candidates from small parties collectively receive slightly more than 0.2%.
- The first round leaves the right-wing camp with a significant advantage going into the runoff.
- Center-right and libertarian candidates who exit the race receive a combined 7.60%, or more than 9 million votes, with most of their voters historically opposing left-wing forces.
- The governing coalition loses ground after Lula da Silva falls behind in the strategically important state of Minas Gerais in southeastern Brazil, where victory has traditionally been seen as a guarantee of a national win.
Turnout
- Voter turnout exceeds 78.93% in the general election, with more than 124.9 million citizens voting out of nearly 158.7 million registered voters.
- The abstention rate reaches about 21.1%, with more than 33.3 million people not voting.
- Valid votes total 118.8 million, or 95.23%, while blank ballots account for 1.84%, or 2.29 million votes, and spoiled ballots account for 2.93%, or 3.66 million votes.
Runoff
- Brazil will hold the runoff of the presidential election on October 25.
- Both finalists will participate in a series of in-person debates and work to mobilize undecided voters in the largest metropolitan areas of southeastern Brazil over the next three weeks.
Statements by runoff candidates
- Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva said Brazil’s presidential race is entering its decisive phase and that efforts to mobilize voters will resume immediately.
- The incumbent president acknowledged that his campaign had anticipated a first-round victory.
- Lula da Silva also called the vote a "lesson in democracy" and personally thanked millions of Brazilians for fulfilling their civic duty by going to the polls.
- Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing Liberal Party candidate, expressed confidence that he would win the presidential runoff and said the country’s decades of left-wing rule were drawing to an end.
- Bolsonaro promised to run a "clean campaign" and noted that he is the only presidential candidate to have officially committed to ending presidential reelection.
Impact of results on relations with Russia
- Brazil’s policy toward Russia is unlikely to undergo significant changes regardless of the presidential election outcome, international affairs journalist, translator and Latin America expert Oleg Yasinsky told TASS.

Majority of Ukrainians believe Zelenskyy should not run for second term – survey
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
11:25:00 EEST
17:25:00 KST

Majority of Ukrainians believe Zelenskyy should not run for second term – survey
More than half of Ukrainians believe that Volodymyr Zelenskyy should serve only one term as president and should not run for a second term in the next election.
Source: a poll conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on 12-21 September
Quote: "Now 53% believe he should be limited to one current term (up from 46% in December 2025). Meanwhile, 42% believe he should participate in the next election (down from 45%). The remaining 5% were undecided."
Details: KIIS notes that there is a clear correlation between the level of trust in the president and support for him running in the election.
"If among those who completely trust the president, 85% support his participation in the elections, then this indicator decreases to 53% among those who rather trust and to, respectively, 20% and 7% among those who rather or completely do not trust," the sociologists said.
For reference: The survey was conducted on 12-21 September. A total of 1,002 respondents aged 18 and over living in all regions of Ukraine under Ukrainian government control were interviewed by telephone based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers. The sample did not include residents of territories temporarily outside the Ukrainian government's control (although some respondents were internally displaced persons who had moved from occupied territories). The survey also did not include Ukrainian citizens who left the country after 24 February 2022.
Under normal circumstances, the statistical margin of error for a sample of this size (with a 95% confidence level and a design effect of 1.3) would not exceed 4.1% for figures close to 50%, 3.5% for figures close to 25%, 2.5% for figures close to 10% and 1.8% for figures close to 5%.
In wartime conditions, there is a certain systematic deviation in addition to the formal margin of error mentioned above. However, the sociologists believe that the results remain highly representative and allow for a fairly reliable analysis of public opinion.

India in talks with Russia and Ukraine to end conflict – FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:24:55 UTC
17:24:55 KST

India in talks with Russia and Ukraine to end conflict – FM
India has moved “beyond advocacy” in the Russia-Ukraine conflict and is now holding talks with both Moscow and Kiev on Black Sea shipping, grain, and energy exports, as well as possible non-attack arrangements, Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has said. 
New Delhi has become more directly involved in recent months after years of calling for dialogue and diplomacy, Jaishankar said at the Munich Leaders Meeting in New Delhi. India is trying to help first on the safety of shipping in the Black Sea, while discussions have expanded to other immediate concerns shared by the two sides.
“We have conversations with both Russia and Ukraine in this regard,” he said, describing talks over grain and energy exports and “non-attack possibilities” as ongoing. 
Ukraine separately acknowledged India’s increased involvement. Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga said last week that New Delhi had submitted the most comprehensive of four ceasefire proposals being considered by Kiev, alongside initiatives from Türkiye, Egypt, and the US. 
Kiev is prepared to consider an energy and Black Sea ceasefire if it includes a halt to attacks on energy facilities and port infrastructure, Sibiga said. Ukraine says it is also open to an unconditional ceasefire along the line of contact.
Russia has also welcomed India’s efforts. President Vladimir Putin said last week that Prime Minister Narendra Modi raises the Ukraine conflict at every meeting and has “very good ideas” aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions. Modi urged Putin in August to move from “endless war” to an “end of war.”
India’s diplomatic engagement is unfolding as New Delhi also faces increased US pressure over its purchases of Russian energy. A recently passed US law would allow Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major purchasers of Russian oil, including India and China. New Delhi has warned that such measures could damage bilateral relations and disrupt global energy markets.
Russian crude, which accounts for more than 40% of India’s oil supplies, is crucial for the energy security of the world’s most populous nation. However, New Delhi is also seeking to preserve its commercial relationship with Washington amid prolonged trade negotiations.
India has maintained that the Ukraine conflict will ultimately be resolved through diplomacy and negotiations rather than restrictions on trade. Jaishankar said last month that New Delhi was in continuous contact with both sides and was looking for ideas that could help mitigate or end the fighting.

Senior Iranian military officer says US forces have moved 1,000 km away from Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:23:32 UTC
17:23:32 KST

TEHRAN, October 5. /TASS/. US forces have moved more than 1,000 km away from Iran’s border, the head of the Advisory Group to the Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said.
"The Americans have fled and moved more than 1,000km away from our borders. That was not their choice but the result of the influence of the Islamic Republic and the might of the IRGC ground force," Rear Admiral Ali Fadavi said live on public broadcaster.
According to the senior Iranian military officer, for the first time ever, US warships were absent from the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf of Oman, and the northern Indian Ocean. The Strait of Hormuz has been under control of Iran for several months already, he emphasized.
Nor has the United States achieved any of the goals it set during the war, Fadavi continued. Jointly with Muscat, Tehran has developed and adopted navigation rules for the Strait of Hormuz, despite Washington’s attempt to influence the situation in the region, he said.
Apart from that, the top IRGC commander noted, captains have had to navigate the southern Strait of Hormuz because of their insurance and financial obligations as he warned that vessels traversing this route can be "subjected" to actions by the Israeli Army at any moment. Meanwhile, a mere 3 to 4 million bpd of oil, or much less than before the war, is now shipped along an alternative route outside the one designated by Tehran, he concluded.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding calling for an immediate ceasefire on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, the United States resumed large-scale attacks on Iran overnight to July 8, having accused it of breaching the existing agreements concerning the Strait of Hormuz, a global chokepoint for approximately 25% of oil and some 20% of LNG supplies.
The Trump administration recently signaled an end to any large-scale use of force against Iran and a transition to economic pressure on the Islamic Republic through sanctions instead.

Swiss divided on early foreign language education

Swiss divided on early foreign language education
The reform of language teaching in primary schools is stirring debate in Switzerland. Left-wing parties defend early language teaching for national cohesion, while the centre-right Radical-Liberal party defends federalism.
On June 12, the Swiss government submitted two proposals for the new Languages Act for consultation. This consultation period ended on Monday. The debate centred on whether to introduce one national language and English in primary school, or a second national language from primary school through to the end of lower secondary education.
+ Young Swiss must learn second national language, says government
The Green party supports the first option, while the Social Democratic party favours the second should a revision prove necessary. The Radical-Liberals reject both options.
Swiss teachers support the second option, subject to adjusted objectives and sufficient funding. Cantons are also divided. Canton Fribourg, fore example, supports the first option, as does Valais.
Several cantonal parliaments in German-speaking Switzerland wish to postpone French lessons until secondary level.

Germany denies Russian art student a visa citing ‘security threat.’ Rights advocates call it a dangerous precedent.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:21:46 UTC
17:21:46 KST

Germany denies Russian art student a visa citing ‘security threat.’ Rights advocates call it a dangerous precedent.
The German Embassy in Moscow has denied a study visa to a graduate of the Design program at the Higher School of Economics (HSE) who had been accepted into a similar program at a German art university. Molnia, a human rights project for students, reported the refusal after reviewing the letter denying the visa.
In the letter, the embassy cited the risk that knowledge gained at the German university could be misused and pose a threat to Germany’s security and interests. “When weighing your personal interest in entering the country against the public interest in preventing a threat, it was determined that the public interest carries greater weight,” the embassy wrote in its response.
European universities could previously deny admission to students in technical fields over the risk of “knowledge being used for unintended purposes.” “This is the first time we have seen the phrase ‘security threat’ applied to a graduate of an arts program with no ties to government structures or military developments,” Molnia said.
Molnia called the case a dangerous precedent and promised to continue helping the student.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in early September that German authorities would tighten control over the entry of Russians in response to the sabotage at Leipzig Airport. He did not specify how the entry rules would change.

Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said an emergency regional sanitary commission had met after reports of a suspected “highly dangerous infectious” disease case. He said all identified contacts had been placed under medical observation, with no symptoms reported and laboratory tests returning “negative.”

TikTok, Instagram push museums to rethink how art is displayed
Old hand-scribbled "___ was here" tags are giving way to social media content, prompting Estonian museums to adapt how they present art for Instagram and TikTok audiences.
Like stores swapping out their seasonal displays, museums rearrange their exhibitions several times a year to keep visitors engaged. At the Pop and Contemporary Art Museum (PoCo) in Tallinn, the focus last week was on setting up its fall display.
Owner Linnar Viik said the museum tracks visitor movements and social media posts to identify works that are getting overlooked.
"We have to do something to draw more attention to them, move them around," he said.
The art museum, which boasts works by big names including Andy Warhol, Banksy, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, also knows how long visitors typically stay: about 45 minutes, or roughly the length of a Netflix episode. But individual works get much less attention.
"Before the COVID pandemic, people spent 20 to 25 seconds looking at a work that caught their attention in a museum," Viik said. "Now that's dropped to about ten to 15 seconds."
That makes it important for museums to create moments visitors want to share online.
Instagrammable stops
PoCo has five or six deliberately "Instagrammable" spots located throughout, including by Estonian street artist Edward von Lõngus' "Dance of Death," which has generated tens of thousands of photos taken from the same angle.
While traditional media coverage in Finland or Sweden can bring in more visitors than social media, Viik said students curating new exhibitions are also tasked with making them easy to share online.
Curator Karl Markus Mäekivi said a recognizable name or an unusual message can prompt people to snap pictures, but the right lighting and deliberate placement can also encourage visitors to stop and take a look.
State museums take a somewhat different approach, putting less emphasis on social media and more on helping people slow down and spend time with art.
Take the pressure off
At the Adamson-Eric Museum in Tallinn, visitors can grab a worksheet designed to encourage slower, more deliberate viewing.
"Visitors can choose one work that speaks to them for whatever reason and then use these questions to notice details they might otherwise miss in a hurry," curator Karin Vicente said.
Vicente said enjoying art doesn't require a scholarly approach so much as the confidence to take your time.
"It's okay not to look at everything or feel like you have to get through the whole building in half an hour," she said, "I look at what I like. Then the pressure comes off, and there's no need to hurry anymore."
--
Editor: Aleksander Krjukov, Aili Vahtla

Yemen military announces broad range of strikes against Houthis in bid to retake lost territory
The Yemeni military announced on Monday that it will launch a broad set of strikes against Iran-backed Houthi targets in an attempt to retake lost territory. The Houthis launched an offensive in September, which killed hundreds of combatants on both sides, according to UN figures, and has since become the most active front in the wider Middle East war.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The Yemeni military announced a broad set of strikes against Houthi targets on Monday, after the government declared a new campaign to retake all territory even as the Iran-backed group made fresh gains on the ground.
The declared offensive sets a lofty goal for the beleaguered Saudi-backed government a month after losing swathes of the country's Red Sea coastline and territory around the Bab al-Mandab Strait – a key chokepoint for international shipping.
Read moreYemen's government declares counter-offensive as Houthis cut vital route to besieged city
The Houthis, at war against the internationally recognised government, launched a lightning offensive in September that has killed hundreds of combatants on both sides and, according to UN figures, forced more than 145,000 people to flee their homes.
While the war in Yemen predates the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, the fighting there has in recent weeks become the most active front in the wider conflict.
Hours after the government announcement, Yemen's military spokesman said its forces launched over 1,000 "strikes against artillery and rocket launcher positions, defensive fortifications, approach and reinforcement routes, supply lines and logistics assets, combat reinforcements" belonging to the Houthis.
The government strikes, however, have yet to blunt ongoing Houthi advances on the ground.
On Sunday, the group effectively encircled the key city of Taiz after cutting the main supply route linking the city to the interim government capital of Aden.
Vast humanitarian crisis
"It is a significant development, but I think it is still too early to say that we are witnessing a decisive turning point," Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told AFP.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen's long-running civil war.
The fighting in Yemen has also drawn in Saudi Arabia – leader of an anti-Houthi military coalition since 2015 – with the group regularly claiming attacks on the kingdom's territory in recent weeks and declaring a blockade of its ships in the Red Sea.
Yemen is one of the poorest countries in the world and has been gripped by a vast humanitarian crisis since the civil war broke out in 2014.
That year the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the Saudi-backed government, before going on to take control of much of the country's north, with Riyadh's international coalition intervening the following year.

&quot;Hornets&apos; Nest&quot; a year later: expert examinations, investigation, and the struggle of the families of deceased Odrex patients
Ukraine

2026-10-05

"Hornets' Nest" a year later: expert examinations, investigation, and the struggle of the families of deceased Odrex patients
Kyiv • UNN
Almost a year has passed since the release of the documentary film “Hornets' Nest.” The families of deceased patients spoke about the current status of investigations and court proceedings concerning the circumstances of treatment at Odrex.
Almost a year has passed since the publication of the documentary film "The Hornet’s Nest", in which relatives of deceased Odrex patients shared their truth about treatment at the Odesa clinic. According to them, it resulted in complications, enormous bills, and the deaths of their loved ones. Even before the film was released, its subjects contacted law enforcement authorities. The UNN investigated what stage the investigation and court proceedings have reached.
Seven years without an expert examination — the case concerning the death of Svitlana Huk’s husband
Svitlana Huk’s story began back in 2019. Her husband turned to Odrex with a thymus tumor. According to the widow, doctors convinced the family that surgery was necessary and that the treatment had positive prospects.
After the surgery, the man’s condition sharply deteriorated, and several days later he died in intensive care.
Svitlana said that the family paid about $42,500 for the treatment. After her husband’s death, the clinic filed a lawsuit demanding that the widow pay an additional approximately UAH 900,000. This concerns civil case No. 522/19678/19, filed by Dim Medytsyny LLC, operating under the Odrex brand, against Svitlana Huk to recover a debt under a medical services agreement.
For her part, Huk filed a lawsuit against Dim Medytsyny LLC. Her civil case No. 522/10741/22 concerns the protection of consumer rights in the provision of medical services, partial invalidity of the transaction, and compensation for material and moral damages.
In addition to the civil disputes with the clinic, criminal proceedings No. 12022162510001375, registered under Part 2 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, are also ongoing. As part of these proceedings, the investigation must establish the circumstances surrounding Svitlana Huk’s husband’s treatment and provide them with a criminal-law assessment. However, after seven years, the case has still not reached the key stage — a full forensic medical examination.
And this is despite the fact that the examination is supposed to answer whether the treatment strategy was chosen correctly, whether the surgery was justified, whether the doctors complied with medical standards, and whether there is a causal link between their actions and Svitlana’s husband’s death.
However, Huk has been unable to obtain such a conclusion for years. The case materials were sent to expert institutions repeatedly, but the examination was never carried out.
Kyiv twice explained its refusal to conduct the examination by citing the absence of a pathological autopsy and the impossibility of reliably establishing the cause of death. Among the reasons for its refusal, Lviv cited the absence of an approved list of paid services, as well as the fact that the entries in the inpatient medical record had been made in Russian, which, according to the bureau’s position, prevented their objective examination.
At that point, the plan was to translate the documentation into Ukrainian and send the materials to the experts again. However, as Svitlana Huk told UNN , it has still not been possible to obtain the necessary expert conclusion.
Even as part of the criminal proceedings, Kyiv refused to conduct the examination for the third time,
Olha Melai — questions about the documents and a blocked investigation
Olha Melai’s husband underwent chemotherapy at Odrex. Because he needed regular drug infusions, he was offered the installation of a special port — a procedure that clinic staff described as minimally invasive and uncomplicated. However, after the intervention, Ihor Melai ended up in intensive care in critical condition and later died. In total, the treatment and medications cost the family more than UAH 2.5 million.
After her husband’s death, Olha had questions about the medical documentation: according to her, the discharge summary contained practically no information either about the port insertion itself or about the consequences of the intervention. The widow contacted law enforcement authorities and handed investigators copies of documents confirming payment for the treatment, while the investigator said that the medical record was to be submitted for a forensic medical examination.
Melai contacted law enforcement. Based on her statement, criminal proceedings No. 42025163030000200 are being investigated under Part 3 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. She provided the investigators with copies of documents confirming payment for treatment, and the investigator said that he intended to submit the medical record for a forensic medical examination.
Not limiting herself to the criminal proceedings, Melai contacted the Ministry of Health and asked it to verify the medical records concerning her husband’s treatment at Odrex for discrepancies and possible falsification. The Ministry instructed the Health Department of the Odesa Regional Military Administration to conduct a clinical and expert assessment; however, the inspection could not be carried out. The Department explained that the Odrex clinic had not provided the patient’s medical documentation, citing its seizure by law enforcement as part of the criminal proceedings.
After that, Melai herself contacted the police, asking them to grant the Department access to the seized materials. At the same time, she submitted requests to the National Health Service of Ukraine and the eHealth system to verify the data concerning her husband’s treatment and his electronic medical records.
Thus, almost a year after the criminal proceedings were opened, the question of what exactly happened during Ihor Melai’s treatment and whether any violations occurred still remains without a final answer.
Khrystyna Totkailo’s father was promised that his voice would be preserved
In August 2024, Khrystyna Totkailo learned that her father had cancer. The family lives in Kyiv, so they initially contacted Feofaniya Hospital. According to Khrystyna, after a consultation, the doctors concluded that aggressive chemotherapy before radical surgery was too risky in his case.
According to Khrystyna, surgeon Ihor Bielotserkovskyi was also present at that consultation. He was the one who suggested that the family contact the Odesa-based Odrex clinic, where his wife, oncologist Maryna Bielotserkovska, worked. Khrystyna recalls that the family was told that this was where her father could receive treatment in a way that would preserve his larynx and voice.
At Odrex, the man was prescribed a five-day course of chemotherapy, with another course planned. He was also fitted with a feeding gastrostomy. Khrystyna said that she repeatedly asked staff to monitor its condition and change the dressings, but, according to her, there was no proper care for several days. Before he was discharged, it was discovered that a through-and-through opening had formed in the area of the gastrostomy.
After returning to Kyiv, her father’s condition deteriorated sharply: his kidneys began to fail, and wounds appeared in his mouth. Khrystyna claims that she did not receive clear answers to her questions about the prescribed treatment and her father’s condition.
The family paid more than UAH 250,000 for the treatment. It was not possible to save her father—he died. After his death, Khrystyna contacted law enforcement.
After his death, Khrystyna contacted law enforcement. Based on her statement, criminal proceedings No. 42025163030000197 are being investigated.
Recently, I was informed that the investigator in the case had been changed and that the documents had been sent for examination. For now, this is all the information I have about the progress of the proceedings. It is difficult for me to obtain more detailed information because I am in Kyiv, while the investigation is being conducted in Odesa,
Several years have already passed, yet the families still have not received definitive answers. The investigations have been accompanied by delays, changes of investigators, and difficulties in carrying out examinations. At the same time, the relatives of deceased Odrex patients continue to fight for the right to know the truth about what happened to their loved ones.

The Trump administration is pursuing deals with allied nations to extend its offensive to land across multiple Latin American countries. Guatemala denied reaching such a deal. Ecuador launched similar missions with the U.S. in March.
President Trump has said the U.S. is in "armed conflict" with cartels in Latin America and has justified the attacks as a necessary escalation to stem the flow of drugs into the U.S. and fatal overdoses claiming American lives. But his administration has offered little evidence to support its claims of killing smugglers.

It explained that 134,422 buildings were completely destroyed, while 13,848 sustained severe damage and around 328,627 housing units were damaged.

Brazil's right-wing Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro secured a surprise lead over President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s election, sending it to a runoff in three weeks.
In a result that defied opinion poll projections showing Lula in the lead, Flavio Bolsonaro scored 47% of the vote to the incumbent's 45%.
If Bolsonaro triumphs in the Oct. 25 election, the Latin American powerhouse will join a steady rightward march in the region in recent elections, a trend championed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The election results included a series of landslide wins for the right in parliament in a massive setback to Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in office to cement his legacy.
"I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round. The game is about to start. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people," the 80-year-old said.
The veteran leftist has branded the election a battle between democracy and "barbarism," warning voters that Brazil's sovereignty was at stake in the face of U.S. pressure.
Flavio Bolsonaro was a little-known senator a few months ago when his father anointed him his political heir, unable to run himself as he serves a 27-year sentence for an attempted coup after losing a 2022 election bid.
However, his father's powerful name won over the country's conservative base and he slid past Lula despite a campaign marked by scandals and mudslinging.
"I am truly happy with the result," Flavio Bolsonaro said after results came through, hailing the "very real possibility" of a run-off victory.
Voters in the deeply polarized nation were jaded by familiar choices and few voted with conviction.
Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, said she had planned to vote for Lula, as she always has. But "when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes."
Carolina Botelho, a political scientist at the Rio de Janeiro State University, said that the leading candidate in the first round has won every election in Brazil since the end of the country's military dictatorship in 1985.
With 56 million votes, Flavio Bolsonaro's first round performance outdid that of Jair Bolsonaro in 2018, when he was elected and 2022.
It emerged during the campaign that Flavio Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic "Dark Horse" about his father.
For many voters, this did little to move the needle.
"Things are truly terrible. As far as I'm concerned, the left just doesn't work anymore," said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, in the Rocinha favela, saying he was fed up with the "horrible" expense of basic goods.
Flavio Bolsonaro highlighted Sunday that as president he will have the possibility of appointing four justices to the powerful Supreme Court – which convicted his father and has been at the center of key political and criminal scandals.
The elections proved a triumphant comeback for the Bolsonaro family after Jair Bolsonaro lost a re-election bid in 2022, leading to violent riots in the capital and his conviction last year for attempting a coup.
Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro and another one of Jair Bolsonaro's sons, Carlos Bolsonaro, both secured seats in the senate.
Jair Bolsonaro's youngest son Jair Renan, 28, was elected as a federal lawmaker.
Flavio has cast himself as more "moderate" than his firebrand father, but his critics were concerned.
"Flavio is a danger to Brazil, he represents a step backward. We can see everything his father did...He really destroyed Brazil," said Anderson de Almeida, a 45-year-old doorman.
Trump had said he was watching the election "very closely," but did not endorse Flavio Bolsonaro.
The US president has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.
Lula repeatedly warned him not to "meddle" in the elections.
Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction for 18 months.
The charges, thrown out on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him.
In his third term he oversaw a drop in inflation and unemployment, but voters complain about a high cost of living and as in many Latin American nations, citizens are fed up with high levels of crime and violence.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's Rita Chou (周婕妤) won her second Women's 9-Ball World Championship after defeating defending champion Seo Seoa of South Korea 3-1 in Sunday's final in Bali, Indonesia, per UDN.
The 39-year-old Chou, nicknamed the "Big-Eyed Girl," earned NT$1.75 million (US$55,000) in prize money. The victory also made her the second Taiwanese woman to win the annual pool tournament twice, matching Liu Hsin-mei's (柳信美) record from 1999 and 2002. She previously won the world title in 2023.
