Seo defeated two other Taiwanese players, Chou Chia-chia (周家嘉) and Chiang Shui-ching (江水淨), on her way to the final.
President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) congratulated Chou after her victory, praising her performance and encouraging Taiwan's billiards players to continue competing internationally.
The Ministry of Sports said in a press release that Taiwan's billiards players have achieved increasingly strong results at international competitions and that it will continue providing resources and logistical support to help athletes compete on the world stage.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Kaohsiung-based Taiwan International Shipbuilding Co. held the keel-laying ceremony for the second of six Coast Guard ocean patrol vessels in Kaohsiung on Friday.
A keel is the ship's structural foundation that runs along the bottom center from the bow to the stern, according to a press release. Laying the keel marks the official start of a ship's construction.
Siraya, the first of the six cutters, was launched on Nov. 1, 2025. It is named after one of the country's Indigenous groups, and other ships in the class will follow the same pattern.
The builder said the new patrol ships use reinforced steel for the hull and frame. The front uses an axe bow design that anchors the vessel for added stability in rough seas.
The builder said the displacement volume is about 5,000 metric tonnes. It added that the ship has a hybrid propulsion system for 30-day missions from cold, high-latitude regions to the tropical Indian Ocean.
The builder said the ships will secure maritime safety, enforce fishery laws, and support salvage operations. It noted that the ships will be delivered by 2031.

Taiwan High Speed Rail to add rush-hour non-reserved trains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
08:00:06 UTC
17:00:06 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan High Speed Rail Corporation will add two southbound trains per hour on Friday evenings, with most cars offering non-reserved seating, to ease crowding during peak travel hours.
The additional service will operate every Friday between 5 p.m. and 9 p.m., THSRC said last Monday. Eight extra southbound trains will depart from Nangang or Taipei during the four hours and terminate at Taichung, per CNA.
All cars on the additional trains will offer unreserved seating except business class. THSRC said the busiest section for unreserved passengers is north of Taichung, where heavy crowds can also affect travelers with reserved seats.
The changes follow severe crowding during the Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers' Day holiday period. A record 347,970 passengers used the high-speed rail on Sept. 24, while nearly 1.79 million traveled between Sept. 24 and 29, according to Economic Daily News.
Some passengers with reserved seats nearly missed their trains because of the crowds. Business-class passengers also complained that people with unreserved tickets had entered their cars.
To increase capacity, the operator will reverse trains directly at station platforms before sending them back into service. The arrangement will allow trains to begin their return journeys within about 12 minutes and reduce waiting times for northbound passengers, per TVBS News.
Before the regular Friday service begins, the new arrangement will first be used on Thursday during the National Day holiday travel period. Two extra southbound trains per hour will run to Taichung that day, while selected services will provide nine to 11 cars with unreserved seating.
A late-night train will also be added on Thursday, followed by an extra northbound service on Friday. The measures are intended to increase capacity before new trains enter service next July, per CTEE.

Estonia is moving troops closer to the border with the Russian Federation and preparing for a possible conflict — FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:59:41 EEST
16:59:41 KST

Estonia is moving troops closer to the border with the Russian Federation and preparing for a possible conflict — FT
Kyiv • UNN
Estonia is transferring a brigade to Jõhvi, 50 km from the border with the Russian Federation, and implementing an active defense strategy. The country is purchasing HIMARS and Chunmoo.
Estonia is redeploying a key brigade from the city of Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 kilometers from the Russian border, as part of launching an “active defense” strategy in preparation for possible aggression by russia. Estonian officials told the Financial Times, reports UNN.
Details
According to officials, Estonia is continuously moving troops closer to the border with Russia and purchasing weapons capable of striking deep into Russian territory, as this frontline NATO country prepares for possible aggression by moscow beyond Ukraine.
However, Estonia’s armed forces and intelligence chiefs do not believe that russia is seeking a full-scale war with NATO, at least over the next two years, but they are convinced that the russian federation is preparing for a possible future conflict with this Baltic state. This has prompted the country, which has no air force of its own, to adopt an “active defense” strategy.
“We have to start at the border and win the first battles,” said Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of Estonia’s First Brigade, the country’s main combat force.
Under the new strategy, his unit will be permanently redeployed from Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 km from the Russian border, where large new facilities for housing soldiers are currently being built.
“Deterrence is not working. The critical period for resolving this issue for all of us in the Baltic countries is the next one to four years,” said a representative of Estonian military intelligence.
“For deterrence to be credible, we must make aggression against us unthinkable. Our goal is clear: to keep the enemy and the devastation of war away from Estonian territory,” Estonia’s Ministry of Defence emphasized.
In May, the Estonian government introduced the term “active defense” into its national security concept. Since then, the country’s armed forces have begun a quiet but radical reorganization. From Tapa, Estonia’s main military base, elite units are being permanently redeployed to positions closer to the Russian border. In addition to the new base in Jõhvi, a base designed to accommodate 1,000 servicemembers is also being built in the border city of Narva.
Over the past year, the country has signed contracts to purchase nine American Himars multiple-launch rocket systems, M57 ballistic missiles with a range of up to 300 km, as well as nine South Korean Chunmoo MLRS units with a similar range. It should be noted that the distance from Estonian border bases to Russia’s St. Petersburg is 260 km.
During the decade following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2014, Estonian military strategists developed a defense doctrine shaped by the country’s history and geography. Under this approach, in the event of aggression, the country’s conscripts would rapidly mobilize and conduct a tactical, almost guerrilla-style defense to impede Russian forces and inflict losses on them until NATO reinforcements arrived.
However, observing russia’s actions in Ukraine, Estonia’s military leaders concluded that such a plan would not work. They now believe that the kremlin does not care about losses, fighting to retain captured territory even after everything on it has been destroyed.
Estonia now plans to fight for every inch of territory and deliver powerful strikes against russia hundreds of kilometers behind the front line from the first day of any invasion.
At the same time, Tallinn’s greatest concern is the possible end of the war in Ukraine, after which russia could redeploy tens of thousands of battle-hardened troops to NATO’s borders. Estonian intelligence believes that this is precisely why the Baltic countries need to use the coming years to strengthen their defenses and deter russia.

Shipowners seek protection from drones after wave of attacks in the Black Sea and the Middle East - FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:53:08 EEST
16:53:08 KST

Shipowners seek protection from drones after wave of attacks in the Black Sea and the Middle East - FT
Kyiv • UNN
Following attacks in the Black Sea and the Persian Gulf, shipowners have sharply increased demand for counter-drone systems. Protecting a tanker costs around $500,000.
Commercial shipping companies are rushing to strengthen their fleets' protection against drones following a wave of attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and the Middle East. Financial Times reports, writes UNN.
Details
Counter-drone specialists, including Marss, Drone Defence and D-fend, said they had seen a sharp increase in the number of inquiries from shipowners, with particularly strong interest among companies involved in transporting oil and gas cargoes and operating in the marine energy infrastructure sector.
Commercial vessels, the publication writes, are increasingly becoming targets of attacks in the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea, as parties to conflicts seek to disrupt critical supply chains for goods, while shipowners willing to operate in dangerous waters are setting record freight rates for their vessels.
D-fend Solutions Chief Marketing Officer Jeffrey Starr told the Financial Times that the company, founded by Israeli cybersecurity experts and specializing in taking control of hostile drones before safely landing them, was seeing "huge demand" from the shipping sector.
"We are seeing shipowners, shippers and naval forces facing an asymmetric threat that is driving a significant increase in inquiries about our technologies," he said. "This threat from unmanned aircraft is no longer confined to areas of intense combat."
According to Chief Executive Richard Gill, rival company Drone Defence has recorded an increase in inquiries from oil tankers and gas carriers, as if shipowners can protect their vessels, "they will be able to choose riskier routes."
John Stawpert, maritime director at the International Chamber of Shipping, said the threat posed to the industry by drones had increased in recent years, "from both surface and airborne platforms, and this is particularly relevant in areas of active conflict, such as the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea and the Black Sea."
According to the International Maritime Organization, more than 20 sailors have been killed in the Persian Gulf by drone and missile strikes since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in late February, while around 30 people have been killed in the Black Sea this year.
The cost of chartering a supertanker to pass through the Strait of Hormuz reached a historic high of $1.2 million per day last week for voyages to China, compared with an average of about $79,000 per day in September last year.
Marine energy infrastructure, including pipelines, cables and wind farms, has also become a target, the publication notes. European security services report surveillance using drones and, in some cases, covert attacks, while NATO countries are increasingly voicing concern over Russian interference in European waters, the publication writes.
According to several counter-drone specialists, until recently demand for anti-drone technology at sea came mainly from superyacht owners seeking protection from paparazzi.
"Superyachts were one of the areas where it all began ... and a significant number of top yachts are protected by the Nidar system," said Marss Development Director Rob Bullock.
The company is now seeing a "step change" in the development of vessels serving the offshore oil and gas industry, as "the technology and software for integrating it have reached a price point at which the costs of lost days due to such threats justify the investment."
Nidar systems operate by using onboard surveillance technologies, such as radar and cameras, to detect approaching threats. More advanced systems may include kinetic means of response, depending on the laws of the region in which the vessel operates.
Drones can also be disabled by jamming GPS signals or disrupting their control frequencies.
Hill said that a radar system with cameras and a signal-jamming system would cost approximately $500,000 for an oil tanker. Ships that cannot afford such technologies resort to more primitive means of protection against drones, such as nets and suspended water tanks, to confuse the drones or cause them to explode before they reach critical parts of the ship, the publication writes.
The key task for counter-drone companies is to develop systems capable of accurately targeting drones in conditions of heavy seas and withstanding exposure to corrosive salt water.
Starr said that D-Fend, whose technology was used to protect U.S. ports during this year's FIFA World Cup, had created a "reinforced, protected version" of its system for maritime applications, which had become "an excellent growth driver."
But keeping pace with the constantly changing threat is an ongoing struggle.
"It's an endless cycle," Bullock said. "Just when you think you've deployed the best thing you've ever deployed, it changes. Everything is moving so fast."

Russian authorities said a 27-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute was hospitalized on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia. She died during the night of Oct. 1-2.
Russian media reported that she had contracted pneumonic plague, although authorities have not publicly confirmed that diagnosis.
One version reported by Russian media said the woman had recently returned from a work trip to Buryatia, where a plague outbreak had been detected near the border with Mongolia.
Another theory suggested she may have accidentally broken a test tube containing the plague bacterium at a laboratory.
Russia’s consumer protection watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, rejected the laboratory accident theory, saying no emergency involving pathogenic microorganisms had been recorded.
Hospital quarantined, 189 people hospitalized
The Shelekhov hospital where the woman died was placed under quarantine. Authorities identified 189 people who had been in contact with her and hospitalized them for observation.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Irkutsk Region Governor Igor Kobzev said on Oct. 2 that none of the hospitalized people showed signs of the disease and that laboratory tests had returned negative.
The following morning, authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk urged residents to temporarily avoid traveling to Shelekhov and neighboring settlements because of the reported plague death.
The warning was later deleted.
What is plague?
Plague is a serious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. It has several forms, including bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic plague.
People most commonly contract plague through bites from infected fleas carried by rodents.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread between people through respiratory droplets. Unlike bubonic plague, it can therefore spread directly from person to person.
The disease can be treated with antibiotics if detected early. Without treatment, however, pneumonic plague can be rapidly fatal.
Russia’s last recorded case was in 2016
Russia’s last officially recorded human case of plague was reported in 2016 in the nearby Altai region.
A 10-year-old boy contracted the disease after skinning a marmot and developing an infection through damaged skin. He survived after receiving timely medical treatment.
The reported case in Irkutsk has not been publicly confirmed as plague by Russian health authorities, leaving the circumstances surrounding the woman’s death unclear.

Planning next year’s ultra-luxury escape? All-inclusives, celebrations and privacy are among the experiences driving high-end traveller habits.
Is it too early to start thinking about New Year’s resolutions? Well, if more travel in 2027 has been on your mind, perhaps a luxury trip should make that list, too.
Offering inspiration for high-end tourism, Virtuoso’s 2027 Luxe Report draws on insights from more than 3,100 travel advisors across more than 50 countries to reveal what will shape luxury travel in the coming year.
According to those surveyed by the global network of agencies, 59% of advisors predict spending on trips will increase modestly and 13% forecast a significant increase, while a further 23% expect spending to remain at 2026 levels.
This suggests that luxury travellers are “not simply maintaining current levels but accelerating their prioritisation of meaningful experiences and investing more in access, quality and time”, Virtuoso said, adding that “value and safety” have become increasingly important in deciding where they go and how they travel.
In 2027, Europe is set to dominate the luxury travel map, with seven of the top 10 most popular global destinations. Following Japan in first place, Italy, France, Greece and Spain make up the top five, while Croatia, South Africa, Portugal, the UK and the US are in the top 10.
Celebrating milestones, excitement to explore a new destination, and spending time with loved ones are the top three reasons why affluent travellers will be jetting away next year.
Other leading travel trends include multigenerational family travel, immediate family travel, and expedition cruising.
Top ‘ultraluxe travel’ experiences
Virtuoso’s survey found that advisors saw a 47% increase in “ultraluxe travel”, which covers exclusive use, private or exceptionally high-end experiences.
So, what will shape the experiences of the high-end traveller next year?
Luxury all-inclusive experiences
All-inclusive experiences top the ultraluxe travel list for 2027. In a separate report, Virtuoso said that “these days, the best all-inclusive properties are rewriting the script”. The company added that “tasting menus take the place of buffets, private villas reign over cookie-cutter rooms, and service is genuine and personal, never transactional.”
Celebration travel
From destination weddings and anniversaries to family gatherings, graduations and milestone birthdays, celebration travel ranks second among the ultraluxe travel experiences. According to Virtuoso’s research, Greece, Bali, Maldives, Italy and French Polynesia rank among the top five honeymoon destinations for 2027.
Privacy
With social media’s ability to quickly turn obscure destinations into must-see, overcrowded spots overnight, for the luxury traveller, privacy means avoiding the queues and camera clicks, while being able to move through the world with minimal friction.
Hyper-personalised experiences
Luxury travellers are no longer satisfied with splurging on a trip abroad just for the sake of it. They are instead pursuing encounters that are personal. According to the report, personal enrichment and education ranked eighth on the top 10 motivations for why the affluent will travel next year.
From the tarmac to bed and board, luxury travellers’ tastes are shifting from generic, off-the-shelf experiences to ones shaped by their exact preferences, which provides a sense of exclusivity. This can include private tours or one-of-a-kind dining experiences catered around their preferences.
Active and adventure trips
Rounding up the ultraluxe travel experiences list are active and adventure trips, with “seeking adventure” ranking 10th among affluent travellers’ top motivations for travel in 2027. Virtuoso’s research found Antarctica, South Africa, Iceland, Costa Rica and Kenya as the top five most popular adventure travel destinations for next year.

Russia Hides Potential Pneumonic Plague Outbreak After Fatal Lab Breach

Russia Hides Potential Pneumonic Plague Outbreak After Fatal Lab Breach
A health scare in Siberia is raising questions over what Russian authorities are trying to hide, as public warnings vanish, officials avoid naming the infection, and emergency measures quietly expand.
A suspected case of pneumonic plague has triggered emergency measures in Russia’s Irkutsk region after a 28-year-old employee of an anti-plague research institute died and nearly 200 people were placed under medical observation, while Russian officials have avoided publicly identifying the disease.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Sun on October 3, Daria Shipilova, 28, who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, reportedly died from plague, prompting the isolation of 189 people and an emergency response involving Russia’s top infectious disease official.
Shipilova was hospitalized in the town of Shelekhov with severe pneumonia-like symptoms before her death. The Shelekhov district hospital was subsequently placed under quarantine as health authorities began tracing people who may have come into contact with her.
Russian outlet Lyudi Baikala reported that Shipilova worked as a laboratory technician and may have been exposed on September 25 after breaking a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen. The circumstances of the reported incident have not been officially confirmed.
Despite the scale of the response, authorities in the Irkutsk region have stopped short of publicly confirming pneumonic plague. Governor Igor Kobzev referred only to a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection,” saying identified contacts had been placed under medical observation and had so far tested negative.
Russia’s chief sanitary official and head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, rushed more than 2,600 miles from Moscow to Irkutsk to oversee the emergency response, according to The Sun, yet Russian authorities have still refused to publicly name the infection behind the alarm.
The Sun reported that 189 people were isolated—114 in one hospital, 63 in another, and 12 at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute. Antibiotics reportedly disappeared from some pharmacy shelves amid panic buying, while authorities canceled public events.
The head of neighboring Buryatia, Alexey Tsydenov, initially said Shipilova had died from plague, only to later soften his statement to say she “may have died from plague.”
The information surrounding the suspected outbreak has also begun disappearing. Authorities in Baikalsk deleted a warning urging residents to avoid travel to Shelekhov, while Kremlin-linked REN TV removed five posts mentioning plague.
Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov, now based in the US, told The Sun that Popova’s personal intervention suggested the situation was “terrible” and “critical,” while accusing authorities of concealing the full circumstances surrounding the case.
Despite the quarantine, emergency response and nearly 200 people being placed under observation, Russian officials continue to publicly describe the case only as a suspected “particularly dangerous infection.” As of October 4, however, authorities said those under observation showed no symptoms and had tested negative.
The suspected plague case comes amid broader concerns over infectious diseases in Russia. In September, researchers identified the drug-resistant tuberculosis strain EurA1.1 in several Russian regions, while the country recorded around 48,000 tuberculosis cases in 2025, including tens of thousands involving drug-resistant forms of the disease.

Waste management, farmers feel the squeeze as diesel prices soar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:41:00 UTC
16:41:00 KST

Waste management, farmers feel the squeeze as diesel prices soar
Estonia's rising diesel prices are putting pressure on waste collection businesses and farmers alike, leaving both grappling with sharply higher operating costs.
Amid the ongoing crisis in the Middle East, diesel prices in Estonia have climbed to around €2 a liter this fall. For waste management provider Eesti Keskkonnateenused, the increase means it may have to negotiate higher waste collection fees with local governments before the end of the year.
Southern regional manager Mart Laidmets said waste collection contracts are generally signed with local governments for several years at a time, with an option to extend them, but such sharp fuel price hikes are difficult to anticipate.
"We have no choice but to negotiate with local governments about whether and by how much they are willing to raise prices," Laidmets told ERR, adding that the company was already close to the limit of how much it could offset rising costs through greater efficiency.
Eesti Keskkonnateenused's southern region operates a fleet of about 30 vehicles, using roughly 60,000 liters of diesel a month to serve Tartu, Estonia's second-largest city, as well as further-flung regions including Setomaa Municipality.
Higher fuel costs are also being passed on by the company's transport partners, Laidmets noted, including those hauling waste and other loads between Tartu, Tallinn and Võru.
'Where can I save that money?'
Farmers are feeling the impact as well. Jõgeva County grain farmer Tõnis Soopalu said filling up his tractor's 450-liter tank has soared, more than doubling from €270 to €550. That's enough fuel, he noted, for a single workday.
During the busiest periods, when combines and grain dryers are running, his farm can go through more than 1,000 liters of diesel a day.
"When it comes to cutting costs, the big question is, where can I save that money?" Soopalu asked. Cutting back on inputs can reduce yields, while skipping necessary work or stopping the dryer could damage the grain.
While the farmer said there was no reason for panic yet, he acknowledged the volatility was making it harder to plan costs. Rising natural gas prices are another concern as well, because gas is used to produce nitrogen fertilizer.
"If oil prices stay this high, we've seen before that it's not sustainable for very long," Soopalu said. "Right now, it's a question of how much will be produced, whether it will be produced at all and what availability will look like. There's plenty to worry about."

Bpost increases cost of sending parcels and letters from 1 January 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:39:15 UTC
16:39:15 KST

From 1 January, Belgian postal services provider Bpost is increasing rates for sending letters and parcels. On average, a stamp will cost around 8 per cent more. Sending a small parcel from a post office will cost 40 cents more.
Bpost increases cost of sending parcels and letters from 1 January 2027
According to Bpost, the price rises are necessary because “Belgians’ postal habits continue to change rapidly.”
The postal operator bases its claim on the most recent study by the Belgian Institute for Postal Services and Telecommunications (BIPT). In 2025, only 22 per cent of respondents said they still sent letters, compared with 41 per cent five years earlier.
“As volumes fall, the cost per letter rises for us. This is because the costs of staff and sorting centres remain the same,” says spokesperson Mathieu Goedefroy. “That is why the price increase is unavoidable.”
Here’s how the prices are changing
Standard postage stamp: 1.63 euros becomes 1.77 euros
Priority postage stamp: 2.52 euros becomes 2.73 euros
Registered post: 9.85 euros becomes 10.76 euros
Sending a parcel at the post office: 8.60 becomes 9 euros
Post within Europe: 3.07 euros becomes 3.36 euros
International post: 3.29 euros becomes 3.58 euros
Another important point to note: older stamps will remain valid next year as well.
Parcels to cost 4.5 per cent more on average
Sending parcels is therefore also set to become more expensive. To send a parcel from a post office using the ‘bpack 24h’ service – for parcels within Belgium that are usually delivered the next working day – you currently pay 8.60 euros. Bpost is raising this to 9 euros.
Prices for other domestic parcels are rising by an average of around 4.5 per cent, depending on the weight and type of parcel. According to Bpost, anyone wishing to send a parcel as cheaply as possible is advised to send it outside peak periods, create a shipping label online and have the parcel delivered to a collection point.
Surcharge during peak month
As in previous years, a €1 surcharge will be applied during the busy period between Black Friday and Christmas, as the number of parcels rises sharply at this time.
These price rises may not be the end of the story. According to Bpost, depending on inflation, prices could be increased by up to a further 3 per cent in the course of 2027.

The motion was opposed by four of the Greens’ five MPs, and is expected to face a legal challenge under equality laws. Polanski did not take a side but justified the motion’s broad argument by pointing to the death toll in Gaza.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Lichtenstein condemned the motion: “I don’t think it’s helpful, and it doesn’t make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians.”
Asked if she would remain in the party, she said: “I haven’t decided yet. Certainly it’s quite possible that I will leave the party, and I’m giving it a little time, and to talk with colleagues.”
The motion says Zionism – the movement for a Jewish state – should be “treated as any other form of racism”. It calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.
Some Jewish Greens have expressed concern that this will mean they could face disciplinary action for belonging to Jewish organisations that officially support Zionism, even synagogues. Supporters of the motion, which was led by a group called Greens for Palestine, have said this would not happen.
Asked about this issue, Lichtenstein said she was less worried about being personally targeted than about the potential impact on organisations. She said: “I’m not concerned about people accusing me of supporting Israel’s right to exist, and therefore, I’m a racist, which of course is not the case. I’m just concerned that this is a very bad motion …
“What concerns me is that the party might accuse UK organisations, Jewish organisations, and also Israeli-Jewish and joint Arab-Jewish organisations, of being Zionist and therefore racist. I support an awful lot of those sorts of organisations that are working against the occupation, and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians.”
The idea of calling for a single Palestinian state was not an issue for all Jewish Greens, Lichtenstein said, but party policy had been that it should be “up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future, one state or two”.
The chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, described the motion as “poisonous antisemitism” and a “threat to British Jews and to Britain”.
He said he was “appalled” by the motion, claiming the Green party had resurrected a “discredited and dangerous slander” first promoted by the Soviet Union.
“All decent people will see this for what it is: poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain,” he said.
Israel barred Polanski from entering the country in retaliation for the motion, which the Israeli foreign ministry said “constitute[d] a clear antisemitic text”.
It is understood some Green members are consulting lawyers over whether the policy could be challenged for breaching equalities legislation.
Adam Wagner KC, the barrister who led a case that concluded Jeremy Corbyn’s Labour party broke equalities laws over antisemitism, said such a case would have a good chance of success. “I think there is a strong risk that the motion as passed contravenes the Equality Act 2010, which applies to political parties, as it will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally,” he said.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action against Thames Valley police to challenge the legality of search warrants that led to his arrest earlier this year, a judicial spokesperson has said.
A private high court hearing is due to take place before Mr Justice Hilliard on Thursday to determine whether documents related to the the former Duke of York’s call for a judicial review can be made public; with Thames Valley police in opposition.
The legal fight stems from the issuing of warrants by an Old Bailey judge that allowed police to raid Mountbatten-Windsor’s residence on the Sandringham estate, and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files.
A high court judge subsequently granted him permission to challenge the legality of the force’s actions over the searches.
According to the Daily Telegraph, which first reported Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal challenge, it represented the first time a member of the royal family had challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on his 66th birthday in relation to allegations that when he was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.
Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with the late financier.
Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on 19 February and interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.
Misconduct in public office can cover a wide range of conduct, including sharing confidential financial information, financial misconduct, wilful neglect of duty and sexual misconduct. It also covers corruption and improper interference, conflict of interest, perverting the course of justice, dishonesty or fraudulent conduct, and misconduct leading to personal gain.
Thames Valley police said: “Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”
Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for comment.

However, Japan has claimed the Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan islands and a group of small uninhabited islands as its own. The Russian Foreign Ministry has repeatedly emphasized that Russia’s sovereignty over these territories, which is established under international law, is beyond doubt.
On October 1, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the 23rd meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club that Moscow seeks good and neighborly relations with Tokyo. According to the president, both countries have areas of mutual interest. However, Russia’s approach to ties with Japan has not changed, whereas Tokyo’s attitude toward Moscow has, Putin said, emphasizing that Japan had imposed sanctions on Russia.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:33:47 UTC
16:33:47 KST

Pro-Russian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik declared his party the winner in Bosnia and Herzegovina's elections held on Oct. 4.
Dodik was not on the ballot, but Zeljka Cvijanovic from his Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) party is poised to retain her seat in the country's tripartite presidency, according to preliminary results.
The Balkan country held elections for the presidency, shared among the Croat, Serb, and Bosniak ethnic groups, as well as for regional and cantonal governments, under a complex political system established after the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
"If it had not been for (U.S. President) Donald Trump's magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told his supporters, while also thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin, who voiced support for the SNSD before the elections.
Dodik, known for his separatist and pro-Moscow views, served as the president of Republika Srpska — Bosnia's Serb-dominated entity — between 2022 and 2025.
In 2025, he was stripped of office and barred from running for six years for defying the country's international envoy.
With over 95% of the votes counted, Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party (SDP BiH) is set to retain his Bosniak seat in the presidency, and Bosnian Croat nationalist candidate Darijana Filipovic has claimed victory in the race for the Croat seat.
Dodik's SNSD is also expected to retain power in the Republika Srpska local parliament and presidency.
The vote was marked by a relatively low turnout, with 42% of voters casting ballots, down almost 10% from the 2022 elections.

NEW YORK, October 5. /TASS/. The International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) believes that if restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz persist, grain prices in some regions of the world could rise by as much as 80%, ICC Secretary General John Denton said, according to The Wall Street Journal.

“The visit is an excellent opportunity to emphasise the importance that both Switzerland and India attach to this relationship,” he said.He said India-Switzerland ties were based on “shared democratic values as well as on trust and mutual respect”.“My visit is a stepping stone towards further growth, deepening and strengthening of our close, broad and long-standing partnership,” Parmelin said.He also highlighted the significance of the first anniversary of TEPA's implementation, saying it was a moment to assess the progress made by the two sides while looking towards future cooperation.“It is the right moment to celebrate how far we have come together, but even more importantly, to shape our joint future,” he said.During his three-day visit, Parmelin is expected to hold discussions with Indian leaders on trade, investment, science and technology, innovation, mobility, cultural exchanges and people-to-people ties. Regional and global issues, as well as multilateral cooperation, are also expected to feature in the talks.The Swiss president is travelling with a delegation of senior officials and business representatives. It is his first State visit to India and his second visit to the country this year after he attended the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February.
Parmelin will also meet President Murmu, who is scheduled to host a ceremonial banquet in his honour.He is scheduled to attend the second India-EFTA Prosperity Summit on October 7, marking the first anniversary of TEPA's operationalisation.The EFTA comprises Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. This visit will further strengthen bilateral relations, building upon the regular high-level exchanges and deepen cooperation in new areas of mutual interest,” the MEA said.

Steel Dome is Türkiye’s integrated, layered air defense architecture, bringing together radar and other sensors, command-and-control systems and weapons to detect, track, and counter aerial threats across different ranges and altitudes. Its capabilities include long-range air and missile defense, early warning and systems designed to counter drones.

Details
On Monday, the euro plunged to a 17-month low as fiscal concerns in France, amid a sharp collapse in the bond market, heightened fears that the crisis could spread across the region, helping the dollar strengthen despite weak U.S. employment data that reduced expectations of a rate hike in the near term, the publication writes.

According to the available information, the single currency was last down 0.68% at $1.1176, weakening 0.5% against the Swiss franc and falling 0.39% against the pound sterling.
"Bond market turmoil and euro weakness have raised fears that France’s problems could spread to the eurozone, similar to the debt crisis more than a decade ago, and force the European Central Bank to help shore up French debt. Some analysts, however, said it was still too early to judge whether the risk of contagion was increasing," the publication writes.
Meanwhile, Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for the Asia-Pacific region at State Street Investment Management, said that "France’s fiscal position is becoming increasingly unstable, while the market has only been reacting since last week."
"For now, I think this is more a story about a country than a euro crisis," he added.

Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to pass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:22:01 UTC
16:22:01 KST

Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has announced a snap general election three days after rightwing parties torpedoed the emergency legislation his minority government had put forward in response to growing public anger over the country’s housing crisis.
Sánchez, who has been in office since 2018, used a televised address to communicate his decision, which had been widely expected.
Announcing on Monday morning that an early general election would be held on 29 November, the prime minister defended his government’s social and humanitarian record in office and admitted it had made mistakes, but insisted it was time to let the Spanish people have their say.
“It’s up to you now,” he said. “A glance at the horizon shows us that the world is in a very complex era of transformation and transition. It’s a time of great tension, of climate emergency, and of social and technological changes – including highly disruptive advances in artificial intelligence. It is, therefore, a time of great dangers, but also – if we know how to seize the moment – of great opportunities. You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play as well.”
Sánchez’s gamble is being seen as a pragmatic move from a seasoned political risk-taker. His minority coalition government with the small, leftwing Sumar alliance, has faced a tough time in parliament since the prime minister secured his return to office by striking a controversial deal with Catalan pro-indepedence parties in the aftermath of the inconclusive general election in July 2023.
Unable to pass a budget for the past three years, and with his party and inner circle beset by corruption allegations and his government facing enduring pressure over its handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta over the summer, he appears to have decided a snap election is his best chance of survival.
On Monday morning, Sánchez repeated his familiar insistence that the choice was between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would curtail freedoms and turn back the clock on hard-won advances.
“You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility. You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.”
The next general election had been due before the end of next summer.
The government’s efforts to address the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
But the decrees were voted down in congress on Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts. The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a government, said it believedconstruction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis.
The rejection of the decrees met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “shame” and “Your profits; our misery”.
The PP welcomed news of the snap election. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” said the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “These isn’t an election like previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez.”
Vox’s leader, Santiago Abascal, also hailed the decision. “At last we’ll be voting and at last Spain will be able to choose what kind of country it wants to be,” he said. “That’s the only good news Sánchez can bring us these days.”
Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month following the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and saw a huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011 indignados movement spring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square.
Over the weekend, large demonstrations were held across the country as protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000.
Although polls consistently place the PP well ahead of Sánchez’s Spanish Socialist Workers’ party – and show that support for Vox is growing – the prime minister will be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise leftwing voters.
The housing issue has served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of the continuing crisis in Ceuta, which was sparked when around 70,000 people crossed into the territory from neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.
Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years.
In July this year, the prime minister’s brother, David Sánchez, was banned from holding public office for nine years after being found guilty of administrative misconduct relating to his hiring by a socialist-led council in the south-western region of Extremadura.
Meanwhile Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial after a judge charged her with embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation.
David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.

Spanish PM Sanchez calls snap election as pressure mounts over housing crisis
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called an early election for November 29. Facing the electorate now could be risky, as Sanchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Monday he would call an early election on November 29, after parliament rejected housing relief measures proposed by his government.
"To do more, we need to renew and broaden the support of the people," Sanchez, in office since 2018, said in a televised address, adding his aim was "to secure a much broader, progressive majority in parliament".
In recent weeks, Spanish residents have demanded solutions from the government over housing affordability, holding protests in cities across the country after public outrage grew over the televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid last month.
Read moreSpanish lawmakers vote down affordable housing bills in blow to Sanchez’s government
Right-wing opposition parties joined forces to scuttle two emergency decrees in Parliament that included measures to reduce evictions and real estate speculation.
The setback sparked wide speculation that Sanchez could consider moving up a national election from next year.
Sanchez has been Spain’s prime minister since 2018, making him one of Europe’s longest-standing leaders.
Sanchez has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on "tech oligarchs", even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.
Facing the electorate now is a risky move as Sanchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls.
An election defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far-right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the centre ground.
Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of Vox is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Sanchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.
Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions including voices from the far-left to the separatist right to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.
But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.

"Define core work and cut unnecessary tasks" — Burnout risk remains high for workers in Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:18:06 EEST
16:18:06 KST

Workers in Finland have reported a modest improvement in their ability to cope with the demands of their jobs, according to the latest 'How is Finland doing?' study by the Finnish Institute of Occupational Health.
Some 43 percent of working people in Finland now rate their ability to deal with their jobs as excellent, up from 39 percent a year earlier.
But at the same time, the risk of burnout remains high. One in four workers either has an elevated risk of burnout or is likely already experiencing it.
Researchers said administrative demands and conflicting roles contribute to exhaustion. They say workplaces should focus on reducing these pressures.
"We often talk about the amount of work, but it is not necessarily the number one risk factor. What seems to have a greater impact is that rigid operating methods, inadequate tools, the slow flow of information or conflicting expectations create unnecessary friction at work," said researcher Jie Li.
"I would encourage people to define core work and to eliminate tasks that do not support your goals."
Other risk factors include job insecurity, excessive workloads, monotonous tasks, as well as physical strain.
Yle News reporter Hannah Anderson looks into Finland's stressed out workers.

Spain’s Sánchez calls snap elections for Nov. 29
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:13:21 UTC
16:13:21 KST

Spain's Prime Minister attends an extraordinary parliamentary session to vote on a government housing decree on October 2, 2026 at the Congress of Deputies in Madrid. | Javier Soriano/ AFP via Getty Images
Already weakened by the corruption cases battering his Socialist Party, Sánchez took a further knock this summer when he faced fierce blowback over his handling of the ongoing migrant crisis in the North African exclave of Ceuta.
But the bitter topic of unaffordable housing — something that tops the list of voters’ concerns in Spain and which has sparked nationwide protests — has finally prompted Sánchez to call an early election in an apparent bid to seize a campaign battleground he believes could work to his advantage.
Although Sánchez has established a reputation as a master of the political bounce-back, he faces a steep climb to turn this latest crisis to his advantage.
Polls overwhelmingly suggest that the country will vote in an administration led by the center-right People’s Party, currently supported by 34% of the electorate, compared with 26% backing the Socialist Party. The PP would likely partner with the far-right Vox party, which is projected to score 18%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.
In calling for an election, Sánchez warned of the surge of the far right.
“You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you want Spain to play,” he said in his address to the nation.
“You must decide whether to join the far-right wave that drives regression wherever it governs, or whether you want Spain to remain a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he added.
Advertisement
Mixed track record
Sánchez used the televised address announcing the snap elections to highlight what his minority coalition government had achieved since coming to office in 2023.
The prime minister emphasized the strides Spain has made on the economic front, becoming “the fastest-growing economy in the entire European Union, leading in job creation,” and underscored the continued investments in green energy that have made the country a renewables powerhouse.
He also highlighted his own role on the international stage, where he has gained prominence as one of the Western leaders to most forcefully condemn bothTrump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the conflicts in Gaza and Iran, and clashed with tech giants such as Elon Musk.
Sánchez said Spaniards could be proud of a government that “denounces genocidal figures while others remain silent and fights the tyrants, oligarchs, and speculators who seek to destroy our children’s future to line their own pockets.”
While insisting that his government had “transformed Spain into a global benchmark for peace, feminism, and prosperity, allowing us to achieve the best economic, social, and environmental results of any democratic government in our country’s history,” Sánchez also acknowledged that many Spaniards felt “dissatisfaction.”
Average citizens are not feeling the impact of Spain’s strong growth and record employment figures. Inflation outpaces salary gains, leaving most households with little additional purchasing power as prices and housing costs surge.
Advertisement
Moreover, episodes like last year’s Iberian blackout tarnished the prestige of the country’s green energy network, and the international response to the ongoing Ceuta migrant crisis has raised doubts about Spain’s heft on the global stage.
Sánchez admitted his government had made mistakes and “not managed to achieve everything we set out to do.”
“Many injustices remain to be corrected, many social goals to be attained, and many problems to be solved — particularly regarding inequality in public services and access to housing,” he said. “But the fact is that to do more, we need to renew and expand public support in order to undertake the deep reforms required for citizens to reduce these levels of inequality.”
Polls favor conservatives
Although Sánchez has established a reputation as a master of the political bounce-back, he faces a steep climb to turn this latest crisis to his advantage.
The PP, which has called for snap elections almost from the moment Sánchez renewed his hold on power at the end of 2023, reacted to the news with the short tweet: “AT LAST.”
The snap election caught Spain’s fractured far-left parties scrambling to regroup. That’s a problem for Sánchez’s Socialists, who need the groups to their left to unite behind a viable electoral alliance in order to form a fresh coalition government.
Advertisement
With Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz declining to run for reelection, the Sumar group — junior partners in Sánchez’s coalition government – is still searching for a leader, which is expected to be unveiled on Oct. 17, when the party rebrands as the “Broad Front.”
Health Minister Mónica García is the frontrunner to be lead candidate, with Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun running as the main figure in Catalonia.
It remains unclear whether that project will be able to incorporate Spain’s other major far-left party, Podemos, or figures such as longtime housing activist and former Barcelona Mayor Ada Colau, who has signaled a willingness to return to frontline politics.

Mideast oil exports exceeded pre-Iran war levels: Kpler data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:11:51 UTC
16:11:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Mideast oil exports exceeded pre-Iran war levels, according to Kpler data
Middle East oil exports, excluding Iran, surpassed their pre-war levels last week, despite attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from the maritime tracking firm Kpler.
For the first time since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran at the end of February, the weekly average of shipments rose for several days above the pre-conflict average of 18 million barrels per day.
Crude oil exports reached pre-war levels in September, with at least 16.5 million barrels leaving the region excluding Iran, Kpler said on Wednesday.
"Forty percent now bypass Hormuz, and most crude crossing the strait changes tankers offshore," Kpler said, adding that most of the oil flowed through Saudi and United Arab Emirates pipelines.
These figures include flows via the Red Sea, a route increasingly used to bypass the blockade Iran is attempting to impose on Hormuz—where around a fifth of the world's petroleum supplies crossed before the conflict.
Iran still claims control over the strait, and ships without its authorisation risk coming under attack, but more and more are making it out, and alternative routes meant to bypass the waterway are operating at full capacity.
Despite the rebound, experts stressed that the situation was far from normal, and Iran remains deprived of a large share of its own exports by a US counterblockade of its ports.
Saudi Arabia is benefiting from the reactivation of its East-West pipeline, which links the kingdom's main oil fields in the east to its Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea, allowing it to bypass Hormuz.
Shut down on September 11 after being hit by strikes launched from Iraq, the pipeline resumed operations on September 22, Amena Bakr, an analyst at Kpler said last week.
The United Arab Emirates is also able to bypass Hormuz thanks to its pipeline linking Abu Dhabi's fields to Fujairah, a terminal just outside the strait on the Gulf of Oman.
Around 0310 GMT on Monday, Brent North Sea crude for December delivery fell 0.79 percent to $101.44 a barrel.
Its US counterpart, West Texas Intermediate for November delivery, dropped 1.20 percent to $90.02.

Annual inflation eases below 30 pct in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:09:41 UTC
16:09:41 KST

Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation stood at 29.73 percent in September, below market expectations of 30.3 percent, according to official figures released on Oct. 5.
Consumer prices rose 1.84 percent month-on-month, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Oct. 5.
Annual inflation fell below 30 percent for the first time in 57 months [since November 2021], said Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek on a social media post, commenting on the latest data.
“Disinflation is spreading across the board, excluding transportation. In September, food inflation decreased by 8.4 points compared to the same period last year, reaching an annual rate of 27.6 percent,” he noted.
“To limit the impact of recently rising oil prices on inflation, we are gradually phasing out the sliding-scale tax mechanism [eşel mobil] in gasoline following diesel,” he added.
Şimşek noted that the Central Bank calculates that inflation would have been 7 points lower this year had there been no war.
“We are continuing our policies aimed at increasing the supply of housing and food. In 2027, the reduction in inertia in service inflation, particularly in rent and education, and the weakening of commodity price increase effects will contribute to the decline in inflation,” said Şimşek.
According to TÜİK data, food and non-alcoholic beverage prices, one of the largest components of the consumer price index, fell 0.2 percent from the previous month.
Transportation prices increased 2.79 percent, while housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuel costs rose 2.71 percent.
Transportation contributed 0.49 percentage points to monthly inflation and housing added 0.33 percentage points. Food prices reduced the monthly reading by 0.05 percentage points.
On an annual basis, food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose 27.62 percent, transportation costs increased 35.1 percent, and housing prices climbed 39.99 percent.
These groups contributed 6.73, 5.96 and 4.84 percentage points, respectively, to annual inflation.
The core C index, which excludes energy, food and non-alcoholic beverages, alcoholic beverages, tobacco and gold, increased 28.7 percent annually and 2.14 percent monthly.
The B index, which excludes unprocessed food, energy, alcoholic beverages, tobacco and gold, rose 29 percent annually and 2.01 percent month-on-month.
Of the 174 expenditure subclasses tracked by TÜİK, prices increased in 133, declined in 35 and remained unchanged in six.
With September inflation data now released, investors will shift their focus to the Central Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee meeting on Oct. 22, when policymakers are due to announce their next interest rate decision. The bank’s final rate-setting meeting of 2026 is scheduled for Dec. 10.
As widely expected, the Central Bank on July 23 kept its policy rate unchanged at 37 percent, extending its monetary policy pause for a fourth consecutive meeting.
Meanwhile, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan is scheduled to deliver a presentation to lawmakers at the Turkish parliament’s Planning and Budget Commission on Oct. 6.
Karahan is expected to provide a comprehensive presentation covering global developments, the Turkish economy, inflation and monetary policy.

Russia Upgrades Geran-4 Drones With Better Navigation and New Warhead, Ukraine Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:09:37 UTC
16:09:37 KST

Russia has upgraded its Geran-4 attack drones with technology designed to make them harder to disrupt and more accurate, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) agency said.
The new version, which Russia has started using this autumn, can navigate more precisely without relying entirely on satellite signals and carries a new warhead designed to damage bridges and power infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One of the upgrades is a small magnetic sensor made by US company PNI Sensor. It helps the drone understand changes in its position and correct errors in its onboard navigation system, improving its ability to stay on course.
Russia has also added an optical navigation system called “Susanin.” In simple terms, the system uses a camera to compare what the drone sees below with images stored in its computer.
This allows the drone to recognize where it is and follow its planned route even without relying on GPS or other satellite navigation.
A similar system is being used on the newer Geran-5 drone, according to Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
The upgraded Geran-4 also carries a new warhead designed specifically to attack infrastructure. It can use a powerful shaped charge to cut through bridge structures and supports carrying high-voltage power lines.
Russia has also replaced the Chinese-made engine previously used on the drone with a Russian-made version produced at the Alabuga industrial facility in Russia’s Tatarstan.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Most of the drone’s other electronic components remain unchanged, HUR said in a report published on its War&Sanctions portal.
What is the Geran-4?
The Geran-4 is a relatively large, jet-powered attack drone designed for long-range strikes. It is about 3.6 meters (11.8 feet) long, has a 3.05-meter (10-foot) wingspan and can carry a warhead weighing up to 50 kilograms (110 pounds).
It has a maximum takeoff weight of about 450 kilograms (992 pounds). Its cruising speed is around 320 km/h (200 mph), while its maximum speed is 350 km/h (217 mph).
The drone has a reported range of about 770 kilometers (479 miles) and can fly at altitudes of up to 4 kilometers (2.5 miles).
Geran-4 vs. Geran-5
The Geran-5 is a larger and more powerful member of the same family.
It is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and weighs up to 850 kilograms (1,874 pounds) – almost twice as much as the Geran-4. It can carry a warhead weighing up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds).
The Geran-5 has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h (280–373 mph) and a range of about 950 kilometers (590 miles). It can fly at altitudes of up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
In simple terms, the Geran-4 is smaller and lighter, while the Geran-5 is a much larger platform capable of carrying a heavier warhead and flying faster and farther.

Norway to propose temporary ban on AI glasses in some public places
COPENHAGEN – Norway’s government said on Oct 5 it plans to propose a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in selected places, saying it is concerned people could be photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without their knowledge.
The proposal mirrors a broader global backlash against smart glasses equipped with cameras over privacy concerns.
The ban could apply to places where the public regularly gather, such as parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres and public events, the government said in a statement.
“I am worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it,” Digitalisation and Public Governance Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said.
It could also apply to schools, playgrounds and youth clubs and to privacy-sensitive places such as doctors’ offices, swimming pools and gyms with changing rooms.
The government said it was not eyeing a total ban and that private use, and use where others are not at risk of being filmed without consent, would still be allowed.
It said it would examine which technology the ban would cover, including whether it would apply to glasses with camera and audio recording, glasses with camera and AI functions or also other body-worn technology with camera, audio recording and/or artificial intelligence.
The minority government said it would present a Bill to Parliament as soon as possible, and would also set up an expert group to advise on permanent national regulation of body-worn technology. REUTERS

Choosing life: Three years after being taken hostage, former Gaza hostages savor each moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:08:29 UTC
16:08:29 KST

Taken with their children or alone. Held for weeks, months, or years. Confined in captors' homes or Hamas tunnels as war raged above them. Israeli former hostages seized on October 7 say they now cherish even the smallest moments of freedom.
Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack was Israel's single deadliest day. The terrorists rampaged through villages, a music festival and army bases, killing 1,200 people and dragging 251 hostages back to Gaza.
They included civilians, soldiers, men, women, children and elderly people, Israelis and foreign nationals. Most were freed in return for Palestinian prisoners during ceasefires between Israel and Hamas, but dozens were killed in captivity.
"Freedom has completely changed the way I see life," said Emily Damari, 30, who was abducted wounded from her home in Kibbutz Kfar Aza and released in January 2025.
Her ordeal taught her not to take anything for granted, she said. "One day in captivity feels like one week. You want to give up at every moment, but I did not," said Damari, who has recently married and launched a clothing line in Israel.
"Today, I open the fridge, and I say thank you. I drink cold water, and I say thank you. I am thankful for everything, big and little. Gratitude has become central to who I am," said Damari. "Being free, at home, surrounded by my family and my people is something I will never take for granted again."
'I choose life'
Eli Sharabi, 54, was seized from nearby Kibbutz Be'eri. His British-born wife Lianne and their two daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were slain by the attackers. His brother Yossi was taken hostage and killed in Gaza.
In February 2025, Sharabi was released, appearing emaciated and skeletal, after 491 days of captivity, which he says included being held in a tunnel, hungry, shackled, and beaten.
"I learned in captivity how precious every moment and every choice can be, and I carry that understanding with me now. I choose to look ahead, to keep going and to use the life I have in a meaningful way," said Sharabi.
Since his release, he has helped establish the Shalva Sharabi Family Center in the southern city of Ashkelon with the disability charity Shalva, to treat families coping with trauma and disabilities, in commemoration of his own family lost.
"I choose life. I choose to keep living fully, while carrying Lianne, Noiya, Yahel and Yossi with me in everything I do."
His wife and daughters believed deeply in caring for others, he said. "Their kindness and care for others will continue. Families will walk through these doors and receive help, care and hope in a place that carries their name. That gives me strength and makes me very proud," said Sharabi.
Slowly building a future
Hagar Brodutch was seized from Kfar Aza with her three children and her neighbor's daughter, who fled to their house after her parents were killed. They were freed in a brief truce in November 2023.
Life after captivity, she said, can be far more complicated than sometimes portrayed.
"The daily struggle is immense, especially for children. I believe it will take many more years before captivity becomes just a shadow that walks alongside us, rather than something that defines who we are," said Brodutch.
Recently, Brodutch, 43, began taking pastry-baking classes, a passion she has long had.
"This is about much more than learning how to bake. It is about finding a new path, creating something with my own hands, and slowly building a future," she said.
"During my time in Hamas captivity, I began to understand that if I were released, returning to my previous life and working in management might no longer be possible," said Brodutch.
"I chose pastry as a form of therapy, but also as a way to create something new for myself, with the hope that one day it could become my profession," she said.
Kfar Aza was one of the hardest-hit communities in Hamas's attack. Aviva Siegel, 65, was kidnapped with her husband Keith. She was released in November 2023, but Keith was held until February 2025.
Aviva joined the hostage release campaign movement in Israel while her husband was still being held. Their reunion, her children and grandchildren, and even strangers she meets give her strength every day, she says.
"I feel that I’m not alone and that there's so much love in this world, and we need to keep it with both our hands," she said. "I feel very, very lucky to be alive."

General admission tickets to Glastonbury, the UK’s biggest music festival, have sold out in 42 minutes, leaving the lucky few now wondering: Who will be playing?
Following its traditional fallow year, the event – which will take place between 23 to 27 June 2027 – is a cause of both joy and frustration – the latter especially for fans who spend hours in the virtual queue and who still fail to secure a spot at Worthy Farm.
Tickets went on sale yesterday at 10am CET. At 10:42am, See Tickets confirmed that the entire allocation had been snapped up.
“Tickets for @Glastonbury Festival 2027 are now SOLD OUT,” it wrote. “Confirmation emails are going out now. Thank you to everyone who bought tickets this morning and sorry to those who missed out.”
Organisers announced last month that general admission tickets would cost £408 each, including a £5 booking fee – taking the price above £400 for the first time.
That's approx. €480 in total – an increase of nearly £30 (€34) from 2025 and, according to reports from BBC News, part of a steady rise since 2010, when tickets cost £286 (€330).
The price hike led to complaints, with some calling the 2027 price tag "unreasonable", "insane" and "a scam", while many feel like they're being priced out.

Someone else shared: "In 2000 it was £87. That’s an extra £321 in 27 years. The money went up but the music went down. Even accounting for inflation, that should be about £160 today. You pay more money to listen to shit music. How is this fair?"
Still, unconditional Glasto fans who missed out this weekend will have another opportunity to secure a spot when unwanted tickets and those for which the remaining balance has not been paid (buyers were required to pay a £100 deposit, with the remaining £308 due between 1 and 7 April next year) are offered in the spring 2027 resale.
No acts have yet been officially announced for Glastonbury 2027. Early bookmakers’ favourites have included Sam Fender, Taylor Swift, Rihanna and Little Simz, while there is growing speculation that The Rolling Stones, Radiohead and Fontaines D.C. could be in with a shot.

The Glastonbury 2027 line-up is expected to be announced in the coming months. The 2027 edition takes place from 23 to 27 June 2027.

EU accession with restrictions for farmers: Brussels prepares special terms for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
10:08:00 EEST
16:08:00 KST

EU accession with restrictions for farmers: Brussels prepares special terms for Ukraine
The European Commission is proposing significant restrictions on Ukraine's access to the EU agricultural market and farming subsidies even after the country becomes a member of the union.
Source: Financial Times, whose journalists have seen an internal European Commission document on reforming the EU enlargement process
Details: The restrictions are intended to reassure existing EU members, including Poland, France and Italy, which are concerned about competition from large volumes of Ukrainian grain and oilseed products.
The document cites the scale, structure and high productivity of Ukraine's agricultural sector as grounds for considering special arrangements that would significantly restrict financial support and market access, including for wheat and other grains. The EU provides a total of €55 billion in agricultural subsidies annually.
Instead, Brussels is proposing to help Ukraine return to its traditional export markets, where trade has been disrupted by Russia's war.
The proposals are still in draft form and have not been adopted. The FT reports that senior European Commission officials are discussing them ahead of their planned approval on Tuesday.
The reform would also make new member states' access to EU funds conditional on implementing reforms and simplify the procedure for stripping countries of their voting rights for violating the bloc's rules.
Separate accession roadmaps without fixed membership dates are proposed for Ukraine, Moldova, Montenegro and Albania.
Background: In April 2026, Taras Kachka, Deputy Prime Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration of Ukraine, said Ukraine was prepared to postpone receiving EU agricultural subsidies for several years in order to accelerate its accession. He said the terms of such a delay would need to be negotiated.

Government wants “anti-democratic views” screening for citizenship applicants and will postpone citizenship bill after full review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-05
07:03:09 UTC
16:03:09 KST

The Danish government wants people applying for citizenship to be screened for anti-democratic views and statements, arguing that citizenship should only be granted to people who are loyal to Denmark and share what it describes as Danish values.
This is stated in a press release by the Danish Immigration Ministry.
The proposed screening system would look for views that conflict with fundamental freedoms and human rights. The government wants the system to become part of a new political agreement setting the criteria for obtaining Danish citizenship.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov said the government believes citizenship should not be granted to people who support terrorism, favor sharia law or oppose gay rights.
“We have the strictest immigration policy ever. We must continue to have that, and of course that also applies to foreigners who want to become Danish citizens,” Bødskov said.
“That is why the government believes that a model should be introduced where we screen future applicants for Danish citizenship for anti-democratic views. Danish citizenship should only be for those who are loyal to Denmark and who have embraced Danish values. Of course, we should not give it to people who, for example, praise terrorism, support sharia and oppose the rights of homosexuals.”
The government said Danish citizenship should only be granted to people whose values are consistent with principles such as freedom, equality and tolerance.
An expert group has already been appointed to examine whether such a screening system can be established and, if so, how it should work. The group is expected to complete its work around the end of the year.
After that, the government plans to begin political negotiations on a new agreement covering the requirements for becoming a Danish citizen.
Government seeks broad political agreement
The government wants the future citizenship agreement to have broad support across the political center, including backing from at least one party to the right of the government.
Bødskov said citizenship rules were too important to be decided by a narrow parliamentary majority.
“The citizenship area is too important for us to make agreements with a narrow majority. Broad cooperation is therefore important,” he said.
“We should be able to come together broadly in the Folketing on an agreement. In this way, we can ensure a long-term agreement that makes it absolutely clear that Danish citizenship is only for those who carry Danish values in their hearts.”
The Folketing is Denmark’s national parliament.
Citizenship bill to be introduced again in 2027
The government also plans to delay the citizenship bill L 98, which lapsed when the election was called, and introduce it again in the first half of 2027.
Before doing so, the Immigration and Integration Ministry will carry out a new and complete review of every applicant included in the bill to check that they still meet the requirements for Danish citizenship.
That means people who had already gone through the application process and had been included in L 98 will have their cases screened again before the bill returns to Parliament.
For those applicants, the decision adds another period of waiting before they can formally be granted citizenship.
The government statement does not explain what would happen if an applicant’s circumstances change during that additional waiting period and they no longer meet one of the requirements, for example because they lose their job. It only says that all applicants will undergo a renewed full review before the bill is reintroduced.
The government expects L 98 to return in the first half of 2027.
The new political agreement on citizenship requirements, including any future screening model, will apply to applicants who have not yet been included in L 98.
